    Onboarding guide

    14. Module System, Composition & Configuration

    What this chapter covers. This is the wiring layer, the code that turns a pile of layered assemblies into a running host. It answers three questions a new host author asks: how does the process discover and assemble its modules?, in what order does DI get built so the decorators wrap the right handlers?, and where do the dozens of appsettings.json knobs land as typed objects? The cast is small but load-bearing: the IModule contract and its IModuleSeeder sidekick; the ModuleLoader that discovers and Kahn-sorts them; the two extension(IServiceCollection) DependencyInjection composition roots (Application and Infrastructure) plus the MmcaApplicationPipelineBuilder and the DecoratorPipelineSeal marker that together make the ordering rule enforceable instead of merely documented; the AssemblyReference / ClassReference assembly anchors that Scrutor and the architecture tests pin to; the two data-source attributes (UseDataSourceAttribute, UseDatabaseAttribute); the settings types this chapter owns, ApplicationSettings / ModulesSettings / ModuleSettings / QueryCachePipelineSettings in Application plus the Infrastructure sections MessageBusSettings, SmtpSettings, SchedulerSettings and PushNotificationSettings (the persistence, auth, caching and outbox sections the same root binds are documented in group 07, group 08, group 09 and group 04); the cloud-neutral null-object defaults a vendor adapter package replaces (NullNativePushSender, NullPushDeviceRegistrar, NullFileStorageService) with the vendor-free NativePushPayloads builder the push adapters share; the two startup posture checks, StartupConfigurationSummaryService and CloudAdapterTripwire with its carrier CloudAdapterTripwireOptions, plus the ChannelJoinAuthorizerMissingWarningService that names an open push-channel posture once; the broker transport boundary (IBrokerTransport, MessageBusProviders, BrokerTransportContext, BrokerTransportPolicies), the transport-neutral broker model it is written against (BrokerTopology, BrokerSubscription, BrokerConsumerKind, BrokerNaming, BrokerHeaders, BrokerWire, OutgoingBrokerMessage, IncomingBrokerMessage, IBrokerPublisher, IBrokerReceivePipeline and the BrokerDisposition family Completed / Redeliver / DeadLetter), and the two built-in transports RabbitMqBrokerTransport and PostgreSqlBrokerTransport with their internals; the cross-replica locking pair (RedisDistributedLock, InProcessDistributedLock); the host-scoped job runner (ScheduledJobRunner), the ExceptionChain renderer background work records its failures with, and the PeriodicBackgroundService base the other fixed-interval sweeps derive from; the broker-side consumer machinery a host composes (IBrokerConsumerBuilder and its BrokerConsumerBuilder, the BrokerReceivePipeline behind IBrokerMessageConsumer, and UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> with its UpcastDispatch cache) with the boot-time EventUpcasterStartupValidator; the scoped TenantContext and the ambient-context carriers that let a hop off the request call stack act as the identity that queued the work (AmbientOrigin with its published OriginSnapshot and RestoreHandle, ScopedUserOverride, ImpersonatingCurrentUserService, ConsumerOriginRestore); the internal-command queue a host composes for deferred work (IInternalCommand, IInternalCommandScheduler, IInternalCommandAdministration with its InternalCommandDeadLetter projection, the InternalCommandNameAttribute that keeps a rename from orphaning rows and the InternalCommandExecution marker (with its Scope handle) that tells a handler it is running on the durable path, plus the ready-made commands the framework ships on it, IDeleteBlobInternalCommand handled by DeleteBlobInternalCommandHandlerBase<TCommand>, and DeleteUserPushInstallationsInternalCommand handled by DeleteUserPushInstallationsInternalCommandHandler); the two resolvers that answer a composition question a plain settings property answered badly, ApplicationNamespace and SmtpTransportSecurity; and the shared Users use-case bases that two apps compose into their own Identity modules. The detailed per-type sections follow; this overview shows how the pieces fit together at runtime.

    [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] (assesses whether modules can be enabled, disabled, and deployed independently with minimal coupling) is the lens this whole chapter is built around: the module system is the boundary that lets MMCA.ADC run as either a single monolith host or four separate service processes from the same module code, configuration-switched. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] also run throughout: composition is where the inward-pointing dependency rule gets physically realized (Infrastructure references Application references Domain references Shared), and where cross-cutting concerns are registered once for every module rather than per-feature. The ADRs that explain why this shape exists are ADR-059 (the module contract itself), ADR-008 (service-extraction topology), ADR-006 (database-per-service) and ADR-014 (the decorator pipeline whose ordering rule this chapter enforces).

    The module contract and the boundary it creates

    A module is the unit of cohesion above a feature slice: Conference, Engagement, Identity, Notification. Each one implements IModule (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Modules/IModule.cs:7): a display Name (IModule.cs:12), an optional Dependencies list of other module names (IModule.cs:17), a RequiresDependencies flag (IModule.cs:23), and one Register(services, configuration, applicationSettings) method (IModule.cs:28) that wires all of that module's services. Three of those five members are default-implemented on the interface (Dependencies => [] at IModule.cs:17, RequiresDependencies => false at IModule.cs:23, and an empty-bodied RegisterDisabledStubs at IModule.cs:34), so a leaf module is just Name plus Register. ADC's modules are deliberately thin: ConferenceModule (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/ConferenceModule.cs:16) is barely more than a dozen lines. Its Register forwards to an AddConferenceModule(applicationSettings) extension method (ConferenceModule.cs:30-31), and its RegisterDisabledStubs (ConferenceModule.cs:22-27) registers a DisabledSessionBookmarkValidationService and a DisabledEventLiveValidationService so a host that disables Conference still has those cross-module contract types resolvable in DI.

    That last detail is the crux of the extraction boundary. RegisterDisabledStubs plus RequiresDependencies is what makes one module assembly boot in two topologies. When Conference runs in its own service, that host names only the Conference module's assembly, so Engagement does not run there and no Engagement stub is ever registered, yet Conference's GetSessionBookmarkCountHandler still needs Engagement's IBookmarkCountService. The host's pipeline therefore registers a typed gRPC client pointed at the real Engagement process with a Replace registration, which displaces a disabled stub where a host has one and otherwise simply adds the adapter (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/Program.cs:332-336, :359). Application code never learns which path it got; the transport choice lives entirely at the composition edge (ADR-008). [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] applies here: this is a clean strategy / null-object pairing (real service, disabled stub, remote client) rather than scattered if (moduleEnabled) checks.

    Discovery and Kahn-ordered registration

    ModuleLoader (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Modules/ModuleLoader.cs:16) is the engine. Its one DiscoverAndRegister overload (ModuleLoader.cs:59-65) takes the assemblies to scan as a required parameter: there is no AppDomain-scan convenience, and the parameter doc says why, because an AppDomain scan only sees assemblies already loaded, so a module assembly that is referenced but not yet touched by any code path would be silently absent from discovery (ModuleLoader.cs:49-54). The scan guards each GetTypes() call so one bad reference never aborts the whole pass: a ReflectionTypeLoadException keeps every type that did load, so one unloadable type does not make the assembly's modules vanish, and any other failure drops just that assembly; both shapes log at Error, because a module that silently fails to register is an outage that looks like a configuration choice (ModuleLoader.cs:69-97). It then instantiates every concrete IModule via Activator.CreateInstance (ModuleLoader.cs:99-102) and every concrete IModuleSeeder into a case-insensitive dictionary keyed by ModuleName (ModuleLoader.cs:104-107).

    Ordering is Kahn's topological sort (ModuleLoader.cs:284-334) over the modules' declared Dependencies. Kahn's algorithm is BFS over a dependency graph: compute each module's in-degree (count of unprocessed dependencies, ModuleLoader.cs:289), build the reverse adjacency list of dependents (ModuleLoader.cs:292-305), seed a queue with the zero-in-degree modules (ModuleLoader.cs:308-309), and as each is emitted decrement its dependents' in-degrees, enqueuing any that reach zero (ModuleLoader.cs:318-322). A dependency name that was never discovered is skipped rather than treated as an edge (ModuleLoader.cs:299-300); validation catches it later. If fewer modules come out than went in, the remainder form a cycle and the loader throws with the offending names (ModuleLoader.cs:326-331). The payoff is an ordering where a module's DI registrations always exist before any dependent registers, which matters because the CQRS decorator pipeline (below) can only wrap handlers that are already in the container.

    For each sorted module the loader checks ModulesSettings.IsModuleEnabled (ModuleLoader.cs:114). A disabled module gets RegisterDisabledStubs called, has the exact service descriptors that call added recorded (ModuleLoader.cs:120-122), and is listed in DisabledModuleNames (ModuleLoader.cs:124); an enabled one runs ValidateModuleDependencies then RegisterEnabledModule (ModuleLoader.cs:128-129) and contributes its seeder if one was found (ModuleLoader.cs:131-134). Registration is also where per-module configuration is loaded by convention: before calling module.Register(...) the loader adds modules.{name}.json and, when an environment name is passed, modules.{name}.{environment}.json to the configuration builder (ModuleLoader.cs:187-191), so a module can ship its own config file. Dependency validation (ModuleLoader.cs:138-171) is microservice-aware: a dependency that is disabled in-process but listed in that consumer's ModuleSettings RemoteDependencies is treated as satisfied remotely, and only a RequiresDependencies = true module with a genuinely unsatisfied dependency throws, with an error message that spells out the three ways to fix it (ModuleLoader.cs:152-160). Every step emits a [LoggerMessage]-generated structured log (ModuleLoader.cs:336-358), so the startup log tells you exactly which modules loaded, in what order, and how long each took (ModuleLoader.cs:193-196).

    Trusting configuration is not quite enough, so the loader offers a second, post-build gate: ValidateRemoteDependencies(serviceProvider) (ModuleLoader.cs:214-236) walks every remote-declared dependency, resolves each service type the disabled module's stub had registered, throws when one does not resolve at all, and logs a warning when it still resolves to the stub implementation (ModuleLoader.cs:238-259). That converts a forgotten gRPC-client registration from a first-request mystery into a startup failure. It is a capability, not a habit: today only MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Modules/ModuleLoaderTests.cs calls it, and no ADC or Store host does. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] is the category at play in both this method and the log messages above.

    The loader is not called from inside AddApplication(), and a host no longer constructs it by hand either. AddModuleHost in the API layer (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/ModuleHostExtensions.cs:51) binds and validates ApplicationSettings and ModulesSettings (ModuleHostExtensions.cs:61-76), constructs the ModuleLoader with the host's bootstrap logger, registers it as a singleton (ModuleHostExtensions.cs:78-82), and hands back a ModuleHostContext whose RegisterModules method is the discovery step (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/ModuleHostContext.cs:66-77). Discovery deliberately does not run inside AddModuleHost: it has to land inside the application pipeline described next, and its position relative to a host's other steps is a per-host decision (ModuleHostContext.cs:12-19). After discovery the loader also drives startup data through SeedAllAsync (ModuleLoader.cs:268-274), which invokes each collected IModuleSeeder.SeedAsync in registration order. IModuleSeeder (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Modules/IModuleSeeder.cs:8) is a two-member interface, ModuleName (IModuleSeeder.cs:13, matched case-insensitively against an IModule Name) and SeedAsync(serviceProvider, cancellationToken) (IModuleSeeder.cs:18), deliberately separate from IModule so seeding runs after the whole container is built and a real IServiceProvider exists.

    The two composition roots, and the pipeline that seals them

    Service registration itself lives in two static DependencyInjection classes, each using a C# extension(IServiceCollection services) block (see primer §4 for the extension(T) syntax, and ADR-106 for why the public DI surface is written that way). The Application root (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:28) exposes AddApplication() (DependencyInjection.cs:36), which registers the core singletons (IDomainEventDispatcher at :34, IEventUpcasterRegistry at :40, INavigationMetadataProvider at :42, IEntityQueryPipeline at :43) and pulls in the framework's own FluentValidation validators by assembly (DependencyInjection.cs:59). Each of those four singletons is registered with TryAddSingleton, so a host that registered its own first keeps it. The upcaster registry is registered unconditionally on purpose: with no upcasters it is an empty registry whose operations are the identity, so both delivery paths can depend on it without a null check (DependencyInjection.cs:39-43, ADR-090), and individual upcasters accumulate through AddEventUpcaster<TSource, TTarget, TUpcaster>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.Extensibility.cs:81).

    The Application root also owns ScanModuleApplicationServices<TAssemblyMarker>() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:28-30) and its Assembly-typed overload (DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:46), the Scrutor convention scan every module's AddXModule call makes: domain-event and integration-event handlers as singletons (DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:51-63), DTO mappers, the opt-in IEntityDTOProjector<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> projectors, request mappers and update appliers scoped (DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:65-103), command and query handlers scoped (DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:105-115), validators from the module assembly (DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:117), and finally a reflection pass that TryAdds a CommandRequestValidator<,> for every command implementing ICommandWithRequest<T> (DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:119-135) so an explicit validator still wins.

    The order of these calls is a hard contract in exactly one respect, and it is the reason AddApplicationDecorators() (MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:132) must come last. Decorators are registered with Scrutor's TryDecorate, which wraps existing registrations, so every module's concrete handlers must already be in the container or there is nothing to wrap, and a handler registered afterwards runs completely unwrapped with nothing failing at startup to say so (DependencyInjection.cs:208-211). Rather than leaving that as a comment, the framework enforces it. AddApplicationDecorators() finishes by calling SealPipeline, which TryAdds a singleton instance of the private marker DecoratorPipelineSeal (DependencyInjection.cs:169, :294, :307-308), and every registration entry point that contributes handlers (ScanModuleApplicationServices, AddEntityCrud, AddEntityUpdateVerb, AddEntityUpdate, AddMmcaApplicationPipeline itself) opens with ThrowIfPipelineSealed, which scans the collection for that marker and throws a message naming the offending call (DependencyInjection.cs:329-338). The whole sequence is available as one call, AddMmcaApplicationPipeline(configure) (DependencyInjection.cs:226-235): it runs AddApplication(), invokes the callback with a MmcaApplicationPipelineBuilder (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/MmcaApplicationPipelineBuilder.cs:12) whose ScanModule<TAssemblyMarker> (:27), ScanModules(params Assembly[]) (:41) and Register(Action<IServiceCollection>) (:62) steps are where module discovery, gRPC clients and broker messaging go, and then closes with AddApplicationDecorators(). The builder's constructor is internal precisely so it cannot be created outside that call, because outside it nothing keeps the decorators last (MmcaApplicationPipelineBuilder.cs:9-14). A third guard, VerifyDecoratorPipeline() (DependencyInjection.cs:263), is never called automatically: it is the hook an architecture fitness test calls after replaying a host's own registration sequence, and it reports every ICommandHandler<,> / IQueryHandler<,> descriptor that still carries an implementation type, which after decoration is proof that nothing wrapped it (DependencyInjection.cs:272-304). MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:68 and MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/ApplicationPipelineCompositionTests.cs:160 are its callers today.

    AddApplicationDecorators also encodes the execution order via TryDecorate's reverse-registration rule (registered innermost first, MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:149-167), so the command pipeline ends up FeatureGate -> Authorization -> Logging -> Caching -> Validating -> Timeout -> Transactional -> handler and the query pipeline FeatureGate -> Authorization -> Logging -> Caching -> Validating -> Timeout -> handler (ADR-014). The rationale for each position is written out in the method's own doc comment (MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:102-130): authorization sits outside caching so a denied request neither reads nor populates the cache, validation sits outside the transaction so an invalid command never opens one, and the timeout budget sits inside validation and outside the transaction so it covers the database work and cancels it rather than leaving it open. The decorator types themselves (for example FeatureGateCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, AuthorizationCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult> and TimeoutCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>) are documented in the CQRS-pipeline chapter; this chapter owns only the wiring of them. An optional MiniProfiler pair is registered separately by an opt-in AddApplicationProfiling() (MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:198), never by AddApplicationDecorators(); the composed service host makes that call after the sealed pipeline when ApplicationSettings:UseMiniProfiler is true (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.ServiceHost/ServiceHostBuilderExtensions.cs:162-165). [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] and [Rubric §1, SOLID] (open/closed) live here: cross-cutting behavior is added by wrapping, not by editing handlers.

    The Infrastructure root (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:48) exposes AddInfrastructure(configuration) (DependencyInjection.cs:58), which binds most of the settings types in this chapter, registers the three save interceptors as singletons (DependencyInjection.cs:62-71), the persistence stack (data-source service and resolver, entity registry, the scoped and singleton context factories, repositories, unit of work, DependencyInjection.cs:60-131), Scrutor-scans the framework's own EF entity configurations (DependencyInjection.cs:134-139), adds caching (DependencyInjection.cs:141), registers the refresh session store and its retention sweep behind the same flag that maps the table (DependencyInjection.cs:169-213), and enrolls three startup checks through TryAddEnumerable, so a host whose modules each call AddInfrastructure still runs each once: a validator that fails the host on a bad upcaster graph (DependencyInjection.cs:230-231), the one-line StartupConfigurationSummaryService (:214-215), and the CloudAdapterTripwire carried through ValidateOnStart by CloudAdapterTripwireOptions (:221-223), both described in the settings section below. The outbox hosted services are conditional: the method reads MessageBusSettings, calls EnsureOutboxAvailableForProvider, and adds OutboxProcessor plus OutboxCleanupService only when IsOutboxEnabled, otherwise registering OutboxDisabledNoticeService so the choice is visible in the log (DependencyInjection.cs:256-268, ADR-100). The OutboxMessages table stays mapped either way, so flipping the flag is never a migration (DependencyInjection.cs:250-255). It closes by composing the internal-command queue (AddInternalCommands, DependencyInjection.cs:275), running AddServices() (:254) and then layering the impersonation decorator over whatever ICurrentUserService that left registered (:256-263), both described two sections below. Optional add-ons sit alongside the root: the class is partial, split by concern across sibling files, so AddCommonHybridCache (DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:158), AddScheduledJobs (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:37), AddTwoFactorAuthentication (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:40), AddEmailConfirmation (:68), AddLegalAcceptance (:104), AddStoredPermissionGrants (:139), AddAuditTrail (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:108), AddMultiTenancy (DependencyInjection.cs:320), AddServices (:315), AddEntityConfigurationAssembly (:373), AddStronglyTypedIds (:401), AddNpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator (DependencyInjection.Persistence.cs:24), AddNotificationInfrastructure (DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:23), AddPushNotifications (:38), and the broker pair AddBrokerMessaging (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:48) and AddBrokerTransport (:159), the registration call an adapter package's transport goes through. Native push, file storage and a non-built-in broker are not registered by any method of this class: each arrives from a vendor adapter package that replaces a core default (see group 28).

    AddCaching (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:30) also registers this chapter's one cross-replica primitive: an IDistributedLock that resolves to RedisDistributedLock when the host has an IConnectionMultiplexer registered, and to the warn-once InProcessDistributedLock otherwise (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:109-123). The Redis implementation is the standard SET key token NX PX ttl acquire (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Concurrency/RedisDistributedLock.cs:67) with a compare-and-delete release script (RedisDistributedLock.cs:36-37, evaluated at :114), handing back a RedisLockHandle that releases exactly its own acquisition, once (RedisDistributedLock.cs:91, :101). That release runs after the guarded work has already committed, so a Redis fault there is logged rather than thrown and the key falls back to expiring on its TTL, and a release that finds the key already gone logs that the section was not exclusive (RedisDistributedLock.cs:106-129); the fallback is exclusive only inside one process, which is exactly what its warning says out loud (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Concurrency/InProcessDistributedLock.cs:74-75), and its InProcessLockHandle simply removes the key from a ConcurrentDictionary (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:79-91). A multi-replica host that registers no Redis client therefore gets one execution of the guarded section per replica. [Rubric §29, Resilience] and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] both touch this pair: the degradation is deliberate, announced, and never silent.

    Opt-in platform features are composed the same way

    Four capabilities are registered beside the roots rather than inside them, and they share one discipline: registering a feature is not the same as turning it on. AddScheduledJobs(configuration) (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:36) binds SchedulerSettings and enrolls ScheduledJobRunner through TryAddEnumerable rather than AddHostedService, precisely so two modules calling it cannot start two runners racing for the same rows (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:44-48); individual IScheduledJob implementations arrive through AddScheduledJob<TJob>() (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:72), each registered scoped so the runner can resolve it in a fresh scope per execution. AddAuditTrail(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:108) binds AuditTrailSettings, adds the AuditTrailSaveChangesInterceptor and the AuditTrailReader that projects the trail's rows, and contributes its own retention job (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:110-124), which only actually runs when the host also enabled the scheduler. AddMultiTenancy(configuration) (DependencyInjection.cs:320) binds TenancySettings and registers TenancySettingsValidator as an IValidateOptions<TenancySettings> through TryAddEnumerable (DependencyInjection.cs:322-330); note what it does not do, because that is the design: TenantSaveChangesInterceptor and ITenantContext, whose scoped implementation TenantContext reports IsResolved = false until a request calls SetTenant (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/TenantContext.cs:25, :28, registered at DependencyInjection.cs:348) unless it was constructed inside a background hop, in which case it starts with the tenant that hop restored (TenantContext.cs:19, see the deferred-work section below), are registered unconditionally by AddInfrastructure and AddServices and stay inert until a tenant is resolved, so the framework can never sit in the half-wired state where entities carry ITenantEntity but the write-side guard is off (DependencyInjection.cs:68-71, :315, ADR-073). Finally AddUserDataExportSection<TSection>() (MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.Extensibility.cs:38) accumulates IUserDataExportSection contributors into the one IEnumerable the export handler fans out over. The governing ADRs are ADR-074, ADR-075, ADR-073 and ADR-076; [Rubric §30, Compliance & Data Governance] is the category the trail and the export both serve.

    ScheduledJobRunner (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobRunner.cs:40) is the one of these with real runtime machinery, and it reuses the outbox's idioms wholesale. It is a BackgroundService that returns immediately (after one log line) when Scheduler:Enabled is false (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:86-91), waits out a 15-second startup delay so migrations finish first (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:70, :95), then loops: run one cycle that reconciles the ScheduledJobs rows against the registered jobs, claims due rows with a lease, executes and stamps the outcome (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:103-108, :213), and smart-waits until the earliest upcoming occurrence capped at Scheduler:PollingIntervalSeconds (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:123-131). A claim attempt is a single filtered ExecuteUpdateAsync against the still-unleased predicate, so two racing replicas both issue it and exactly one matches (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:438-448); it returns a JobClaim carrying either this replica's lock token or null when another replica won the row (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:450), which is what makes an occurrence run exactly once across a scaled host. The persisted row is ScheduledJobEntry (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobEntry.cs:20), deliberately not an auditable entity: it is framework bookkeeping with an explicit claim lease instead of a concurrency token, and it is host-scoped, living in the Default data source only (ScheduledJobEntry.cs:8-19), on whichever relational engine Scheduler:DataSource names (SQL Server unless set, and never Cosmos because the table is relational, SchedulerSettings.cs:48-55), which each cycle resolves before touching the table (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:226-227). SchedulerMetrics (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/SchedulerMetrics.cs:16) publishes the MMCA.Common.Scheduler meter with a run counter tagged by job and outcome (SchedulerMetrics.cs:28-31), a duration histogram (SchedulerMetrics.cs:39-42) and a schedule-lag histogram (SchedulerMetrics.cs:50), the same shape BrokerMetrics (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/BrokerMetrics.cs:18) uses for the MMCA.Common.Broker meter's fault and circuit-open counters (BrokerMetrics.cs:30, :43). So [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] is covered by instruments rather than by log scraping.

    Two more composition-time shapes sit beside those registrations. The first is the base class the other periodic sweeps derive from: PeriodicBackgroundService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Hosting/Background/PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:20) factors the fixed-interval pattern into one place, an IsEnabled gate evaluated once at startup (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:38), a StartupDelay defaulting to 15 seconds (:31), then ExecuteCycleAsync on an Interval loop (:25, :50) whose failing cycle is logged and never kills the loop (through an overridable LogCycleFailure, :45-46, so a derived sweep can keep its own message and the event id its dashboards and tests key on, :40-43), with every wait going through an injected TimeProvider so a test can drive it on a fake clock (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:7-11); its own doc comment records that the outbox processor deliberately does not use it, because a signal-driven smart wait is not a fixed interval (:13-15). The second is the broker side of AddBrokerMessaging. There is no per-consumer fault consumer: a message whose handlers exhaust every retry and redelivery is dead-lettered by the framework's receive pipeline, which logs it and counts broker.fault.count at that point (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:11-13; the pipeline is described in the broker section below). A retired contract is bound instead to UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:29) through RegisterUpcastedIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>, which upcasts each message to its terminal contract through IEventUpcasterRegistry and dispatches the handlers registered for that contract, so handlers are written once against the newest event type while producers still publishing the old one keep being delivered, with deduplication still keyed on the original message id (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:10-25, ADR-090). Registering both kinds for one type is refused at registration rather than left to run the handlers twice (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:18-19, enforced at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:51-58). Because the terminal type is known only at runtime, handler resolution goes through UpcastDispatch (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/UpcastDispatch.cs:15), which caches the closed handler interface and a compiled invoker per terminal type so reflection stays off the per-message path (UpcastDispatch.cs:7-14, used at UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:97). The upcaster graph those hops depend on is checked at boot by EventUpcasterStartupValidator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:20), an IHostedService that AddInfrastructure enrolls through TryAddEnumerable (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:231): resolving the registry is the check, because its constructor rejects a duplicate source, a self-mapping and a cycle, so a misconfigured host fails to start instead of dead-lettering events hours later (EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:7-17, :23-29).

    Deferred work, and the context that travels with it

    The last two things AddInfrastructure composes are a queue for work a request wants done later, and the machinery that lets whatever drains a queue act as the identity that filled it. AddInternalCommands (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:141, called at DependencyInjection.cs:275) binds InternalCommandsSettings, registers the origin capture, the scheduler and the operator surface scoped (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:160-161, :166), and then takes the outbox's posture deliberately: the table is mapped either way, and InternalCommands:Enabled decides only whether the processor and its retention sweep run (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:174-177) or a disabled-notice hosted service says so once in the log (:179, rationale at :130-139).

    IInternalCommand (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/InternalCommands/IInternalCommand.cs:38) is the whole application-side contract, a marker over ICommand<Result> with no second handler interface: a deferred command is executed by the same ICommandHandler<TCommand, TResult> a synchronous one is, so every decorator (feature gate, authorization, logging, validation, timeout, transaction) applies to the deferred execution exactly as it does inline (IInternalCommand.cs:11-16). The two rules that follow from a row in a table are stated on the interface itself: the payload must round-trip through System.Text.Json, and execution is at-least-once because a host that dies between the handler's commit and the row's stamp re-runs the row once the lease expires, so handlers must be idempotent (IInternalCommand.cs:19-29). IInternalCommandScheduler (IInternalCommandScheduler.cs:16) writes the row on the caller's own unit of work: scheduling from inside an ITransactional command commits with the aggregate change or rolls back with it (IInternalCommandScheduler.cs:9-14), which is the outbox's atomicity guarantee applied to work the host wants to do rather than to a message it wants to publish. With a transaction active the row is only enrolled, and when no later save follows the transactional pipeline saves it just before the commit; with none active the row is saved at once, flushing whatever else is pending on that context (IInternalCommandScheduler.cs:34-43). Both overloads return Result<Guid> (IInternalCommandScheduler.cs:45-48, :59-62), the handle the administration surface takes. A row stores the command's assembly-qualified CLR name unless InternalCommandNameAttribute (InternalCommandNameAttribute.cs:25) declares a stable identity, the internal-command twin of EventNameAttribute on the outbox side, with the same drain-then-rename caveat because the attribute changes only what new rows store (InternalCommandNameAttribute.cs:12-17). IInternalCommandAdministration (IInternalCommandAdministration.cs:17) is the operator half: count the pending backlog, page the dead letters as InternalCommandDeadLetter rows (IInternalCommandAdministration.cs:99) whose command payload is deliberately not projected because it can carry personal data (:86-89), requeue them (attempts reset, the lease and dead-letter stamp cleared, LastError kept on purpose, :48-53), and purge completed rows on demand. Every method returns a Result, because an unknown source name is an expected failure an admin screen renders rather than an exception. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] and [Rubric §29, Resilience] are the categories: without this surface, a command that exhausted its attempts has no way back into execution except hand-edited production SQL.

    The framework ships one ready-made use of the queue, for the case an inline call handles worst: deleting a blob that a committed change left orphaned. IDeleteBlobInternalCommand (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/InternalCommands/IDeleteBlobInternalCommand.cs:21) adds a single BlobName (IDeleteBlobInternalCommand.cs:24) to IInternalCommand, because a delete run in the post-commit tail is best effort (a storage outage, a deploy or a crash leaks the blob with nothing left that knows about it) while a row scheduled on the same unit of work survives all three (IDeleteBlobInternalCommand.cs:9-13). An implementation is a small record carrying only the name, with an InternalCommandNameAttribute so a later rename cannot strand rows in flight (IDeleteBlobInternalCommand.cs:16-18). DeleteBlobInternalCommandHandlerBase<TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/InternalCommands/DeleteBlobInternalCommandHandlerBase.cs:28) is the idempotent handler the at-least-once rule asks for: a successful delete completes the row, a NotFound answer is already the state the command asks for and so also returns Result.Success() instead of retrying forever, and any other failure is returned unchanged so the processor's backoff retries it (DeleteBlobInternalCommandHandlerBase.cs:45-64, rationale at :13-18). A consumer derives one sealed subclass per command, so the handler scan registers a closed ICommandHandler<TCommand, Result> that the decorators wrap, and overrides only BlobKind (default "Blob", DeleteBlobInternalCommandHandlerBase.cs:38) to label its log lines (:20-23). ADC does this twice, for avatars (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteAvatarBlob/DeleteAvatarBlobInternalCommandHandler.cs:20) and for session assets (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/SessionAssets/UseCases/DeleteSessionAssetBlob/DeleteSessionAssetBlobInternalCommandHandler.cs:20); Store has no subclass. The storage side is ADR-045.

    Context propagation is the other half, and it is one helper rather than one per mechanism. AmbientOrigin (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/AmbientOrigin.cs:21) is the single place the framework captures and restores the five values a hop off the call stack needs (user id, roles, permission claims, tenant, correlation id), so a deferred command, an outbox row and a broker message all carry the same set the same way (AmbientOrigin.cs:10-19). Roles travel as one comma-separated value bounded by the column width, MaxRolesLength = 512 (AmbientOrigin.cs:40), keeping only the whole leading roles that fit, because cutting a name mid-word would restore a role nobody holds (AmbientOrigin.cs:55-60); the flattener is null-tolerant on purpose, because ICurrentUserService.Roles is a default interface member that hand written test doubles routinely leave unstubbed and a null there must read as "no roles", never as a capture that throws inside a save (AmbientOrigin.cs:47-53). Permission claims are the opposite trade: FlattenPermissions (AmbientOrigin.cs:110) writes them as a JSON array at full fidelity, because a dropped permission would deny a deferred command the inline request was allowed to run and no delimiter is safe for an arbitrary permission name (AmbientOrigin.cs:97-107), and ParsePermissions (:135) reads a malformed value back as no permissions rather than failing the hop (:128-132). The mfa claim is deliberately not carried: a step-up proves a live interaction, so an IRequiresMfa command cannot run deferred (AmbientOrigin.cs:163-167). The capture sites are the internal-command origin capture (InternalCommandOriginCapture, .../Persistence/InternalCommands/InternalCommandOriginCapture.cs:34), the outbox writer (.../Persistence/DbContexts/Factory/DbContextFactory.cs:158) and the broker publisher (.../Messaging/BrokerMessageBus.cs:105); the restore sites are the internal-command processor (.../Persistence/InternalCommands/Processing/InternalCommandProcessor.cs:483), the OutboxProcessor (.../Persistence/Outbox/Processing/OutboxProcessor.cs:508) and the consumers.

    Restore (AmbientOrigin.cs:254) does two things. It writes the captured values onto the scope it was given, tenant first because the tenant routes the scoped context factory, then the principal, then the correlation id (AmbientOrigin.cs:268-277); the principal is always overwritten or cleared so a reused scope cannot let one message's user answer for the next, while the tenant is set only when the scope has not already resolved a different one, because a tenant cannot change within a scope (AmbientOrigin.cs:214-224, :294-303). And it publishes what the scope ended up with as an OriginSnapshot (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/AmbientOrigin.cs:353) on an AsyncLocal (AmbientOrigin.cs:26, read through Current at :34, published at :279-285), returning a RestoreHandle (AmbientOrigin.cs:340) whose Dispose puts back whatever origin was published before (AmbientOrigin.cs:265-266, :287, :342). The publication exists because integration event handlers are singletons that open their own scope from the root factory, a scope the direct restore never reaches; so TenantContext, ScopedUserOverride and CorrelationContext seed themselves from Current once, when constructed (AmbientOrigin.cs:230-241, TenantContext.cs:19, ScopedUserOverride.cs:30, CorrelationContext.cs:13), and a handler's own scope still runs as the original interaction. The snapshot is a six-value record (user id, roles, permission claims, tenant, correlation id, authentication type, AmbientOrigin.cs:353-359) whose BuildPrincipal (:363) rebuilds the claims principal through the same AmbientOrigin.BuildPrincipal the direct restore uses (AmbientOrigin.cs:179-206, :271): the user id as sub, each role as a role claim and each permission as a permission claim, so deferred work is granted exactly as the inline request was (AmbientOrigin.cs:154-160). Suppress (AmbientOrigin.cs:331) withdraws the published origin behind the same handle type for the one place an explicit choice must win over an enclosing hop, TenantDataSourceTargets CreateTenantScope (.../Persistence/DataSources/TenantDataSourceTargets.cs:105). Every restore site holds the handle for the whole row or message (using var origin, for example UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:68), so the next one cannot inherit it.

    A restore lands in ScopedUserOverride (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ScopedUserOverride.cs:27), a per-scope carrier holding the principal that did not arrive over HTTP (ScopedUserOverride.cs:30, set at :36). The principal itself is never a live ambient value: a scope created during a hop copies the published origin once, at construction, and owns that copy from then on, so nothing is shared or mutated across scopes, and an HTTP request (which never publishes an origin) resolves an empty carrier and reads straight through to the HTTP principal (ScopedUserOverride.cs:17-26). It exposes Clear() (:50) because the outbox processor keeps one scope for a whole batch and without an explicit clear a row raised by a user would answer for every later row raised by the system (ScopedUserOverride.cs:42-49). The carrier is read by ImpersonatingCurrentUserService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ImpersonatingCurrentUserService.cs:20), which decorates rather than replaces whatever ICurrentUserService the host registered: with no override every member reads straight through to the inner service, so an HTTP request behaves exactly as it did before the decorator existed (ImpersonatingCurrentUserService.cs:25-35), and claim values are parsed in the invariant culture exactly as CurrentUserService writes them (:46-50). AddInfrastructure applies it with Scrutor's TryDecorate after AddServices() has run its own TryAddScoped, guarded on the presence of the ScopedUserOverride registration so a host whose modules each call AddInfrastructure does not stack one wrapper per call (DependencyInjection.cs:279-286). The broker side of the same restore is ConsumerOriginRestore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:20), the one step of the restore that knows about a transport (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:13-19): its Apply (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:31) reads the headers BrokerMessageBus stamped (user id, roles, permissions, tenant, correlation id) from the delivered message's string dictionary, hands them to AmbientOrigin.Restore, and returns the restore handle the consumer holds for the whole consume (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:45-52, the permissions header at :49). It is shared by every consumer the receive pipeline dispatches to, both IntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (.../Messaging/Consumers/IntegrationEventConsumer.cs:76) and UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:64), each calling it before the inbox is touched because under database-per-tenant the restored tenant routes the inbox store (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:59-63), so a message reaching a retired contract is restored exactly as one reaching the current contract. The user id is transported as text and parsed back, and a malformed value is treated as a publisher bug that yields no identity rather than a reason to fail the consume (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:35-43); every broker header is a string in the first place, so a broker that widens or retypes application properties cannot change what the receiver reads (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerHeaders.cs:3-7). [Rubric §11, Security] is the lens: the identity a background execution acts as is captured from the request that queued it, never assumed or elevated.

    The broker transport boundary

    AddBrokerMessaging (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:63) owns everything that is the same on every broker and hands only the byte-moving part to one IBrokerTransport (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/IBrokerTransport.cs:22). The transports are framework code with no third-party messaging library underneath (ADR-118), and the contract states the division itself: the framework owns the topology, the wire format, the receive pipeline (origin restore, inbox, retry, redelivery and dead-letter decisions), the outbox-only publish path and the tracing, while a transport publishes an outgoing message to a topic, delivers each message on the host's queue to the receive pipeline, and carries out the disposition the pipeline returns (IBrokerTransport.cs:7-15). RabbitMQ and PostgreSQL are built in and every other transport ships in an adapter package, so the core packages never reference a vendor SDK (IBrokerTransport.cs:16-20). The contract is three members: a Name compared case-insensitively against MessageBus:Provider (IBrokerTransport.cs:28), a MaxRedeliveryDelay that is null when the broker has no delay cap (:35; Amazon SQS caps a message delay at 15 minutes, :30-34), and Register(services, context) (:51), which adds a singleton IBrokerPublisher and a hosted receiver for the host's queue, and which runs while AddBrokerMessaging runs so a missing namespace or connection string throws at startup rather than at the first publish (IBrokerTransport.cs:37-47). IBrokerPublisher (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IBrokerPublisher.cs:9) is called only by BrokerMessageBus, which the outbox processor drains through, so a publish the broker did not accept must throw and surface to the outbox's retry and circuit breaker (IBrokerPublisher.cs:3-8, PublishAsync at :18). MessageBusProviders (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/MessageBusProviders.cs:10) names the three values the core handles itself, InProcess (the default when the setting is absent, MessageBusProviders.cs:16), RabbitMq (:19) and PostgreSql (:27), and keeps a small map from the adapter-supplied names (AzureServiceBus, AmazonSqs) to the package and call that provide them, used only to make the registration error actionable (MessageBusProviders.cs:29-39). ResolveBrokerTransport constructs a built-in transport directly, otherwise takes the last registered IBrokerTransport whose name matches, otherwise throws naming the package to reference (or the AddBrokerTransport call to make) and the available providers (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:199-232); an adapter therefore calls AddBrokerTransport (:174, a TryAddEnumerable singleton that rejects an empty name, :178-183) before the host calls AddBrokerMessaging.

    The registration order inside AddBrokerMessaging is a sequence of startup guards. It returns at once for InProcess (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:72), fails a broker paired with an explicitly disabled outbox because the outbox is a broker host's only publish path (:80, rationale at :234-255), resolves the transport (:84), and then requires Application:Namespace (:89, :257-281): every topic is prefixed with it, so services that fell back to their own application names would publish and subscribe on different topics and lose every cross-service event with no error anywhere. Consumers are declared next. The configureConsumers callback receives an IBrokerConsumerBuilder (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:16) with two calls, RegisterIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (:26) and, for a retired contract, RegisterUpcastedIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (:40). There is one queue per host, so two services consuming the same event never compete for one queue and there is no per-consumer endpoint configuration to get wrong (IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:9-14). The internal BrokerConsumerBuilder (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:12) records one BrokerSubscription (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerSubscription.cs:11) per event, tagged with its BrokerConsumerKind (BrokerConsumerKind.cs:4) and named through BrokerNaming (BrokerNaming.cs:13), throws on a second registration of the same event in either kind (BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:47-58), and maps each subscription to the closed IntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> or UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:36-45), which AddBrokerMessaging registers scoped (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:105). The collected subscriptions become the host's BrokerTopology (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerTopology.cs:10): the application namespace, the one queue (MessageBus:QueueName or the application name, DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:94-96) and the subscriptions in registration order, with a constructor that rejects a duplicate event name a second time (BrokerTopology.cs:25-34). A host that consumes nothing still has a topology: it publishes, and its transport creates no queue (BrokerTopology.cs:7-8). The method then registers the receive pipeline (:109), Replaces the bus interfaces (:119, :125) and the inbox store (:132-147), and calls transport.Register last, so the transport sees every framework registration above it (:150-158).

    The transport receives a BrokerTransportContext (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportContext.cs:11): the topology, also registered as a singleton so a hosted receiver can take it from DI (BrokerTransportContext.cs:34-38), the bound MessageBusSettings (:41), the connection string resolved from MessageBus:ConnectionString, then ConnectionStrings:rabbitmq, then ConnectionStrings:messaging, or null so the transport keeps its own default host (:43-48), and the configuration for transport-specific keys (:51).

    Every delivered message goes through one IBrokerReceivePipeline (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IBrokerReceivePipeline.cs:16), whose single ProcessAsync takes an IncomingBrokerMessage (IncomingBrokerMessage.cs:11) and returns a BrokerDisposition (IBrokerReceivePipeline.cs:22). Its implementation, BrokerReceivePipeline (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:26), restores the publisher's trace context as the parent of a Consumer span, resolves the subscription from the event-name header, deserializes the body, and runs the subscription's consumer (inbox, origin restore, handlers) through the non-generic IBrokerMessageConsumer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/IBrokerMessageConsumer.cs:12) with in-process exponential retry, each attempt in a fresh DI scope (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:12-19). The disposition is a closed record family (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerDisposition.cs:8): Completed (:14, shared as Complete at :11), Redeliver carrying a delay and the next redelivery count (:24), and DeadLetter carrying a reason and a detail (:33); a transport applies it and decides nothing itself, because retry counts, intervals and dead-letter policy live once, in the pipeline (BrokerDisposition.cs:3-7). An unknown event name or a body that does not deserialize is dead-lettered at once as unknown-event or poison (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:29, :32, :124-144); a message whose retries all fail is redelivered while intervals remain (:166) and is dead-lettered as handler-failed after that (:35, :176), with one Error log and one broker.fault.count increment at that point (:17-19). It never throws for a handler or payload failure: only the host's own cancellation escapes, and the transport then leaves the message unacknowledged so the broker delivers it again (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:20-23). On the wire, OutgoingBrokerMessage (OutgoingBrokerMessage.cs:13) is what a publisher sends, BrokerHeaders (BrokerHeaders.cs:8) names the transport-level headers (event name, the message id the inbox dedupes on, the redelivery count, W3C trace context, :10-29), and BrokerWire (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/BrokerWire.cs:12) holds the two pieces both hops must agree on: the MMCA.Common.Messaging trace source (BrokerWire.cs:19) and body JSON options identical to the outbox payload's, so an event that round-trips through the outbox round-trips through the broker in the same shape (:27-37).

    BrokerTransportPolicies (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:16) holds the receive-side policies as pure functions of MessageBusSettings, so the pipeline and every transport read one definition (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:3-8). RetryDelay (:27) doubles RetryMinIntervalSeconds per retry up to RetryMaxIntervalSeconds, so the defaults wait 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds (:18-23). BuildRedeliveryIntervals (:52, :65) maps the second-level intervals (one minute, ten minutes, one hour by default, MessageBusSettings.cs:190), drops non-positive entries because a zero interval would turn the second level into a hot loop, and clamps each to the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:42-75); the pipeline reads the clamped set once, at construction (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:72). In-process retry absorbs a blip measured in seconds, redelivery an outage measured in minutes or hours, and every in-process retry is exhausted before a redelivery is asked for (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:9-15). The backpressure knobs, ResolvePrefetchCount (:85) and ResolveConcurrentMessageLimit (:98), are range-guarded in code rather than by [Range], because AddBrokerMessaging binds the section with Get<MessageBusSettings>(), which never runs DataAnnotations, and a value of zero or less leaves the transport's own default in place (:77-82).

    Two transports are built in, written against the same contract an adapter implements. RabbitMqBrokerTransport (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:24) runs on RabbitMQ.Client. Its topology, named by RabbitMqNames (RabbitMqNames.cs:19), is a durable fanout exchange per topic, one durable queue per host bound to the exchange of every event it consumes, {queue}-error for dead letters, and a {queue}-delay-{seconds}s queue per redelivery interval whose message time to live returns each message to the host queue, so delayed redelivery needs no broker plugin; publishes are persistent and confirmed, and connections recover automatically (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:11-17). Register (:33-61) adds a RabbitMqPublisher (RabbitMqPublisher.cs:10) over a RabbitMqChannelOperations (RabbitMqChannelOperations.cs:12) and a RabbitMqConnectionSource (RabbitMqConnectionSource.cs:11) with a RabbitMqProvisioner (RabbitMqProvisioner.cs:16), returns early when the topology has no subscriptions (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:46-49), and otherwise adds a hosted RabbitMqReceiver (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:21) whose concurrency is ConcurrentMessageLimit or else the processor count and whose prefetch is PrefetchCount or else twice the concurrency (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:88-105). The connection string must be an amqp:// or amqps:// URI or registration throws; with none the client's localhost:5672 default applies (:19-21, :70-86). RabbitMqDispositionApplier (RabbitMqDispositionApplier.cs:21), RabbitMqHeaders (RabbitMqHeaders.cs:11) and IRabbitMqOperations (IRabbitMqOperations.cs:9) complete the internal set. PostgreSqlBrokerTransport (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:36) keeps topics, queues and delayed redeliveries in three tables of one PostgreSQL database, defined by PostgreSqlTransportSql (PostgreSqlTransportSql.cs:24), and is core rather than an adapter because any PostgreSQL is the broker (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:10-15). A publish inserts one row per subscribed queue in one statement and wakes the receivers with pg_notify; a receiver claims rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED under a renewed lease and falls back to polling; a redelivery pushes the row's visible_after out, so there is no delay cap; and a dead letter moves the row to {schema}.dead_letters (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:16-22). Register (:61-94) adds the PostgreSqlMessageStore (PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:16) singleton and the PostgreSqlPublisher (PostgreSqlPublisher.cs:13), then the PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator (PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator.cs:12) when MigrateOnStartup is on, ahead of the receiver because hosted services start in registration order (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:75-79), and finally the PostgreSqlReceiver (PostgreSqlReceiver.cs:23) with its PostgreSqlReceiverOptions (PostgreSqlReceiverOptions.cs:11, PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:86-93); IPostgreSqlMessageStore (IPostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:10), PostgreSqlClaimedMessage (PostgreSqlClaimedMessage.cs:14) and PostgreSqlDispositionApplier (PostgreSqlDispositionApplier.cs:17) complete the set. Unlike RabbitMQ there is no default host, so a missing connection string fails registration (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:111-117). Its own keys bind from MessageBus:PostgreSql into PostgreSqlTransportSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlTransportSettings.cs:8, :11): a Schema and Role that both default to transport (PostgreSqlTransportSettings.cs:14, :38-42) and MigrateOnStartup, on by default (:36), which a host whose database user cannot create a role and a schema turns off, creating the schema out of band with the same idempotent DDL (:30-35). When an INpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator is registered (an RDS, Cloud SQL or Entra token provider), the transport runs on the same shared NpgsqlDataSource the PostgreSQL contexts use for that connection string, the startup migration included (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:30-34, :103-109). [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] and [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] are the lenses: the broker is a strategy chosen by configuration, behind one contract, with the vendor code outside the core (ADR-066, ADR-118).

    Assembly anchors

    Several pieces of machinery need a Type whose Assembly identifies a layer: Scrutor's FromAssemblyOf<T>() scans, FluentValidation's AddValidatorsFromAssemblyContaining<T>(), and the architecture rules' per-package anchor. That is what the AssemblyReference / ClassReference pairs are, one per layer (Application, Infrastructure), each a trivial static class AssemblyReference holding Assembly / AssemblyName statics (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/AssemblyReference.cs:5-9) beside a non-static class ClassReference (AssemblyReference.cs:11) for the places a generic constraint forbids a static type. AddApplication uses the Application pair for the common validators (MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:59) and AddInfrastructure uses the Infrastructure pair to scan entity configurations (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:134-139). They are deliberately behavior-free; their whole job is to name an assembly for the scanning and governance tooling. A related, test-only assembly anchor lives in CreateMigrationProofTable (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests.MigrationsFixture/CreateMigrationProofTable.cs:24): a real EF migration for the framework's one SQLite context kept in its own tiny library, because EF selects migrations by the [DbContext] they carry and a migration compiled into the test assembly would make every test that names that assembly see a pending migration (CreateMigrationProofTable.cs:11-21).

    Configuration binding, the Settings family

    Everything a host operator tunes arrives as a strongly-typed settings object bound from an appsettings.json section, each carrying a static readonly string SectionName so the section name lives next to the shape it binds. The pattern in AddInfrastructure is uniform: services.AddOptions<T>().Bind(configuration.GetSection(T.SectionName)).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() (for example ConnectionStringSettings at MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:73-76), so misconfiguration fails fast at startup rather than lazily on first use (ADR-070). There are no ISettings facade interfaces over these types: consumers take IOptions<T> (or the concrete singleton, for the two dictionary-shaped ones) directly. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices] apply: ValidateOnStart plus DataAnnotations ranges (for example OutboxSettings BatchSize is [Range(1, 1000)] with a default of 50, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Outbox/Administration/OutboxSettings.cs:15-17) turn a config typo into an immediate, descriptive boot failure.

    The Application-layer settings drive composition itself. ApplicationSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Settings/ApplicationSettings.cs:8) carries UseMiniProfiler, MaxPageSize (default 500), MaxExportRows ([Range(1, 10_000_000)], default 100,000) and DatabaseInitStrategy (default "Migrate", ApplicationSettings.cs:14-43), and is passed by value into every IModule.Register. ModulesSettings is a Dictionary<string, ModuleSettings> bound from the "Modules" section (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Settings/ModulesSettings.cs:7-10) whose IsModuleEnabled and IsDependencyRemote helpers (ModulesSettings.cs:18-32) the loader queries; note that a module absent from configuration is treated as disabled (ModulesSettings.cs:19). ModuleSettings carries the per-module Enabled flag (default true, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Settings/ModuleSettings.cs:9) and the RemoteDependencies list (ModuleSettings.cs:37) that flips a dependency from "in-process" to "satisfied by an extracted service", with a worked monolith-after-extraction config example on the property itself (ModuleSettings.cs:24-35). One more Application-layer settings class exists for a layering reason rather than a composition one: QueryCachePipelineSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Settings/QueryCachePipelineSettings.cs:20) exposes the single Cache:PopulateLockTimeout knob the caching query decorator needs, because that decorator lives in Application and Application cannot reference Infrastructure where CacheSettings binds the rest of the same section (QueryCachePipelineSettings.cs:4-18, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Caching/CacheSettings.cs:18-22); AddCaching binds both from the same section so they cannot drift (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:48-56).

    The Infrastructure settings cover the rest of the platform. AddInfrastructure binds them here even though several belong to other chapters by subject (persistence in group 07, auth in group 08, caching in group 09, the outbox in group 04): the binding discipline is this chapter's, the types are theirs. Starting with the database ones, ConnectionStringSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DataSources/ConnectionStringSettings.cs:12) has no required property at all: SQL Server is the default engine, but a host may run entirely on SQLite or Cosmos, and may declare its databases through the DataSources section instead (ConnectionStringSettings.cs:3-11). What is required is that the host can reach some database, and that rule spans two sections, so it cannot be a data annotation: ConnectionStringSettingsValidator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DataSources/ConnectionStringSettingsValidator.cs:30) is registered as an IValidateOptions<ConnectionStringSettings> via TryAddEnumerable (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:83-84) and passes only when the top-level section names a database on any engine or one DataSources entry does (ConnectionStringSettingsValidator.cs:47-53, :56-72), failing with a message that lists both shapes because which one is missing depends on whether the host is a single-database monolith or a database-per-module one (ConnectionStringSettingsValidator.cs:38-45). DataSourcesSettings with its per-entry DataSourceEntrySettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DataSources/DataSourceEntrySettings.cs:19) is the logical-to-physical source map for database-per-service, built directly from Get<Dictionary<...>> rather than through the options pipeline (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:86-90) because a root-level dictionary section does not bind that way, with a constructor that rejects an empty or reserved "Default" key (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DataSources/DataSourcesSettings.cs:27-40).

    The rest of the platform sections follow the same discipline: MessageBusSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/MessageBusSettings.cs:13), whose Provider is a plain string defaulting to MessageBusProviders.InProcess (MessageBusSettings.cs:25) rather than an enum, because any value beyond the three built-in names selects a transport an adapter package registers (the boundary is described in its own section below). The same Provider resolves the inbox and outbox defaults, both on for any broker and off for InProcess unless set explicitly (MessageBusSettings.cs:142, :185). AddBrokerMessaging short-circuits entirely for InProcess (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:72-75) and otherwise Replaces both IMessageBus and IEventBus with their broker-backed counterparts (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:119, :125, ADR-066); OutboxSettings (batch size, retries, polling and processing intervals, lease, retention) consumed by the OutboxProcessor; PersistenceSettings, whose single CommandTimeoutSeconds defaults to the 30 seconds the framework applied implicitly before the section existed (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/PersistenceSettings.cs:21-22); the JWT/JWKS group (JwtSettings, the JwtSigningAlgorithm enum (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/JwtSigningAlgorithm.cs:21), and JwksSettings, whose Enabled defaults to false so an HMAC-only deployment does not start advertising an RSA key set by accident, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/JwksSettings.cs:30-33); and the delivery channels, SmtpSettings and PushNotificationSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/PushNotificationSettings.cs:8, section PushNotifications, with the hub path defaulting to /hubs/notifications and a MaxConnectionsPerUser of 20, PushNotificationSettings.cs:11, :25, :50), bound with ValidateOnStart by AddPushNotifications (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:43-46). OS-level push (ADR-044) and managed file storage (ADR-045) have no settings type and no implementation in the core packages at all, because the core is cloud-neutral: AddServices registers a null-object default behind each contract, NullNativePushSender and NullPushDeviceRegistrar (DependencyInjection.cs:377-378) and NullFileStorageService (DependencyInjection.cs:385), each through TryAdd, and a vendor adapter package (MMCA.Common.Azure, MMCA.Common.Aws or MMCA.Common.Gcp) replaces it when its own section is enabled and complete (DependencyInjection.cs:373-376, :356-358; the adapters are in group 28). Image normalization is deliberately not a framework service: decoding needs a native image library every consumer of the package would otherwise carry (DependencyInjection.cs:382-384). Application code therefore always resolves something. What the core does keep is the vendor-free half of push, NativePushPayloads (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/NativePushPayloads.cs:13), pure System.Text.Json builders for the FCM v1 message and the APNs alert (NativePushPayloads.cs:20, :42) that the Notification Hubs and SNS adapters send, while the FCM adapter maps the same fields onto FirebaseAdmin's typed message, so one notification looks the same whichever cloud delivered it (NativePushPayloads.cs:5-12). [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] again: a null object, not a nullable dependency. AddPushNotifications does not share that adapter shape: it always adds SignalR, adds the Redis backplane when a redis connection string is present, replaces the in-app notification sender and live-channel publisher with their SignalR-backed implementations, and Replaces SignalR's default user-id provider with the claim-based one, because AddSignalR has already registered its own and a TryAdd would never take effect (DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:45-67).

    A null-object default is right for a host that never switched a channel on and wrong for one that did, so AddInfrastructure closes the gap with a startup tripwire. CloudAdapterTripwire (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:32) is an IValidateOptions over the empty CloudAdapterTripwireOptions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwireOptions.cs:8), a type whose only job is to ride ValidateOnStart so the check runs with the other startup validators before any hosted service starts (CloudAdapterTripwireOptions.cs:3-7). When NativePush:Enabled is true (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:35) and INativePushSender still resolves, in a scope, to NullNativePushSender, the host fails with a message naming each adapter package, its registration call and the keys it needs (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:62-82); otherwise a deployment that lost the adapter call would start, pass its health checks and silently drop every push (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:16-22). File storage is deliberately not checked, because a FileStorage section is routinely shared configuration and so does not declare intent, and a host that does store files without an adapter is not silent anyway: NullFileStorageService fails every upload with FileStorage.NotConfigured (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:24-29). Beside it, StartupConfigurationSummaryService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:35) is an IHostedService that writes one Information line at start naming the posture the host actually resolved: the MMCA.Common version stamped on the assembly at build time, the release tag or 0.0.0-dev (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:49-52), the configured database engines, the bus provider with its EnableDelayedRedelivery value, the cache mode and the tenancy mode (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:55-74). It logs names and flags only, deriving the engines from whether a connection string is set and never from its text (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:20-23), and it names the cache tier without resolving ICacheService, so a Redis-backed host does not open its connection at startup (:93-104). It also emits the one Warning a RabbitMQ host with delayed redelivery off needs, because a handler failure that outlasts the in-process retries then dead-letters instead of being rescheduled (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:82-85, :25-30). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] covers both: "which version, which bus, which cache?" is answered by the first lines of the log. One binding is deliberately elsewhere: JwtSettings is bound by the API layer's AddCommonAuthentication (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.Authentication.cs:136-137), so a host that skips authentication never pays for a JWT section it does not have.

    The three opt-in feature sections follow the same shape with one extra rule worth reading closely. SchedulerSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/SchedulerSettings.cs:16) and AuditTrailSettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/AuditTrail/AuditTrailSettings.cs:16) each make Enabled (default false) the single gate over both the behavior and whether the backing table is mapped into the model at all (SchedulerSettings.cs:10-14, AuditTrailSettings.cs:10-15), so a host that never opts in keeps exactly the migrations it had. Their tunables are ranged the same way (PollingIntervalSeconds default 30 and LeaseSeconds default 300, SchedulerSettings.cs:28-46; RetentionDays default 90, AuditTrailSettings.cs:37-38), and per-job retiming lives in ScheduledJobOverrideSettings bound from Scheduler:Jobs:{Name} (SchedulerSettings.cs:63, :66-74). TenancySettings (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Tenancy/TenancySettings.cs:51) adds the collection-binding subtlety: ResolutionOrder and ExcludedPathPrefixes bind as empty lists and the framework reads EffectiveResolutionOrder / EffectiveExcludedPathPrefixes instead (TenancySettings.cs:82, :106), because the configuration binder ADDS to a pre-populated collection rather than replacing it, so a non-empty default would leave a host running the framework's entries as well (TenancySettings.cs:42-49). Its per-tenant database routing is pure configuration: TenantEntrySettings (TenancySettings.cs:127) keys TenantDataSourceOverrideSettings (TenancySettings.cs:144) by physical data source name, and TenancySettingsValidator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Tenancy/TenancySettingsValidator.cs:24) fails the boot when an override names a source that does not exist, when it declares no connection string at all, or when the resolution order names TenantResolutionStrategy Host, which is defined but not implemented (TenancySettings.cs:22-28). Every one of those failures is a misconfiguration that would otherwise surface as silent cross-tenant behavior, which is exactly the bug class tenancy exists to prevent, so it is worth a failed boot. [Rubric §11, Security] is the category there.

    Two composition questions are answered by a small resolver rather than by a settings property, because a bound property cannot distinguish "configured false" from "never configured" and the safe answer differs by environment. ApplicationNamespace (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/ApplicationNamespace.cs:35) is the one name every piece of shared infrastructure is namespaced by: Redis cache keys, distributed-lock keys, distributed rate-limit counter keys, the Redis output-cache InstanceName, the SignalR Redis backplane channel prefix and the broker's endpoint prefix (ApplicationNamespace.cs:7-12). It resolves the explicit Application:Namespace key when set (:32, :54-60), otherwise the host's application name, otherwise the "app" fallback (:35), and sanitizes the result to characters that are safe in a Redis key, a channel name and a queue name (:43-44). Composition reads it where the shared resource is wired: AddPushNotifications for the backplane channel prefix (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:59), AddBrokerMessaging for the endpoint prefix when MessageBus:EndpointPrefix is blank (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:100-102), and the cache-key builder (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Caching/CacheKeyPrefix.cs:95). The default is per-application rather than empty because two hosts pointed at one Redis or one broker otherwise share every keyspace, and NotificationHub ships in the framework, so its backplane channel name is identical in every consumer and a user-targeted push in one application reaches the other application's clients holding the same numeric user id (ApplicationNamespace.cs:15-26). SmtpTransportSecurity (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Mail/SmtpTransportSecurity.cs:26) has the same three-step shape for TLS: the explicit Smtp:EnableSsl key, then configuration, then secure unless the host says it is Development (SmtpTransportSecurity.cs:29, :37-49). SmtpEmailSender resolves it once at construction (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Mail/SmtpEmailSender.cs:57) through the overload that also logs one startup warning when a non-Development host turned TLS off for a configured relay, so that decision is visible in the logs of the deployment that made it (SmtpTransportSecurity.cs:51-58). Development keeps the permissive default because local development targets MailDev, which offers no TLS (SmtpTransportSecurity.cs:21-25). [Rubric §11, Security] covers both: the secure value is the one you get by configuring nothing.

    The two routing attributes

    Two attributes, both in MMCA.Common.Infrastructure, both Inherited = true so they ride down a configuration class hierarchy, encode where an entity is stored declaratively: the per-entity half of the database-per-service strategy (ADR-006). UseDataSourceAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:13-18) names the engine (DataSource: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Cosmos or SQLite) and is carried by the provider-specific configuration base classes, so choosing a base class chooses the engine with no change to the entity (see primer §2). UseDatabaseAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/UseDatabaseAttribute.cs:21-26) names the logical database on that engine; its documented resolution order (UseDatabaseAttribute.cs:9-14) is the attribute value, then the module name derived from the entity's namespace (the segment before Domain), then "Default".
