    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.ExportUserData · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/IUserDataExportSection.cs:105 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: a static holder for one string constant: the sentence a data subject reads when a section of their export could not be produced and the app supplied no reason of its own.

    • Depends on: nothing. It is a single const string, which is why it is Level 0 even though the export pipeline around it is not.

    • Concept introduced, the caller-safe failure message. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy and Data Governance] assesses whether privacy obligations are met in the product rather than in a policy document: a data-subject access request has a legal deadline, so a partially unavailable package that says so plainly is a better answer than a failed request (ADR-076). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses what leaves the trust boundary: this text reaches an end user, so it is deliberately generic and carries no exception message, stack trace, peer address, or connection string; the detail goes to the log instead, through the handler-local ExportSectionUnavailable source-generated log message on ExportUserDataHandlerBase<TUser, TQuery> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:202). [Rubric §13, Observability and Operability]: splitting the audience in two (generic sentence out, full exception in) is the pattern, not an oversight.

    • Walkthrough: one member, public const string UnavailableReason (IUserDataExportSection.cs:112-113), whose value is "This section could not be retrieved. The data is unchanged; the export can be requested again later." The XML doc records the intent (IUserDataExportSection.cs:107-111): the subject learns the section is incomplete and retryable, and learns nothing about the internal failure. const rather than static readonly because the value is compile-time and callers use it in default-parameter position and in object initializers.

    • Why it's built this way: two call sites need the identical wording, and having them share a constant is what keeps a degraded section indistinguishable whether the section itself reported unavailability or the handler caught an exception on its behalf.

    • Where it's used: as the fallback in UserDataExportSectionResult.Unavailable when the caller passes no reason (IUserDataExportSection.cs:99), and directly in ExportUserDataHandlerBase<TUser, TQuery>'s catch block when a section throws (ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:196).

    UseDataSourceAttribute

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:14 · Level 1 · class (sealed attribute)

    • What it is: the companion attribute to UseDatabaseAttribute. Where that one names the logical database, this one declares the database engine (DataSource: CosmosDB, Sqlite, or SQL Server) an entity type configuration targets. It is Level 1 rather than Level 0 because, unlike the pure-BCL UseDatabaseAttribute, it references the first-party DataSource enum.

    • Depends on: the DataSource enum (from MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces.Infrastructure.Persistence, imported at UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:1) and System.Attribute (BCL).

    • Concept: engine selection for the multi-engine persistence layer, the sibling of the logical-name routing introduced under UseDatabaseAttribute. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] again: the framework supports SQL Server, Cosmos, and SQLite simultaneously, and this attribute is how a configuration announces which engine's rules apply. In practice it is carried on the provider-specific configuration base classes (EntityTypeConfigurationSQLServer/Cosmos/Sqlite), so a concrete configuration inherits its engine, while UseDatabaseAttribute selects which database on that engine.

    • Walkthrough:

      • [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, Inherited = true, AllowMultiple = false)] (UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:13), same inheritance and single-use semantics as UseDatabaseAttribute so a provider base class propagates the engine to derived configurations.
      • Primary-constructor parameter dataSource (UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:14) of type DataSource.
      • DataSource get-only property (UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:17) exposing the chosen engine. The XML doc (UseDataSourceAttribute.cs:5-11) records that it is read by DataSourceService at model-building time to populate the entity-to-data-source cache that UnitOfWork uses to route each entity to the correct ApplicationDbContext.

    • Why it's built this way: keeping the engine on an attribute (inherited from a provider base class) means an entity's engine and database are both declarative metadata the registry can scan up front, which is what lets routing happen without first building an EF model (ADR-006).

    • Where it's used: on the per-engine EntityTypeConfiguration* base classes and, through inheritance, every concrete configuration under them; read by DataSourceService / EntityDataSourceRegistry.

    UserDataExportSectionResult

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.ExportUserData · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/IUserDataExportSection.cs:47 · Level 1 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: what one IUserDataExportSection hands back: either its payload, or the fact that the payload could not be produced plus a caller-safe reason.

    • Depends on: UserDataExportSectionDefaults (Level 0, for the fallback reason string). BCL only otherwise (object, ArgumentException). It is the application-layer twin of the wire DTO UserDataExportSectionDTO that the handler copies it into.

    • Concept introduced, "unavailable" as a first-class value rather than an exception. [Rubric §29, Resilience, Reliability and Business Continuity] assesses how a system behaves when a dependency is down. In a fan-out over N contributors, an exception is the wrong currency: it either aborts the whole package or gets swallowed. Modelling the negative outcome as a value (Available = false plus a reason) means the degraded case is visible in the document the data subject receives, and the caller cannot forget to handle it. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns]: the two named static factories are the only construction paths, so an instance is always in one of exactly two legal shapes, the same private-construction discipline value objects use elsewhere in this codebase.

    • Walkthrough

      • Four init members: required string SectionName (IUserDataExportSection.cs:50), required bool Available (:53), object? Data (:60), and string? UnavailableReason (:67). The two required members are the ones a result is meaningless without; the two nullable ones are mutually exclusive in practice.
      • Data is typed object? on purpose (:55-59): every contributor publishes its own DTO shape and the export is serialized as one JSON document, so the payload type cannot be known here. Its doc marks it PII by design: never log it, never cache it.
      • UnavailableReason (:62-66) is documented as reaching the data subject, so it must never carry internal exception detail.
      • Complete(sectionName, data) (:73-83) guards with ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(sectionName) (:75) and returns Available = true. Note that a null payload is legal here: a section that provably holds nothing for this user returns a complete result with an empty body, which is a truthful answer rather than an unknown one (IUserDataExportSection.cs:11-14).
      • Unavailable(sectionName, reason = null) (:91-101) applies the same name guard (:93) and falls back to UserDataExportSectionDefaults.UnavailableReason when the caller supplies none (:99).

    • Why it's built this way: a sealed record with init members gives structural equality and immutability for free, which matters because these instances flow straight into a document that must not be mutated after assembly (ADR-076).

    • Where it's used: the return type of IUserDataExportSection.ExportAsync (IUserDataExportSection.cs:38), consumed by ExportUserDataHandlerBase<TUser, TQuery>'s RunSectionAsync, which copies its four fields into a UserDataExportSectionDTO (ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:177-183). Produced by every concrete section, for example Store's SalesUserDataExportSection returning Complete with an empty payload for an account with no linked customer (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/SalesUserDataExportSection.cs:45) and with the mapped payload otherwise (:56).

    IUserDataExportSection

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.ExportUserData · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/IUserDataExportSection.cs:20 · Level 2 · interface

    • What it is: the contributor contract for a data-subject export. One implementation is one module (or one cross-service peer client) that holds personal data keyed by user and can hand it over on request.

    • Depends on: UserDataExportSectionResult (Level 1, its return type) and the UserIdentifierType alias. Nothing external beyond Task and CancellationToken.

    • Concept introduced, the accumulating-registration extension point. [Rubric §5, Vertical Slice] assesses whether a feature's pieces cluster inside the boundary that owns them: the export document is assembled centrally, but what each module contributes is written and registered by that module, so adding personal data to a module means adding one section, not editing a central projection. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: a section may be backed by an in-process repository read or by a gRPC client to an extracted peer, and the export handler cannot tell the difference. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy and Data Governance]: this is the mechanism by which "all personal data we hold about you" stays complete as modules are added, which is the obligation ADR-076 exists to discharge. [Rubric §29, Resilience]: sections are explicitly best-effort, and the contract says so in its own remarks (IUserDataExportSection.cs:8-14): a throwing section degrades to Available = false and the export still succeeds, because one unreachable peer must never deny a data subject the rest of their data.

    • Walkthrough: two members.

      • string SectionName { get; } (IUserDataExportSection.cs:27), the stable name the section is published under in the document ("Engagement", "Sales"). The doc calls it part of the contract rather than a label to reword, because it appears verbatim in the package a data subject reads.
      • Task<UserDataExportSectionResult> ExportAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (IUserDataExportSection.cs:38-40). Its doc states the tolerance explicitly: throwing is permitted, and the handler degrades the section, but returning UserDataExportSectionResult.Unavailable is preferred where the reason is known (:34-37).
      • Registration is a separate one-liner: AddUserDataExportSection<TSection>() does TryAddScoped<TSection>() plus TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IUserDataExportSection, TSection>()) (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.Extensibility.cs:38-44). TryAddEnumerable is the load-bearing call: registrations accumulate across modules while the same type registered twice is added once, and registration order becomes document order (DependencyInjection.Extensibility.cs:19-26). The lifetime is scoped, so a section runs inside the request's unit of work and may take scoped dependencies (DependencyInjection.Extensibility.cs:27-30).

    • Why it's built this way: the alternative, a central export handler that knows every module's data, would couple the Identity module to every other module and would break the moment one of them was extracted into its own service. Fan-out over an injected IEnumerable<IUserDataExportSection> keeps that knowledge inside each module and turns extraction into a change of what the section calls, not of who contributes.

    • Where it's used: injected as IEnumerable<IUserDataExportSection> into ExportUserDataHandlerBase<TUser, TQuery> (ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:51). Implemented by EngagementUserDataExportSection and NotificationUserDataExportSection, registered in that order (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:74-75), and by Store's SalesUserDataExportSection (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/SalesUserDataExportSection.cs:22), registered by its Identity module (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/IdentityModule.cs:40). Two more implementations exist only as test doubles that pin the degradation contract, ThrowingSection and CancellingSection (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/ExportUserDataHandlerBaseTests.cs:309 and :320).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: whether a given section's peer is reachable in a given environment is a deployment fact, not a source fact. The source settles only that an unreachable peer degrades one section.

    BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase<TCommand>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:41 · Level 4 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared start-two-factor-enrollment workflow: load the account's two-factor state, refuse if already enabled, resolve the account's display name, mint a fresh TOTP secret, and start the enrollment in the store in protected form (BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:41, :55-101).

    • Depends on: ITwoFactorService, ITwoFactorStore, ITwoFactorSecretProtector and an ILogger as primary-constructor parameters (:41-45); implements ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> closed over Result<TwoFactorSetupResponse> (:45). TCommand is constrained to IUserScopedRequest (:46), the narrowest of this family's command constraints: this workflow reads only the caller's id and carries no request payload. Its one audit line is a private source-generated [LoggerMessage] method, TwoFactorEnrollmentStarted (:115-116), which is why the class is declared partial (:41). Externals: Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.

    • Concept introduced: a fresh secret on every call, never a reuse. An interrupted enrollment must not leave a secret live that somebody who saw the first QR code could still key an authenticator with, so HandleAsync calls twoFactorService.GenerateSecret() unconditionally rather than resuming a prior attempt (:86, comment at :83-85).

      [Rubric §11: Security] assesses secret-material handling. The account is checked for an already-enabled factor before a new secret is even generated (:68-74); the store never receives the plaintext secret, only secretProtector.Protect(secret) (:88-90); and the response carries the plaintext secret plus a provisioning URI built by the service, never anything the handler constructs itself (:98-100). The class remarks state the rule: only the account owner gets the plaintext key, once, in the response.

    • Walkthrough: one virtual member, one method and one abstract hook.

      • HandlerName (:52): protected virtual, defaulting to GetType().Name, the same source-stamping pattern used by every other handler base in this family.
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:55-101): null-guards the command (:59); loads the two-factor state (:61), returning Error.NotFound when absent (:62-66); returns a Conflict (Authentication.TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled) when already enabled (:68-74); resolves the account label through the one abstract hook (:76), failing NotFound when it comes back blank (:77-81); generates the secret (:86); starts the enrollment in the store with the protected secret (:88-90), propagating its failure untouched (:91-94); logs TwoFactorEnrollmentStarted (:96); and returns the plaintext secret and provisioning URI (:98-100).
      • ResolveAccountNameAsync(UserIdentifierType, CancellationToken) (:111-113): protected abstract. The one app-specific step, because each app's User exposes its authenticator label (normally the email) differently.

    • Why it's built this way: enrollment, confirmation, disablement and recovery-code regeneration are four small, independently-testable steps rather than one wide handler, so each app subclass only ever forwards the app-specific lookups its use case actually needs. Each step owns its log message as a private [LoggerMessage] method, so the message text lives beside the only code that emits it. Protecting the secret in the base rather than in each app's store means no app store can persist it in plaintext by omission; the default protector is the data-protection one registered by AddTwoFactorAuthentication (see DependencyInjection).

    • Where it's used: covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs through a test subclass, and end to end with the real protector by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorSecretProtectionEndToEndTests.cs.

    • Caveats: the plaintext secret is returned to the caller in the response; it is up to the transport (HTTPS) and the client to keep it confidential in transit, nothing in this handler encrypts the response further.

    ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase<TCommand>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:39 · Level 4 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared confirm-enrollment workflow: refuse an account whose factor is already active, verify the caller's first TOTP code against the pending secret under a failed-attempt budget, generate a batch of recovery codes, and persist the completed enrollment (ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:39, :54-106).

    • Depends on: ITwoFactorService, ITwoFactorAuthenticator, ITwoFactorStore, ILoginProtectionService and an ILogger (:39-44); implements ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> over Result<TwoFactorRecoveryCodesResponse> (:44). TCommand is an IUserScopedCommand<out TRequest> carrying a TwoFactorCodeRequest (:45). Also uses TwoFactorErrors and TwoFactorAttemptKey (:75), and logs through a private source-generated [LoggerMessage] method, TwoFactorEnabled (:108-109), hence the partial declaration (:39).

    • Concept introduced: the pending secret has to still be there to confirm against, and a wrong code costs budget. The handler reads the state the Begin step wrote and fails with TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorEnrollmentMissing when there is no secret, treating an empty or zero-length secret the same as a missing one (:60-65, TwoFactorSecret is not { Length: > 0 } secret), so a confirm call that races an unstarted enrollment cannot verify against a blank value. A secret that is still stored on an already-active account is refused with an Authentication.TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled conflict (:67-73), because the secret stays stored after enrollment and a time-based code alone would otherwise mint a fresh recovery set (SECURITY M228, remarks at the type). The code is checked through ITwoFactorAuthenticator.VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync, so its time step is accepted once (:82-84); a wrong code increments the per-account counter (:87), the lockout is checked before verifying (:76-80), and success resets the counter (:91), the same way a wrong current password counts in the change-password workflow (ADR-029).

      [Rubric §11: Security] assesses brute-force resistance on secondary credentials. A stolen-token holder cannot enumerate six-digit codes through this endpoint without hitting the exponential lockout. [Rubric §1: SOLID] assesses open/closed. Verification and persistence (CompleteEnrollmentAsync) are delegated to collaborators, so the handler itself contains no cryptographic logic.

    • Walkthrough: one virtual member and one method.

      • HandlerName (:51).
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:54-106): null-guard (:58); load state and fail on a missing/empty secret (:60-65); refuse an already-enabled account (:67-73); derive the counter key (:75) and fail with the lockout errors if locked out (:76-80); verify the submitted code (:82-84), on failure increment the counter and return TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid (:85-89); reset the counter (:91); generate recovery codes (:93); complete the enrollment with their hashes (:95-101); log TwoFactorEnabled (:103); return the plaintext codes to the caller once, in the response (:105).

    • Why it's built this way: recovery codes are only ever returned at this one moment, on the response of the call that completes enrollment, because the store only ever persists their hashes (:95-98, the failure path at :99-101); the plaintext never touches the database.

    • Where it's used: BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase<TCommand> and this type are used together by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs through a shared test subclass.

    • Caveats: a failed VerifyCode does not clear the pending secret, so the caller can retry with a fresh code from the same authenticator entry without restarting enrollment.

    DisableTwoFactorHandlerBase<TCommand>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/DisableTwoFactorHandlerBase.cs:36 · Level 4 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared turn-off-two-factor workflow: check the per-account lockout, challenge the submitted code against the active factor, and disable it in the store only when the challenge succeeds (DisableTwoFactorHandlerBase.cs:36, :50-93).

    • Depends on: ITwoFactorAuthenticator, ITwoFactorStore, ILoginProtectionService and an ILogger (:36-40); implements ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> over Result (:40). TCommand is an IUserScopedCommand<out TRequest> carrying a TwoFactorCodeRequest (:41). Also uses TwoFactorErrors and TwoFactorAttemptKey (:54), and logs through a private source-generated [LoggerMessage] method, TwoFactorDisabled (:95-96), hence the partial declaration (:36).

    • Concept introduced: a distinguishable not-enrolled outcome, behind a lockout. ChallengeAsync returns a TwoFactorOutcome, and the handler treats NotEnrolled as a distinct failure (TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorNotEnrolled, :77-80, comment at :74-76) rather than an idempotent success: the caller just presented a code, and the code was never actually checked against anything, so the response says so rather than silently agreeing. Ahead of the challenge the handler consults the lockout for the account's counter key (:54-59); a challenge failure whose error code is TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalidCode increments the counter (:64-70), and a good challenge resets it (:82). That is the M228 hardening: a wrong code counts against the same budget as a wrong current password in the change-password workflow (ADR-029).

      [Rubric §11: Security] assesses whether the disable path itself is gated. Disabling two-factor cannot happen without a live code challenge, and a stolen-token holder cannot guess codes here without hitting the lockout, so an attacker who only has the session cookie (and not the authenticator) cannot turn protection off.

    • Walkthrough: one virtual member and one method.

      • HandlerName (:47).
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:50-93): null-guard (:52); derive the counter key and return the lockout failure when locked out (:54-59); challenge the code (:61-63), counting a wrong-code failure and returning the challenge errors (:64-72); the NotEnrolled outcome fails distinctly (:77-80); reset the counter (:82); DisableAsync (:84), returning its failure unchanged (:85-88); log TwoFactorDisabled (:90); return success (:92).

    • Why it's built this way: the challenge/store split mirrors the enrollment pair: ITwoFactorAuthenticator owns the live code check, ITwoFactorStore owns the persisted state, and this handler only sequences the two.

    • Where it's used: covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs.

    • Caveats: disabling does not clear previously issued recovery codes from the store on its own; that is ITwoFactorStore.DisableAsync's contract, not visible from this handler.

    RegenerateRecoveryCodesHandlerBase<TCommand>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/RegenerateRecoveryCodesHandlerBase.cs:36 · Level 4 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared regenerate-recovery-codes workflow: check the per-account lockout, challenge the submitted code, then replace the account's whole recovery-code set (RegenerateRecoveryCodesHandlerBase.cs:36, :51-98).

    • Depends on: ITwoFactorAuthenticator, ITwoFactorService, ITwoFactorStore, ILoginProtectionService and an ILogger (:36-41), the widest primary constructor of the four TwoFactor bases; implements ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> over Result<TwoFactorRecoveryCodesResponse> (:41). TCommand is an IUserScopedCommand<out TRequest> carrying a TwoFactorCodeRequest (:42). Uses TwoFactorAttemptKey (:57) and logs through a private source-generated [LoggerMessage] method, TwoFactorRecoveryCodesRegenerated (:100-101), hence the partial declaration (:36).

    • Concept introduced: regeneration replaces, it does not append, and it is not a code oracle. ReplaceRecoveryCodesAsync takes the freshly generated hash set and is expected to overwrite whatever codes existed before (:87-89), so a code from a batch the caller regenerated away is no longer valid, closing off an old code that may have leaked. A wrong code counts against the per-account budget (:67-72, M228, ADR-029), so the endpoint is not an unthrottled code oracle for a stolen-token holder.

      [Rubric §11: Security] assesses whether the regenerate path is itself gated the same way disable is: the lockout check (:57-62) and a live code challenge, with the same NotEnrolled distinct failure, have to succeed first (:64-81).

    • Walkthrough: one virtual member and one method.

      • HandlerName (:48).
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:51-98): null-guard (:55); derive the counter key and return the lockout failure when locked out (:57-62); challenge (:64-66), counting a wrong-code failure (:67-75); the NotEnrolled outcome fails distinctly (:77-81); reset the counter (:83); generate a new code batch (:85); replace them in the store (:87-89), propagating a failure untouched (:90-93); log TwoFactorRecoveryCodesRegenerated (:95); return the new plaintext codes (:97).

    • Why it's built this way: it shares the challenge-then-store shape with DisableTwoFactorHandlerBase<TCommand> and the generate-then-persist shape with ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase<TCommand>, because regeneration is genuinely the union of the two operations.

    • Where it's used: covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs.

    • Caveats: as with ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase<TCommand>, the plaintext codes are returned exactly once, in this response; the store keeps only their hashes.

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.ExportUserData · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/RefreshSessionUserDataExportSection.cs:66 · Level 5 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: one sign-in session as the data subject receives it in the export: when it was issued, when it expires or was revoked and why, and the client and device details recorded for it, with no token hash (RefreshSessionUserDataExportSection.cs:47-52, :66-79).

    • Concept: the export-side projection that keeps credentials material out of a portability document. It applies the [Pii] marking taught in the primer (ADR-005) the same way RefreshSession does, so a log redactor masks the client and device members (:50-51). [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy and Data Governance] assesses whether personal data is identified and handled deliberately: every member here is either a timestamp, the revocation reason, or a [Pii]-marked client or device field, and the token hash and the successor's token hash are simply not members (:19-20).

    • Walkthrough: a positional sealed record of thirteen members (:66-79): CreatedAt, ExpiresAt, nullable RevokedAt and RevocationReason, then nine nullable [Pii] strings (IpAddress, UserAgent, DeviceId, DeviceName, DeviceModel, DeviceManufacturer, DevicePlatform, DeviceFormFactor, DeviceType). The one member is the static factory From(RefreshSession) (:84-102), which null-guards its argument (:86) and copies the fields one for one, mapping the row's ReasonRevoked onto RevocationReason (:92).

    • Why it's built this way: a dedicated export shape, rather than serializing the stored row, makes "never a secret" structural: a field added to RefreshSession does not reach the data subject until someone adds it here.

    • Where it's used: produced only by RefreshSessionUserDataExportSection (RefreshSessionUserDataExportSection.cs:43); pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/RefreshSessionUserDataExportSectionTests.cs.

    • What it is: the framework's own data-subject export section: the account's sign-in sessions, published as the SignInSessions section of the export document, so the access and portability export covers the session metadata the framework itself stores (RefreshSessionUserDataExportSection.cs:7-11, :28, :31).

      • Name (:31): public const string "SignInSessions", returned by SectionName (:34).
      • ExportAsync(UserIdentifierType, CancellationToken) (:37-44): reads every session for the account through IRefreshSessionStore.GetAllByUserAsync (:41; the store contract returns them oldest first, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:58-59), projects each through UserSessionExportDTO.From, and returns UserDataExportSectionResult.Complete (:43).     • What it is: the shared data-subject export workflow (GDPR/CCPA access and portability). It authorizes the caller, loads the account read-only, asks the subclass for the app's own snapshot of that account, fans out best-effort over every registered IUserDataExportSection, and assembles one JSON-ready package the data subject can be handed.

    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork and, through it, IReadRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>; IUserDataExportSection (injected as an IEnumerable); IUserOwnedRequest (the TQuery constraint) and UserOwnershipRule; AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> (the TUser constraint); IQueryHandler<in TQuery, TResult> (the contract it implements); Result / Error; the Shared-layer DTOs UserDataExportDTO and UserDataExportSectionDTO (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Privacy/UserDataExportDTO.cs:15 and :61); and UserDataExportSectionDefaults. Externals: TimeProvider and ILogger (both injected through the primary constructor, ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:50-53), plus the [LoggerMessage] source generator from Microsoft.Extensions.Logging for its one private log method (:201-202).

    • Concept introduced, the template-method handler that owns the workflow and delegates only what is genuinely app-specific. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses deliberate pattern use: this is Template Method applied to a use case, with exactly three extension points (one abstract role check, one abstract projection, one virtual tail) and everything else fixed. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]: the two apps previously carried near-identical export handlers; hoisting the workflow left each subclass with the two decisions that actually differ. [Rubric §30, Compliance, Privacy and Data Governance]: the assembled document is PII by design, so its class doc states it must never be logged or cached, and notes that the caching query decorator is not applicable because the query implements no IQueryCacheable (ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:42-45). [Rubric §29, Resilience]: the fan-out degrades per section rather than failing, since a data-subject request carries a legal deadline (ADR-076). [Rubric §14, Testability]: because authorization arrives inside the query and time arrives as TimeProvider, the whole workflow is exercised with mocks and no host (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/ExportUserDataHandlerBaseTests.cs:17).

    • Walkthrough

      • Shape and constraints (ExportUserDataHandlerBase.cs:49-55): a primary-constructor abstract partial class (partial so the logging source generator can supply the body of its private log method) taking IUnitOfWork, IEnumerable<IUserDataExportSection>, TimeProvider, and ILogger, implementing IQueryHandler<TQuery, Result<UserDataExportDTO>>, with TUser : AuditableAggregateRootEntity<UserIdentifierType> and TQuery : IUserOwnedRequest.
      • CurrentFormatVersion = "1.0" (:61) is stamped into the envelope. Its doc is precise about scope (:57-60): it versions the envelope only, so an app changing its own subject or section payloads does not move it.
      • UnitOfWork is exposed protected (:64) purely so a subject-snapshot override can read further aggregates. HandlerName is virtual and defaults to GetType().Name (:71), so an app subclass named ExportUserDataHandler reports that name in the error payload (:67-70).
      • HandleAsync (:74-122). It null-guards the query (:78), then runs the ownership gate through UserOwnershipRule.CheckOwnership with HasExportPrivilege(query.CurrentUserRole) and the code "User.ExportForbidden" (:81-90), failing fast on rejection.
      • The read (:92-98): unitOfWork.GetReadRepository<TUser, UserIdentifierType>() then GetByIdAsync. The class doc calls this out as a deliberate change from the two pre-hoist app copies, which used the read-write repository: this is a query handler, it never saves, and a no-tracking read is the correct choice for a projection (:37-41). A missing account returns Error.NotFound.WithSource(HandlerName).WithTarget(typeof(TUser).Name) (:96-97).
      • The subject snapshot (:100): one await on the abstract BuildSubjectSnapshotAsync.
      • The fan-out (:102-108): a plain foreach over the injected sections, awaited one at a time. The comment states both reasons (:102-103): sections share the scoped unit of work and its DbContext, which is not thread-safe, and registration order is the published order of the document. This is the one place where the obvious "parallelize the I/O" instinct is wrong.
      • The envelope (:110-117): FormatVersion, GeneratedOn = timeProvider.GetUtcNow(), UserId, the subject, and the section envelopes.
      • The tail (:119): OnExportCompletedAsync, then Result.Success(export) (:121).
      • RunSectionAsync (:166-199) is the degradation boundary. It calls the section, copies the four result fields into a UserDataExportSectionDTO (:177-183), and catches with the filter when (ex is not OperationCanceledException) (:185), so cancellation is not degradation and propagates as cancellation. On any other exception it logs the full exception through its own private source-generated ExportSectionUnavailable (:190, declared at :201-202 at LogLevel.Warning with the template "Data-subject export section {Section} unavailable for user {UserId}; export continues with Available=false") and returns an envelope with Available = false and the generic UserDataExportSectionDefaults.UnavailableReason (:192-197): detail to the log, nothing internal to the subject.
      • The three extension points: HasExportPrivilege(string?) (abstract, :130), the role that bypasses ownership; BuildSubjectSnapshotAsync(TUser, TQuery, CancellationToken) (abstract, :144-147), which fields of the account are portable personal data, asynchronous and given the query because an app may need to read a second owned aggregate (:22-25); and OnExportCompletedAsync(...) (virtual, defaulting to Task.CompletedTask, :159-164), the app's tail for an access-log row or a metric, documented as not mutating the export and as owning its own failures because the export has already succeeded (:149-153).

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-076 records the decision, and the shape deliberately mirrors DeleteUserHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>: the same ownership gate through the same helper, the same privileged-role hook. The credential fields are excluded from the snapshot by contract (:132-136): a password hash and salt and an external-provider key are secrets, not portable personal data. Refresh-token material is not the subject snapshot's concern at all: sign-in sessions reach the export through the framework's own RefreshSessionUserDataExportSection, which projects every session without its token hash. The degraded-section log is Warning, not Error, on purpose: a degraded section is an expected, handled outcome of a best-effort fan-out and the request itself still succeeds (:201). Declaring that log method on the class itself keeps it next to the only call site, while the log category is whatever ILogger the app subclass passes to the primary constructor.

    • Where it's used: subclassed in each app's Identity Application assembly, where the convention scanner picks the concrete subclass up as an ordinary IQueryHandler with no extra registration (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.ModuleScanning.cs:111-115, and the point is spelled out in the export-section registration doc at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.Extensibility.cs:31-36). ADC's ExportUserDataHandler closes it over User and ExportUserDataQuery and overrides only the two abstract members (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/ExportUserDataHandler.cs:32, privilege = UserRole.IsOrganizer at :38, snapshot at :41); Store's does the same with its own User (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ExportUserData/ExportUserDataHandler.cs:34). Behaviour is pinned by ExportUserDataHandlerBaseTests, including a section that throws (.../ExportUserDataHandlerBaseTests.cs:138) and a section that cancels (:217).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the framework also ships an abstract [FeatureGate]-d endpoint, DataExportControllerBase<TQuery> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Privacy/DataExportControllerBase.cs:60-61), but neither app subclasses it: both kept their own export endpoints on top of this handler base, which the ADR records as an unadopted part of the decision.

    • Depends on: nearly every Infrastructure type below it, wired by interface. Persistence: DbContextFactory, PhysicalDbContextFactory, DataSourceService, DataSourceResolver, EntityDataSourceRegistry, FrameworkTableTargets, DefaultEntityConfigurationAssemblyProvider, EFQueryableExecutor, SqlServerUniqueConstraintViolationDetector, EFRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType>, RepositoryFactory, UnitOfWork, AuditSaveChangesInterceptor, DomainEventSaveChangesInterceptor, TenantSaveChangesInterceptor, INpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator, InternalCommandProcessor. Messaging/outbox: IMessageBus/InProcessMessageBus/BrokerMessageBus, IEventBus/InProcessEventBus/BrokerEventBus, OutboxSignal, OutboxProcessor, OutboxCleanupService, OutboxDisabledNoticeService, OutboxAdministration, EfInboxStore/NoOpInboxStore/InboxDisabledWarningService, IBrokerTransport with RabbitMqBrokerTransport/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport, BrokerTransportContext, MessageBusProviders. Cross-cutting: ICacheService with MemoryCacheService/HybridCacheService, CacheKeyNamespace, IDistributedLock with RedisDistributedLock/InProcessDistributedLock, IJwksProvider/RsaJwksProvider, TokenService, LoginProtectionService, PasswordResetTokenService, AuthSessionIssuer, UserSessionsAdministrationService, EFRefreshSessionStore with RefreshSessionCleanupService, TotpTwoFactorService, TwoFactorAuthenticator, EmailConfirmationTokenService, PermissionGrantModelGate, EFPermissionGrantStore, PermissionGrantCache, PermissionGrantRefreshService, StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService, LayeredPermissionRegistry, ClaimBasedUserIdProvider, EventUpcasterStartupValidator, StartupConfigurationSummaryService, CloudAdapterTripwire with CloudAdapterTripwireOptions, ScheduledJobRunner, IAuditTrailReader/AuditTrailReader, AuditTrailCleanupJob, TenantContext, CorrelationContext, NullPushNotificationSender/NullLiveChannelPublisher, NullNativePushSender, NullPushDeviceRegistrar, NullFileStorageService. Settings: ConnectionStringSettings with ConnectionStringSettingsValidator, DataSourcesSettings/DataSourceEntrySettings, MessageBusSettings, OutboxSettings, PersistenceSettings, SmtpSettings, JwksSettings, CacheSettings, QueryCachePipelineSettings, LoginProtectionSettings, PasswordResetSettings, RefreshSessionSettings, LegalAcceptanceOptions, SchedulerSettings, AuditTrailSettings, TenancySettings with TenancySettingsValidator, PushNotificationSettings. Externals: RabbitMQ.Client for the built-in RabbitMQ transport (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.csproj:49; there is no messaging library between the framework and the broker SDKs since MassTransit was removed in v1.316.0, ADR-118), StackExchange.Redis, Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid, Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR, Npgsql, Scrutor. No cloud vendor SDK: those live in the adapter packages (ADR-134).

    • Concept introduced, the mega-composition-root plus the swap-at-the-edge extraction pattern. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses whether wiring lives at the edge rather than in the core: every concrete Infrastructure choice is registered here, not in Application or Domain. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: the method bodies are the framework's default posture, and each optional capability (broker, scheduler, audit trail, tenancy, hybrid cache, push, the identity completions) is a separate opt-in method a host layers on, so the same package runs as a monolith or as an extracted service without recompiling the core. The default everywhere is TryAdd*, meaning a host can pre-register its own implementation and the framework will not clobber it; the places that deliberately break that rule are the broker swap (Replace, DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:119 and :125), AddCommonHybridCache (RemoveAll, DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:188), and AddPushNotifications, which appends the SignalR senders over their null defaults (DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:76-77) and Replaces SignalR's own IUserIdProvider (:67), and each says so in a comment. [Rubric §17, DevOps]: registering a capability is consistently NOT the same as enabling it: the scheduler and the audit trail both stay inert until their Enabled flag is true (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:31-33, :89-92), and the internal-command processor runs only under InternalCommands:Enabled (:174-183), so a host ships the registration and an environment turns it on. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]: the places where a misconfiguration would be silent instead throw or warn at startup, which is the running theme of this file.

    • Walkthrough (in registration order):

      • AddInfrastructure (DependencyInjection.cs:57-266) is the entry point. It registers the model-facing singletons (:59-60) and the three EF save interceptors as singletons because they are stateless with per-save state in a ConditionalWeakTable keyed by context (:62-70), including TenantSaveChangesInterceptor, which is registered unconditionally so a host can never leave the write-side tenancy guard half-wired (:67-70). It registers FrameworkTableTargets once (:96), the set of databases the framework table sweeps (outbox, internal commands, audit trail) visit, and binds SmtpSettings with validation (:98-101). The raw-SQL executor goes through the internal AddRawSqlQueryExecutor helper (:116), which registers IRawSqlQueryExecutor only when the default source is on a relational engine, so a Cosmos-default host fails at resolution rather than on its first statement (:416-426); it is scoped because it reaches the scope's own context through IDbContextFactory, sharing the caller's connection and any open transaction (:113-115). IConcurrencyConflictDetector/EfCoreConcurrencyConflictDetector is TryAddSingleton (:126), the sibling classifier to the unique-constraint detector for a save rejected by a moved concurrency token. Near the end it calls the private AddInternalCommands helper (:252, ADR-114), then AddServices() (:254), then decorates ICurrentUserService with ImpersonatingCurrentUserService via TryDecorate (:256-263), guarded on whether ScopedUserOverride is already registered so a host whose modules each call AddInfrastructure does not stack one decorator per call.
      • Settings binding, and the one rule annotations cannot express. ConnectionStringSettings binds through AddOptions(...).ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() (:72-75), then ConnectionStringSettingsValidator is added through TryAddEnumerable (:82-83) with the reason inline (:77-81): "a host must reach some database" spans the ConnectionStrings section AND the DataSources one, so a SQLite-only host declaring its databases as named sources is legitimate while a host declaring none anywhere is not. The same TryAddEnumerable idiom recurs for every validator and startup check in the file, so two modules calling AddInfrastructure never run one validation twice.
      • The named-data-sources note (:85-89) is load-bearing: DataSourcesSettings is built directly from configuration.GetSection(...).Get<Dictionary<string, DataSourceEntrySettings>>() rather than through AddOptions, because a root-level dictionary section does not bind through the options pipeline. The resolver and the eager entity registry follow immediately (:91-92).
      • The physical-factory warning (:103-109): DbContextFactory is scoped (one per request) and PhysicalDbContextFactory is a singleton that must never be converted to EF context pooling, because each raw context carries per-source constructor state that pooling would silently reuse across databases. Beside them sit the stateless query executor (:111) and the unique-constraint classifier (:118-121), the latter TryAdded so a host on another engine can register its own first and keep it.
      • The Scrutor scan (:132-138) discovers every IEntityTypeConfigurationBase<TEntity, TIdentifierType> in the Infrastructure assembly via FromAssemblyOf<ClassReference>() (:135) and registers each as its implemented interfaces, scoped to match the DbContext lifetime, closing the loop back to ClassReference. AddCaching(configuration) is called immediately after (:140), followed by the PersistenceSettings and OutboxSettings bindings (:144-152).
      • The auth block (:154-190) binds LoginProtectionSettings, PasswordResetSettings and RefreshSessionSettings with their scoped services, registers AuthSessionIssuer scoped (it issues, rotates and revokes the token pair, :174-176) and the administrator's read-only UserSessionsAdministrationService scoped (:178-180), and gates one hosted service: RefreshSessionCleanupService is registered only when RefreshSessions:Enabled is true (:186-190), on the same flag that maps the table. The comment names the failure it avoids (:182-185): an unconditional registration would start a periodic sweep (every CleanupIntervalHours, default 6) in every service of a modular host, all but one of which has no table to sweep. MessageBusSettings and JwksSettings with RsaJwksProvider follow (:192-201).
      • Three startup checks (:203-223), each added through TryAddEnumerable. EventUpcasterStartupValidator (:207-208) fails the host at start on a duplicate source, a self-map or a cycle rather than dead-lettering the first retired-contract message (ADR-090). StartupConfigurationSummaryService (:214-215) writes one Information line per host start naming the resolved posture (version, engines, bus, cache, tenancy) plus the RabbitMQ delayed-redelivery-off Warning (:210-213). CloudAdapterTripwire validates CloudAdapterTripwireOptions on start (:221-223): an enabled NativePush section whose sender still resolves to the inert core default means the vendor adapter call is missing, so the host fails naming the call instead of running with pushes dropped (:217-220).
      • The outbox is a transport decision (:225-250). OutboxSignal is always registered (:225). Then the message-bus section is read eagerly (:233-234), passed to the private EnsureOutboxAvailableForProvider guard (:235), and MessageBusSettings.IsOutboxEnabled decides between the two hosted outbox services (OutboxProcessor plus OutboxCleanupService, :237-241) and a single OutboxDisabledNoticeService (:244). The comment states the trade in full (:227-232): a broker deployment cannot deliver without the outbox, while a single-process host would pay two hosted services, a table and a poll loop for a hop it never takes, and the OutboxMessages table stays mapped either way so flipping the flag is never a migration (ADR-100). The operator surface OutboxAdministration is scoped, because it creates one child scope per data source it visits (:247-250).
      • AddInternalCommands (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:141-179) mirrors the outbox posture: it binds InternalCommandsSettings, registers the signal, the origin capture and IInternalCommandScheduler scoped on the caller's own context factory so scheduling is atomic with the aggregate change (:158-162), and the operator surface IInternalCommandAdministration (:164-167). Only InternalCommands:Enabled adds InternalCommandProcessor plus its cleanup service; otherwise a disabled-notice service (:174-183). The table is mapped unconditionally, so the flag never implies a migration (:135-138).
      • AddCaching (DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:30-126) does two probes in one method, and its IConfiguration parameter is optional. With configuration it binds the key-prefix options plus CacheSettings and the Application layer's QueryCachePipelineSettings (:44-57); without it, both are registered bare so IOptions<T> still resolves to framework defaults instead of failing a host that called the parameterless overload (:58-62, with the reasoning at :34-43). It post-configures RedisOutputCacheOptions.InstanceName to the same key namespace (CacheKeyNamespace.From(sp), :75) when the host left it empty, so two applications on one Redis do not share output-cache entries or tag sets (:64-77, ADR-135). The cache (:79-99): AddCaching registers only the in-process MemoryCacheService (:96-98), where the keyspace is private to the process so no prefix is needed. A shared distributed cache is served only by HybridCacheService, which AddCommonHybridCache registers in place of this one (:162-208), so if an IDistributedCache is registered and is not the no-op MemoryDistributedCache when this factory runs, it throws an InvalidOperationException naming AddCommonHybridCache rather than silently falling back to a per-replica cache (:86-93). The lock: RedisDistributedLock when a multiplexer resolves, keyed by the CacheKeyNamespace (:111-118), InProcessDistributedLock otherwise (:120-122). The comment explains why the lock is registered next to the cache at all (:101-108): all five in-framework callers pair the two (the API idempotency filter, password-reset token redemption, the two-factor authenticator's last-accepted time step, OAuthControllerBase's read-and-burn of a single-use exchange code, and PasskeyChallenges' challenge redemption and passkey deletes).
      • AddCommonHybridCache (DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:162-208) is the opt-in two-level cache (ADR-077). It calls AddHybridCache (:160), then configures HybridCacheOptions through the options pipeline rather than the AddHybridCache callback (:166-180), because the TTL policy comes from the bound Cache section and the callback has no service provider to read it from (:162-165); the host's own hook runs last so it can override anything the framework set (:179). It then deliberately does RemoveAll<ICacheService>() before AddSingleton (:184-198) so the call wins whether it runs before or after AddInfrastructure. The remarks are honest about the cost of that choice (:147-151): RemoveAll does not distinguish the framework's registration from a host's own custom ICacheService, so calling this is a statement that the two-level cache IS the cache. AddCommonHybridCacheWhenRedisConfigured (:219-231) is the guarded form: it calls AddCommonHybridCache only when the named Redis connection string (default redis) is set (:225-228), since with no L2 the hybrid tier degrades to what MemoryCacheService already provides (:208-214).
      • AddScheduledJobs (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:36-50) and AddScheduledJob<TJob> (:72-78) wire the recurring-job feature (ADR-074). The first binds SchedulerSettings with validation (:39-42) and registers ScheduledJobRunner via TryAddEnumerable rather than AddHostedService (:44-48), so a host or two modules calling it twice cannot run two runners racing for the same rows. The second registers one job scoped, both as the concrete type and into the accumulating IEnumerable<IScheduledJob> (:75-76); the doc spells out that the job is scoped because the runner resolves it in a fresh scope per execution and it must hold no state between runs (:66-70).
      • AddAuditTrail (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:107-126) binds AuditTrailSettings (:110-113), registers the trail interceptor as a singleton for the same statelessness reason as the other save interceptors (:115-117), the scoped reader (:119), and, notably, AddScheduledJob<AuditTrailCleanupJob>() (:124). Registering the retention job here rather than in AddScheduledJobs keeps the two features independent, and the remarks state the operational consequence plainly (:97-101): without the scheduler the trail still records every change and nothing is ever purged, so AuditTrail:RetentionDays is inert.
      • AddMultiTenancy (DependencyInjection.cs:297-309) binds TenancySettings and adds TenancySettingsValidator through TryAddEnumerable (:305-306). What it switches on is resolution, not isolation: the filter, the interceptor and ITenantContext are always present and inert until a tenant resolves (:276-280), and a Tenancy:Tenants:{id}:DataSources:{sourceName} override naming a source that does not exist fails startup rather than silently falling back to the shared database (:289-294).
      • The five opt-in identity completions (ADR-116), in DependencyInjection.Auth.cs. AddTwoFactorAuthentication(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:47-66) binds TwoFactorSettings and registers ITwoFactorService/TotpTwoFactorService singleton (pure over its arguments, :54-55), ITwoFactorSecretProtector/DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector singleton plus AddDataProtection(), so the shared secret reaches the app's store only in protected form and a multi-replica host needs the shared key ring (:57-60), and ITwoFactorAuthenticator/TwoFactorAuthenticator scoped (shares the request's unit of work, :62-63). It registers no ITwoFactorStore deliberately, because the account's secret and recovery hashes belong to the consumer's own User aggregate (:31-34). Calling it together with registering the app's store arms the sign-in challenge: provided the app registers AuthenticationValidators by type, the container builds it with the registered authenticator and AuthenticationServiceBase uses it whenever its own twoFactor argument is null, with no change to the app's AuthenticationService constructor; once called, the store is required, and a host that wants enrollment without the challenge overrides ChallengeSecondFactorAsync (:37-44). AddEmailConfirmation(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:80-95) binds EmailConfirmationSettings and registers IEmailConfirmationTokenService/EmailConfirmationTokenService scoped (:88), plus TimeProvider.System through TryAddSingleton (:92), because the token service stamps expiries from the injected clock: AddServices registers the same clock (DependencyInjection.cs:368), and the TryAdd keeps this call self-sufficient without displacing a host's own TimeProvider; an unconfirmed account is refused only once RequireConfirmedEmail is set AND the app's User implements IEmailConfirmableUser (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:75-78). AddSignInLinks(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:107-119) binds SignInLinkSettings with validation (:109-112) and registers ISignInLinkTokenService/SignInLinkTokenService scoped plus TimeProvider.System through TryAddSingleton (:115-116); it issues nothing on its own, since links are sent and redeemed only once the app wires the handler bases and a controller AND Authentication:SignInLinks:Enabled is set (:103-106). AddLegalAcceptance(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:140-149) binds LegalAcceptanceOptions from the Legal section and nothing else: it registers no ILegalAcceptanceService, because the accepted version and instant belong to the app's own User aggregate, so the consumer supplies that implementation plus a controller deriving from LegalAcceptanceControllerBase. It deliberately omits ValidateOnStart, unlike its siblings, since the single Legal:CurrentTermsVersion setting has no invalid value (:142-144). The options reach registration through AuthenticationValidators as an optional constructor argument, so with the setting unset the call changes nothing. AddStoredPermissionGrants(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:175-219) binds PermissionGrantSettings (:177-180); registers the PermissionGrantModelGate singleton (:183), whose presence is what tells ApplicationDbContext to map the grant table for the one data source named by Authentication:PermissionGrants:DataSourceName; the scoped EFPermissionGrantStore (:185); one PermissionGrantCache singleton that answers as both IPermissionGrantCache and IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator, so an edit and the reads that follow it cannot see two different snapshots (:187-193); IRoleAdministrationService/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService (:195); and the PermissionGrantRefreshService hosted service through TryAddEnumerable, so two modules calling it never start two refresh loops (:197-200). It then decorates whatever IPermissionRegistry is registered with LayeredPermissionRegistry via TryDecorate (:205), so it belongs AFTER AddAuthorizationPolicies(); when TryDecorate finds nothing it registers a layered registry over an empty compiled one and offers that same empty instance as IPermissionCatalog, so the stored layer and the administration surface still work standalone (:202-216).
      • AddServices (DependencyInjection.cs:315-364) registers the small services and encodes a subtle lifetime lesson: TokenService is a singleton (:334) with a six-line comment explaining why (:328-333): a scoped lifetime disposed the RSA handle at end-of-request while IdentityModel's static CryptoProviderCache still held the cached signature provider wrapping it, throwing ObjectDisposedException on the next RS256 sign. [Rubric §11, Security] (correct signing-key lifecycle). It also sets the default IEventBus to InProcessEventBus (:336) and the default IMessageBus to InProcessMessageBus (:342), registers ITenantContext unconditionally with the reasoning inline (:321-325), registers TimeProvider.System and SmtpEmailSender (:344-345), and wires the inert no-op defaults for push and the live channel (:346-347), native push (ADR-044, NullNativePushSender and NullPushDeviceRegistrar, :349-354) and file storage (ADR-045, NullFileStorageService, :356-361). The comments name the vendor adapter calls that swap those defaults (Azure, AWS and GCP packages) and state that image normalization is the application's own concern, because decoding needs a native image library every consumer would otherwise carry (:356-360).
      • AddPushNotifications (DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:41-89) binds the settings (:40-43), adds SignalR (:45), adds the Redis backplane only when a redis connection string exists (:47-59) with ChannelPrefix set to the resolved ApplicationNamespace (:56-58), because the channel derives from a hub type every consumer shares, so without it one application's pushes reached another's clients (SEC-Common-53, :50-55). It appends the SignalR senders over the null defaults (:62-63) and Replaces SignalR's DefaultUserIdProvider with ClaimBasedUserIdProvider (:67), since a TryAdd there never took effect and a principal carrying only the raw sub claim got a null UserIdentifier (:64-66).
      • AddBrokerMessaging (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:63-161) is the extraction pivot. It reads MessageBusSettings, falling back to new MessageBusSettings() when the section is absent (:69-70); on InProcess it returns immediately (:72-75), leaving the in-process bus in place; otherwise it re-runs the outbox guard (:80, with the comment at :77-79: a service host that wires the broker without the full infrastructure registration must still fail loudly) and resolves the IBrokerTransport before anything is registered, so an unregistered provider fails without leaving a half-registered broker behind (:82-84). It then requires Application:Namespace (:86-89, SEC-Common-53): every topic is prefixed with the resolved ApplicationNamespace, so two applications on one broker never publish onto each other's topics, and the value must be explicit because the fallback (the host's own application name) differs per service, which would put publishers and consumers on different topics. The host's consumer callback runs against a BrokerConsumerBuilder (:90-92), where each service calls RegisterIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>() (or RegisterUpcastedIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>() for a retired contract) per event it handles (:54-57), and the result becomes one BrokerTopology singleton: one queue (MessageBus:QueueName or the application name) with one subscription per consumed event (:94-99, described at :41-46). It registers one scoped consumer per subscription, resolved by the receive pipeline from a fresh scope per attempt (:101-106), and the singleton IBrokerReceivePipeline as BrokerReceivePipeline, handed the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay (:108-115). It then Replaces the scoped IMessageBus with BrokerMessageBus (:119) and IEventBus with BrokerEventBus (:125), the deliberate exception to the TryAdd rule, because the in-process bus must not run alongside the broker (ADR-066, ADR-118). Last, after the inbox branch below, it calls transport.Register with a BrokerTransportContext carrying the settings, the resolved connection string, the configuration and the topology (:150-158), so the transport sees every framework registration and adds only its IBrokerPublisher and its hosted receiver (:41-46), and a transport configuration error throws at startup. PostgreSqlBrokerTransport registers its schema migrator inside that Register call, ahead of its receiver, because hosted services start in registration order (Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:75-79).
      • The inbox branch (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:132-148) chooses the consumer-side dedup store from settings.IsInboxEnabled, the resolved posture rather than the raw flag (unset means ON for a broker, :127-131): EfInboxStore scoped when on (:134, with TimeProvider.System TryAdded for its ProcessedOn stamp, :138), and when off the singleton NoOpInboxStore (:142) plus an InboxDisabledWarningService hosted service (:147). That second registration is the whole point of the branch: a disabled dedup store looks exactly like an enabled one until a duplicate side effect reaches a customer, so the posture costs one startup Warning to make visible (:144-146).
      • AddBrokerTransport (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:174-186) is how an adapter package (or a host with a transport of its own) makes a provider name selectable: it rejects an empty Name (:178-181) and adds the instance through TryAddEnumerable (:183), so registering the same adapter twice is harmless, and when two transports share a name the last one registered wins. It must run BEFORE AddBrokerMessaging, which picks the transport while registering the broker services (:163-170).
      • The four private helpers (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:189-302) sit outside the extension block. ResolveBrokerTransport (:199-232) returns the built-in RabbitMqBrokerTransport or PostgreSqlBrokerTransport for those names (:201-209), else the LAST adapter transport registered under the name, read straight off the collection because no provider exists yet (:211-221); with no match it throws naming the adapter package and its registration call when MessageBusProviders knows one, and the available providers (:223-231). EnsureOutboxAvailableForProvider (:248-255) throws when a broker transport is paired with an explicitly disabled outbox, and the message says why in operational terms: the outbox is the only publish path a broker deployment has, so the alternative is every cross-service event vanishing while the service looks healthy. EnsureApplicationNamespaceConfigured (:270-281) throws when Application:Namespace is missing or blank, and its message carries the fix (the same value on every service, with an appsettings.json and an environment-variable example). ResolveBrokerConnectionString (:293-302) applies an explicit precedence: MessageBus:ConnectionString, then ConnectionStrings:rabbitmq (what Aspire injects), then ConnectionStrings:messaging; without that fallback a transport would keep its own default host (RabbitMQ's localhost:5672) and never reach the Aspire-allocated container port (:283-292).
      • Retry, redelivery and dead-lettering live in one receive pipeline; the transports only apply its verdict. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]: BrokerReceivePipeline.ProcessAsync (Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:82) dead-letters a message that cannot be read as its event type without retrying it (:115-144), runs the consumer up to RetryLimit + 1 times, each attempt in a fresh scope, waiting BrokerTransportPolicies.RetryDelay between attempts (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:180-197, Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:27), then returns a Redeliver disposition on the next second-level interval (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:165-166), the intervals coming from BuildRedeliveryIntervals clamped to the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:72, BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:65), and a DeadLetter once they are spent (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:170-176). Backpressure is the one policy each transport applies itself, from ResolvePrefetchCount (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:85) and ResolveConcurrentMessageLimit (:98); RabbitMQ defaults the concurrency to the processor count and the prefetch to twice the concurrency (Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:95, :104-105). The Azure Service Bus transport lives in the MMCA.Common.Azure adapter package (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Azure/Messaging/AzureServiceBusTransport.cs:37) and Amazon SQS in MMCA.Common.Aws (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aws/Messaging/AmazonSqsTransport.cs:40), the one transport with a redelivery cap (15 minutes, :65).
      • AddNpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator (DependencyInjection.Persistence.cs:24-37) registers an INpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator through TryAddEnumerable (:28) and a keyed NpgsqlDataSource singleton per distinct connection string (:32-34), so the PostgreSQL contexts and the readiness check share one data source; adapter packages call it from their own registration method (for example AddAwsRdsIamAuthentication), and it is order-independent relative to AddInfrastructure (:12-20).

    • Why it's built this way: the extension(IServiceCollection) syntax keeps every Infrastructure registration on one type without a proliferation of static helper classes (ADR-106), and pushing all concrete choices into one composition root at the layer edge is what keeps Application and Domain free of framework references (ADR-006 for the database-per-service wiring, ADR-007/ADR-008 for the broker/extraction path). Vendor-specific transports, push senders and storage are registered by the adapter packages against the extension points here (AddBrokerTransport, AddNpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator, the Null* defaults), which keeps the core free of any cloud SDK (ADR-134). See the DI-sequence note in MMCA.Common/AGENTS.md: hosts call AddApplicationDecorators() last so Scrutor can decorate handlers already registered, but the relative position of AddInfrastructure is not otherwise ordering-sensitive, and AddCommonHybridCache is explicitly documented as order-independent in both directions (DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:142-148).

    • Where it's used: called from each service host's Program.cs (the reference apps and the extracted MMCA.ADC.* service hosts) after AddApplication(); the optional methods (AddScheduledJobs, AddAuditTrail, AddMultiTenancy, AddCommonHybridCache or AddCommonHybridCacheWhenRedisConfigured, AddBrokerMessaging, AddPushNotifications, the identity completions) are added by the specific hosts that need those capabilities. AddScheduledJobsTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/AddScheduledJobsTests.cs:15) pins the double-registration behavior of the scheduler pair.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the exact set of consuming Program.cs files is in the downstream apps (MMCA.ADC / MMCA.Store / MMCA.Helpdesk), not in this repository, so the precise call sites are Not determinable from source here.

    BrokerMetrics

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/BrokerMetrics.cs:18 · Level 0 · class (internal, static)

    • What it is: the OpenTelemetry instrument set for the broker transport. One meter carrying two counters: integration events the receive pipeline dead-lettered after every retry and redelivery failed, and outbox publishes the circuit breaker refused to even attempt (BrokerMetrics.cs:5-11).

    • Depends on: System.Diagnostics.Metrics (BCL) only (BrokerMetrics.cs:1). Nothing first-party. It is the exact same shape as SchedulerMetrics, for a different feature.

    • Concept: the one-meter-per-feature instrument holder, taught under SchedulerMetrics. What is worth teaching here is which two numbers were chosen. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether a running system can be understood from outside: broker delivery is asynchronous and out of band, so a consumer that keeps failing produces no failed HTTP response anywhere, and the only evidence is a message quietly landing in the dead-letter location. broker.fault.count is therefore the natural alert target for consumer health (BrokerMetrics.cs:25-29). The second counter exists because the class doc insists on a distinction an operator would otherwise have to infer: a publish rejected by an open circuit never reached the broker at all (BrokerMetrics.cs:35-41), which is different from a publish that reached it and failed. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]: those rejected rows stay leased and are retried on a later cycle, so the counter measures fail-fast behavior working as designed rather than data loss.

    • Walkthrough:

      • MeterName = "MMCA.Common.Broker" (BrokerMetrics.cs:21) and the single static Meter built from it (:23). The doc carries the same never-create-a-second-meter warning as the scheduler (BrokerMetrics.cs:13-15), with the failure mode spelled out: a duplicate instance publishes a parallel set of instruments under one name, and a listener enabling one silently misses the measurements recorded on the other.
      • FaultCounter (BrokerMetrics.cs:30-33), broker.fault.count, unit messages, tagged by event_type and queue.
      • CircuitOpenCounter (:42-45), broker.circuit.open.count, same unit, tagged by event_type only.

    • Why it's built this way: internal static readonly instruments created once at type initialization means the recording sites resolve nothing from DI. The meter name is duplicated as a literal in MMCA.Common.Aspire (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aspire/Extensions.Telemetry.cs:314) because that package has no reference to Infrastructure, and the doc records that duplication rather than letting the next reader discover it (BrokerMetrics.cs:8-11). The instruments only move in a host that runs a broker transport, since the in-process bus has no receive pipeline and no broker publish path.

    • Where it's used: BrokerReceivePipeline adds to FaultCounter in AfterRetriesExhausted, once the last second-level redelivery is spent, right after its one Error log, tagging the event type and the host's queue name (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:169-174). OutboxProcessor adds to CircuitOpenCounter on its publish path (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Outbox/Processing/OutboxProcessor.cs:669), where an earlier comment notes that the per-row signal stays on the metric while the log line is per cycle (OutboxProcessor.cs:540).

    [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] applies: this type sits on the path a message takes once it leaves the process (outbox, bus, consumer, or broker plumbing), which is what section 10 scores.

    BrokerWire

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/BrokerWire.cs:12 · Level 0 · class (internal, static)

    • What it is: the handful of wire-format facts the publish side (BrokerMessageBus) and the receive side (BrokerReceivePipeline) must agree on: the JSON options the message body is written and read with, and the trace source both hops report on (BrokerWire.cs:7-11).
