    • Concept introduced: one definition of a contract both ends of a hop share. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] assesses whether a message survives the trip between processes unchanged. A publisher and a consumer that each build their own serializer options can drift apart one setting at a time and only disagree in production, so both ends read the one static instance here. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: the broker hop is where a distributed trace most often breaks, so publish and delivery report on one named source and are parented across the broker through the W3C traceparent header (BrokerWire.cs:14-19).

    • Walkthrough:

      • ActivitySourceName = "MMCA.Common.Messaging" (BrokerWire.cs:19): one Producer span per publish and one Consumer span per delivery (:14-18).
      • MessagingSystem = "mmca" (BrokerWire.cs:22): the messaging.system tag value stamped on both spans.
      • ActivitySource (BrokerWire.cs:25): the single shared source built from the name.
      • JsonOptions (BrokerWire.cs:34-37): ReferenceHandler.IgnoreCycles and otherwise the System.Text.Json defaults, identical to the options OutboxMessage serializes its payload with, so an event that round-trips through the outbox round-trips through the broker in exactly the same shape (:27-33).

    • Why it's built this way: the options are a copy, not a shared reference, because the outbox's instance is private to the persistence layer (BrokerWire.cs:31-33). The source name is a literal that MMCA.Common.Aspire subscribes by name, because that package has no reference to Infrastructure (BrokerWire.cs:16-17, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aspire/Extensions.Telemetry.cs:84).

    • Where it's used: BrokerMessageBus starts the Producer span, stamps messaging.system and serializes the body with JsonOptions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/BrokerMessageBus.cs:70, :73, :83); BrokerReceivePipeline deserializes with the same options and starts the Consumer span named after the host's queue (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:132, :257, :260).

    [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] applies: this type sits on the path a message takes once it leaves the process (outbox, bus, consumer, or broker plumbing), which is what section 10 scores.

    ExceptionChain

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Diagnostics · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Diagnostics/ExceptionChain.cs:25 · Level 0 · class (internal, static)

    • What it is: a one-line renderer for an exception and its causes, used for a background job's LastError column, its log text and its span status (ExceptionChain.cs:5-8).

    • Depends on: BCL only (StringBuilder from System.Text, Stack<T>, AggregateException) (ExceptionChain.cs:1).

    • Concept introduced: record the cause, not the wrapper. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether a failure can be diagnosed from what the system recorded. Wrapper exceptions hide the cause: SmtpException says only "Failure sending mail." while the server's reply sits on InnerException, and recording the outer message alone left 21 dead-lettered attempts in Store production (2026-11-01) with nothing to diagnose (ExceptionChain.cs:11-14). The answer is to walk the chain, not to store stack traces: the column and the span status are read by people, and the processors that need a stack log the exception object itself (:20-22).

    • Walkthrough:

      • MaxLevels = 8 (ExceptionChain.cs:28): the most levels, the outer exception included, one description renders. Separator is " ---> " (:30).
      • Describe(exception) (ExceptionChain.cs:35-63) starts with the outer message, then walks the causes depth first through an explicit stack (:45-46) until it is empty or MaxLevels is reached (:48). Each cause is appended as " ---> {Type}: {Message}", except one repeating the previous message, which adds nothing and is skipped (:53-57). An exception with no cause renders as its bare message.
      • PushCauses (ExceptionChain.cs:65-78) pushes every inner exception of an AggregateException in reverse, so the first one is rendered first (:67-73), and otherwise the single InnerException (:74-77).

    • Why it's built this way: an explicit stack rather than recursion keeps the walk ordered for aggregates nested inside aggregates, and the level cap keeps one pathological chain from flooding a column; callers still fit the result to their column width (ExceptionChain.cs:17-22).

    • Where it's used: OutboxProcessor for a failed row's error (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Outbox/Processing/OutboxProcessor.cs:647), InternalCommandProcessor for a command that threw (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/InternalCommands/Processing/InternalCommandProcessor.cs:500), and ScheduledJobRunner for a failed job run (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobRunner.cs:654). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Diagnostics/ExceptionChainTests.cs.

    InProcessLockHandle

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Concurrency · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Concurrency/InProcessDistributedLock.cs:79 · Level 0 · class (private nested, sealed)

    • What it is: the disposable release token that InProcessDistributedLock hands back on a successful acquire. Disposing it removes exactly the key that acquisition added, exactly once.

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. BCL only: the owner's ConcurrentDictionary<string, byte> and the key are passed into its primary constructor; Interlocked provides the once-only latch, IAsyncDisposable/ValueTask the shape.

    • Concept introduced, the acquisition handle as a scope token. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses whether recurring problems use recognised patterns deliberately; returning a disposable instead of exposing a Release(key) method is the scope-bound-resource shape the IDistributedLock contract mandates, and it is what lets await using release the lock even when the guarded work throws. The token is also what makes release owner-scoped: the handle closes over the key it added, so it cannot free anybody else's acquisition.

    • Walkthrough: the primary constructor takes the owner's held dictionary and the key (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:79); a single int _released field (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:81) is the latch. DisposeAsync (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:83-91) runs Interlocked.Exchange(ref _released, 1) == 0 and only then calls held.TryRemove(key, out _) (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:85-88), so a second disposal is a no-op and the contract's "disposal is idempotent" clause holds. It returns ValueTask.CompletedTask (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:90) because removing a key from a ConcurrentDictionary is synchronous, so there is no state machine to allocate.

    • Why it's built this way: an interlocked latch rather than a plain bool because a handle can be disposed from more than one thread (an await using unwind plus an explicit dispose), and the removal has to happen exactly once, or a late second dispose would evict a key a different caller has since acquired.

    • Where it's used: constructed by InProcessDistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:63) and returned as the contract's IAsyncDisposable?; the API IdempotencyFilter is the caller that disposes it.

    RedisLockHandle

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Concurrency · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Concurrency/RedisDistributedLock.cs:91 · Level 0 · class (private nested, sealed)

    • What it is: the release token for a RedisDistributedLock acquisition. Disposing it runs a compare-and-delete Lua script that removes the Redis key only while it still carries this acquisition's token.

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Externals: StackExchange.Redis (IDatabase, RedisKey, RedisValue, RedisResult) and Microsoft.Extensions.Logging; Interlocked for the latch. Same handle shape as InProcessLockHandle, with real asynchronous work in the release.

    • Concept: the owner-token release, the half of the SET NX PX lock that keeps it honest (the acquire half is taught under RedisDistributedLock). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether a system reports its own degradation: a release that finds nothing to delete is exactly the case where the guarded section outran its time-to-live and stopped being exclusive, so the handle logs a warning naming the key rather than swallowing it. The same applies when the release itself fails: it is best-effort by the IDistributedLock contract, so the fault is logged as a warning and the holder's already-completed work is not turned into a failure.

    • Walkthrough: the primary constructor captures the IDatabase, the already-qualified RedisKey, this acquisition's RedisValue token, and a logger (RedisDistributedLock.cs:91-95), with the same int _released latch (RedisDistributedLock.cs:97). DisposeAsync (RedisDistributedLock.cs:99-130) returns immediately when the latch was already set (RedisDistributedLock.cs:101-104); otherwise it evaluates ReleaseScript with that key and token inside a try (RedisDistributedLock.cs:111-115). The script is if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end (RedisDistributedLock.cs:36-37), one round trip that compares and deletes atomically on the server. A 0 result means the key was already gone or is owned by someone else now, so there is nothing to release and LogLockAlreadyExpired warns (RedisDistributedLock.cs:117-122, message text at RedisDistributedLock.cs:84). Any exception from the release (a Redis fault or timeout) is caught by a deliberate broad catch (Exception) under a justified CA1031 suppression (RedisDistributedLock.cs:124-129) and logged through LogLockReleaseFailed (RedisDistributedLock.cs:87-88) instead of propagating, because the release runs after the guarded work has already committed and the lock expires on its own time-to-live (RedisDistributedLock.cs:106-110). The code comment notes RedisTimeoutException is not a RedisException, hence the broad catch.

    • Why it's built this way: a plain DEL would let a caller whose lock had already expired free the next holder's lock, which is precisely the double execution the lock exists to prevent (RedisDistributedLock.cs:32-34). Doing the comparison inside a Lua script makes compare-and-delete atomic server-side instead of a racy get-then-delete from the client (ADR-017).

    • Where it's used: constructed by RedisDistributedLock.TryAcquireAsync (RedisDistributedLock.cs:72). RedisDistributedLockTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Concurrency/RedisDistributedLockTests.cs:15) asserts the acquire/release pairing against a mocked IDatabase, including the qualified key the handle deletes.

    InProcessDistributedLock

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Concurrency · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Concurrency/InProcessDistributedLock.cs:31 · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed, partial)

    • What it is: the fallback IDistributedLock for a host with no Redis connection registered. It serializes callers inside this one process, and it says so in the log the first time anybody uses it.

    • Depends on: IDistributedLock (the contract it implements, from MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces, imported at InProcessDistributedLock.cs:4), ILogger<InProcessDistributedLock> injected through the primary constructor (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:31), and its own nested InProcessLockHandle. BCL: ConcurrentDictionary, Interlocked, Stopwatch, Task.Delay.

    • Concept introduced, the degraded implementation that announces itself. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether the design survives horizontal scale-out: each replica gets its own instance of this class and therefore its own held-key table, so with more than one replica a section guarded by this lock still runs once per replica (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:11-15). That is correct for a single-replica deployment, for local development, and for tests, and wrong for anything else, which is why the fallback is not silent. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether an operator can see a degraded mode: the first acquisition emits a [LoggerMessage]-generated warning that names both the cause and the fix (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:75-76, "no IConnectionMultiplexer is registered ... Register a Redis client (AddRedisClient) to make it exclusive across replicas").

    • Walkthrough:

      • State. PollInterval is 25 ms (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:34), the gap between acquisition attempts while waiting for a holder. _held is a ConcurrentDictionary<string, byte> with StringComparer.Ordinal (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:36), used as a set: the value byte is a placeholder and only key presence matters. _degradationWarned is the warn-once flag (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:39).
      • Guards and the warning. TryAcquireAsync (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:42-73) rejects a blank key, a non-positive ttl, and a negative wait (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:48-50), then flips the flag with Interlocked.Exchange(ref _degradationWarned, 1) == 0 so a steady state warns once rather than per request (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:52-55).
      • The acquire loop (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:59-72). _held.TryAdd(key, 0) is the atomic test-and-set: it succeeds only for the caller that inserts the key, and that caller gets an InProcessLockHandle (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:61-63). Otherwise, if Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(startedAt) >= wait the method returns null (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:66-69), which is what makes wait: TimeSpan.Zero a single non-blocking attempt exactly as the contract promises. Otherwise it awaits Task.Delay(PollInterval, cancellationToken) and retries (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:71).
      • Exact keys, not stripes. The remarks explain the one design choice that differs from KeyedSemaphoreStripe (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:18-25): stripes let two unrelated keys share a semaphore, which is harmless for a caller that waits indefinitely but not for a bounded wait, where the false sharing turns into a spurious "held elsewhere" answer for a key nobody holds. The table stays bounded by the number of locks held right now, not by every key the process has ever seen, because the handle removes the entry on release.
      • ttl is accepted and ignored (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:26-29). It is validated (InProcessDistributedLock.cs:49) but never used: the TTL exists to bound a holder that died without releasing, and here the holder is a task in this process, so if the process dies the table dies with it.

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-017 makes the lock a registration rather than an optional dependency, so a host always resolves something; this type is the honest floor of that guarantee. Logging the degradation once, instead of silently behaving like a lock, is what keeps "we have a distributed lock" from becoming a false belief in a multi-replica deployment.

    • Where it's used: registered by AddCaching in the Infrastructure composition root when no IConnectionMultiplexer is resolvable (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:120-122, inside the IDistributedLock factory at :84-98; see DependencyInjection), which covers MMCA.Helpdesk, local single-process runs, and tests. Behavior is pinned by InProcessDistributedLockTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Concurrency/InProcessDistributedLockTests.cs:12).

    RedisDistributedLock

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Concurrency · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Concurrency/RedisDistributedLock.cs:24 · Level 2 · class (internal, sealed, partial)

    • What it is: the cross-replica IDistributedLock, implemented as the standard SET key token NX PX ttl Redis lock against a single Redis instance.

    • Depends on: IConnectionMultiplexer and the rest of StackExchange.Redis (IDatabase, RedisKey, RedisValue, RedisResult), ILogger<RedisDistributedLock>, and an optional CacheKeyNamespace (RedisDistributedLock.cs:24-27), which is what puts this type at Level 2 rather than Level 1. It returns its nested RedisLockHandle.

    • Concept: the acquire half of the lock taught in two pieces with RedisLockHandle. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses scale-out correctness: moving the lock into Redis is what makes "only one of these runs at a time" true across replicas instead of true per process, which is the whole reason the abstraction exists (see InProcessDistributedLock for the degraded alternative). [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses failure behavior: the expiry carried on the SET is the crash guard (a holder that dies releases by expiry rather than wedging the key forever, RedisDistributedLock.cs:12-17), and the class documents that it is deliberately single-instance, not Redlock (RedisDistributedLock.cs:19-23), inheriting Redis's failover behavior, which is exactly why the contract is documented as best-effort. The release side honors the same posture: a fault while releasing is caught and logged by the handle (RedisDistributedLock.cs:124-129, see RedisLockHandle) rather than failing the already-committed guarded work.

    • Walkthrough:

      • State. KeyPrefix is "lock:" (RedisDistributedLock.cs:30) so lock entries cannot collide with cache entries in a shared instance. ReleaseScript (RedisDistributedLock.cs:36-37) is the compare-and-delete Lua taught under RedisLockHandle. PollInterval is 50 ms (RedisDistributedLock.cs:40); unlike the in-process poll, each retry here is a network round trip. _keys falls back to CacheKeyNamespace.None when no namespace was injected (RedisDistributedLock.cs:42), so the Cache:KeyPrefix option (when configured) qualifies lock keys the same way it qualifies cache keys.
      • Argument guards. TryAcquireAsync (RedisDistributedLock.cs:45-82) applies the same three checks as the in-process implementation: non-blank key, ttl greater than zero, non-negative wait (RedisDistributedLock.cs:51-53).
      • Key and token. The physical key is _keys.Qualify(string.Concat(KeyPrefix, key)) (RedisDistributedLock.cs:55). The token is a fresh Guid.NewGuid().ToString("N", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) minted per acquisition (RedisDistributedLock.cs:59); the release script matches on it, and that is what makes a release owner-scoped instead of "delete whatever is there now" (RedisDistributedLock.cs:57-58).
      • The acquire loop (RedisDistributedLock.cs:64-81). StringSetAsync(redisKey, token, ttl, keepTtl: false, When.NotExists, CommandFlags.None) (RedisDistributedLock.cs:66-68) is a single atomic conditional set carrying the expiry, so exactly one replica can win a key. On success it returns a RedisLockHandle closing over the database, key, token, and logger (RedisDistributedLock.cs:70-73); once Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(startedAt) >= wait it returns null (RedisDistributedLock.cs:75-78); otherwise it delays one PollInterval and retries (RedisDistributedLock.cs:80).

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-017 replaced the process-local guard around the idempotency filter's execute-then-store window with this, because a striped semaphore stops serializing anything once a service runs more than one replica. Choosing the one-instance SET NX PX lock over Redlock is a stated trade: simpler, dependent on a single Redis, and paired with a contract that tells callers never to lean on it for an invariant persistence can enforce.

    • Where it's used: selected by AddCaching whenever an IConnectionMultiplexer is resolvable (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:109-123, see DependencyInjection), passing the same CacheKeyNamespace the distributed cache gets (DependencyInjection.Caching.cs:83, :91). The one in-framework caller is the API IdempotencyFilter; RedisDistributedLockTests covers the acquire and release commands against a mocked IDatabase.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: whether a given deployed environment actually supplies the redis connection string is an infrastructure/config fact, not a source fact, so "which implementation is live in environment X" is Not determinable from source here; the source only settles that the presence of a registered IConnectionMultiplexer decides it.

    ApplicationNamespace

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Configuration · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/ApplicationNamespace.cs:35 · Level 0 · class (static, partial)

    • What it is: the single shared value every piece of shared infrastructure is namespaced by: Redis cache keys, distributed-lock keys, distributed rate-limit counter keys, the Redis output-cache InstanceName, the SignalR Redis backplane channel prefix, and the message broker's topic prefix (ApplicationNamespace.cs:7-12). Never empty, so isolation is automatic rather than a setting a host has to remember to set (:52-56). A broker host is the one exception to "never has to set it": there the value must be configured explicitly (:28-33).

    • Depends on: IConfiguration and IHostEnvironment (both optional parameters), and its own [GeneratedRegex] source-generated partial property (:49-50). BCL only.

    • Concept: resolution with a fallback chain rather than a required setting. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: two applications sharing one broker or one Redis instance used to share every keyspace by default, so a user-targeted push published in one application reached the other application's clients holding the same numeric user id (SEC-Common-53, ApplicationNamespace.cs:14-21). This type gives every consumer one namespace they can all agree on without each of them inventing its own default. The broker is where the fallback stops being safe: the host's application name differs per service, and every service of one application must publish and consume on the SAME topics, so a broker host has to state the value rather than inherit it (:28-33).

    • Walkthrough: two public constants, one private constant, one generated regex, and two static methods.

      • ConfigurationKey = "Application:Namespace" (:38): the explicit override.
      • Fallback = "app" (:41): used only when neither configuration nor the host environment names the application.
      • HostApplicationNameKey = "applicationName" (:47): the key the generic host writes the application name to (HostDefaults.ApplicationKey, :43-46), read directly when no IHostEnvironment is at hand.
      • Resolve(configuration, environment) (:60-75): prefers the explicit ConfigurationKey (sanitized); otherwise falls back to environment.ApplicationName, then to the raw applicationName configuration key; otherwise returns Fallback. Never returns empty.
      • Sanitize(name) (:84-90): replaces every run of characters the UnsafeCharacters regex flags ([^a-zA-Z0-9_-]+, :49) with -, trims leading/trailing -, and returns Fallback when nothing survives, because a Redis key tolerates almost anything while a broker queue or topic name and a SignalR channel prefix do not, and the whole point is one value every one of its consumers accepts (:77-81).

    • Why it's built this way: a value that is never empty means every consumer (cache key prefix, push channel prefix, rate-limit key) gets isolation whether or not a host ever sets Application:Namespace, without asking every consumer to invent its own default. Override it only when two hosts of the SAME application must share a keyspace, such as a web head and a worker draining one backplane (ApplicationNamespace.cs:22-27).

    • Where it's used: read by CacheKeyPrefixOptions's CacheKeyNamespace.From(IServiceProvider) for the per-application default Redis key namespace (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Caching/CacheKeyPrefix.cs:95, with Sanitize at :129), by the notifications registration for the SignalR channel prefix (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:59), and by the distributed rate limiter's key namespace (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:237). On the broker path AddBrokerMessaging first calls EnsureApplicationNamespaceConfigured, which throws when ConfigurationKey is blank for a broker provider and names the setting to add (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:89, :270-278), then resolves the value and hands it to the BrokerConsumerBuilder and the BrokerTopology that prefix every topic (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:90-97). The keyspace isolation decision is ADR-135. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Configuration/ApplicationNamespaceTests.cs and MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/DependencyInjectionBrokerMessagingTests.cs.

    CloudAdapterTripwireOptions

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Configuration · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwireOptions.cs:8 · Level 0 · class (internal sealed, empty)

    • What it is: an options type with no members. Its only job is to carry CloudAdapterTripwire through ValidateOnStart, so that check runs with the other startup validators, before any hosted service starts (CloudAdapterTripwireOptions.cs:3-8).

    • Depends on: nothing. It is declared as internal sealed class CloudAdapterTripwireOptions; (CloudAdapterTripwireOptions.cs:8), a body-less class declaration.

    • Concept: a marker options type used as a hook into the options validation pipeline. ValidateOnStart only runs IValidateOptions<T> validators for an options type somebody registered, so a check that validates the composed container rather than a configuration section still needs a T to hang on. An empty class is the cheapest such T. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] scores moving failures to the earliest point: this is what places the cloud-adapter check at boot rather than at the first dropped push.

    • Walkthrough: there is nothing to walk; the type has no members. The behavior lives in the two registration lines that use it: services.AddOptions<Configuration.CloudAdapterTripwireOptions>().ValidateOnStart(); and a TryAddEnumerable of IValidateOptions<CloudAdapterTripwireOptions> mapped to CloudAdapterTripwire (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:244-246).

    • Why it's built this way: binding the tripwire to its own options type, rather than to an existing settings class, keeps the check independent of whether any particular section is present, and TryAddEnumerable keeps it to one validator even when several modules call AddInfrastructure. The fail-fast posture is ADR-070.

    • Where it's used: AddInfrastructure (DependencyInjection.cs:244-246) and the validator's generic argument (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:32). Exercised by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwireTests.cs.

    SmtpSettings

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Mail · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Mail/SmtpSettings.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the Smtp section: host, port, credentials, TLS toggle, and the default sender and recipient addresses. Validated by data annotations at startup (SmtpSettings.cs:5-8).

    • Depends on: System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations for [Range] (SmtpSettings.cs:1). Consumed by SmtpEmailSender, the IEmailSender implementation.

    • Concept: the validate-on-start gate taught under ConnectionStringSettings, here guarding a numeric range rather than a cross-section rule. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether avoidable failures are moved earlier: [Range(1, 65535)] on Port (SmtpSettings.cs:21) means a configuration typo such as 0 or 70000 fails the host at boot with a named error instead of surfacing as a socket exception the first time the application sends mail. Note also the named constant instead of a magic number: DefaultSmtpPort = 25 is a public static readonly field (:15) used as the property's own default (:22), so the value is discoverable and testable rather than inlined. [Rubric §11, Security]: Password is a plain string (:28), so it is only ever as safe as the configuration provider that supplies it (user-secrets or Key Vault, never a committed appsettings.json).

    • Walkthrough: two static fields then eight { get; init; } members.

      • SectionName = "Smtp" (SmtpSettings.cs:12) and DefaultSmtpPort = 25 (:15).
      • Host (:18), Port (:22), Username (:25), Password (:28), EnableSsl (:31, defaulting to false), From (:34), To (:37), TimeoutSeconds (:53, [Range(1, 600)], default 30). Every string defaults to string.Empty, so an absent section binds cleanly; only Port and TimeoutSeconds are range-checked. To is documented as the default recipient used by the no-argument SendAsync overload (:36-37).
      • EnableSsl no longer defaults to "off" when the key is unset: SmtpTransportSecurity resolves the effective value, turning TLS on outside Development (SEC-Common-54); the property itself still carries a plain false default because it only records what the host configured, not the resolved posture (:16-24).
      • TimeoutSeconds exists because the .NET default of 100 seconds outlives most callers' own budget: a relay that accepts the TCP connection and then stops answering parks the request thread for the full 100s, and a notification burst parks one per message; 30 seconds keeps a stalled relay inside the caller's timeout instead of outliving it (:41-49).
      • The consumer is deliberately plain: SmtpEmailSender takes IOptions<SmtpSettings> in its primary constructor and snapshots .Value into a readonly field (SmtpEmailSender.cs:12-14), then builds a fresh SmtpClient per send from Host/Port plus a NetworkCredential and the resolved TLS decision (:25-29), and a MailMessage from From (:32-35).

    • Why it's built this way: annotations plus ValidateOnStart cost one line at registration and move an entire class of misconfiguration from run time to boot, the contract ADR-070 describes. Resolving TLS through SmtpTransportSecurity instead of a hard-coded default keeps the failure mode fail-closed outside Development (ADR-122).

    • Where it's used: bound with .ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() in AddInfrastructure (DependencyInjection.cs:80-83); read by SmtpEmailSender.

    PeriodicBackgroundService

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Hosting.Background · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Hosting/Background/PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:20 · Level 0 · class (public abstract partial)

    • What it is: the base class for fixed-interval background sweeps. It contributes four things a hand-written BackgroundService loop usually gets wrong: an enablement gate evaluated once at startup, a startup delay so the host finishes initializing first, a loop whose cycle failures are logged (through an overridable hook) without killing the loop, and every wait routed through an injected TimeProvider so a test can drive it with a fake clock (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:6-11).

    • Depends on: Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.BackgroundService as the base, TimeProvider and ILogger as its two primary-constructor parameters (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:20-22), and the LoggerMessage source generator for its two log methods (:99-103), which is what makes the class partial.

    • Concept introduced, the template method with an injected clock. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses whether a pattern is used where it carries its weight, and this is a textbook template method: the base owns the invariant algorithm (gate, delay, loop, catch, wait) and the subclass supplies only the variable parts through Interval, IsEnabled, StartupDelay, LogCycleFailure, and ExecuteCycleAsync. [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity] assesses whether a background component survives its own failures: the broad catch at :82-86, under a CA1031 suppression whose justification reads "One failed cycle must not stop the background service for the life of the process" (:81), is the whole answer, because an unhandled exception inside ExecuteAsync silently ends a hosted service for the lifetime of the process, and a reconciliation sweep that stops running is a failure nobody notices until the data is wrong. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether an override can keep its own event id: LogCycleFailure is virtual (:45-46) precisely so a subclass can log its own message and event id (for a dashboard that keys on it) while still relying on the base loop to call it. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether time-dependent code can be tested without waiting: Task.Delay(..., timeProvider, ...) (:63, :90) means a FakeTimeProvider advances the loop instantly, which is what PeriodicBackgroundServiceTests and its FakeClockLoop helper rely on (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/PeriodicBackgroundServiceTests.cs, MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/FakeClockLoop.cs).

    • Walkthrough

      • Interval is abstract (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:25): every subclass must state its own cadence, and nothing defaults it.
      • StartupDelay is virtual with a 15 second default (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:31). The doc says why it exists: let the application finish initializing before background work competes with it, and tests override it to shorten the wait (:27-30).
      • IsEnabled is virtual and defaults to true (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:38). It is read once, at the top of ExecuteAsync, and a false logs and returns (:55-59), so the service occupies no thread and no timer for the rest of the process. Flipping the toggle at runtime does not restart it.
      • LogCycleFailure(exception) is virtual (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:45-46): the default writes one generic Error naming the service through the generated LogCycleError. The doc comment spells out why it is overridable: a subclass can keep its own message and its own event id, which dashboards and tests key on (:40-43).
      • ExecuteCycleAsync(stoppingToken) is the abstract single sweep (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:50), and its contract is stated in the doc comment: exceptions are logged and do not stop the loop.
      • ExecuteAsync (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:53-97) is the algorithm. The startup delay is wrapped in its own try whose catch (OperationCanceledException) when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested) returns cleanly (:61-68), so a host stopped during the delay does not log a shutdown as an error. The loop then runs until cancellation (:70), awaiting the cycle, breaking on a shutdown cancellation (:76-80), routing any other exception through LogCycleFailure (:81-86), and waiting the interval under the same cancellation-aware guard (:88-95).
      • The two [LoggerMessage] methods (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:99-103) are source-generated: LogDisabled at Information, LogCycleError at Error with the exception attached and a message that states the recovery ("it will retry on the next interval"). Both stamp GetType().Name, so the log line names the concrete sweep, not the base class; LogCycleError is called through LogCycleFailure rather than directly from the loop.

    • Why it's built this way: the class doc draws the boundary explicitly (PeriodicBackgroundService.cs:12-16): this is for periodic reconciliation and cleanup work, and it is deliberately not what the outbox processor uses, because the outbox's signal-driven smart wait does not fit a fixed interval. The background-work posture is ADR-052, and a fixed-interval sweep is a different thing again from the cron-style recurring scheduler of ADR-074, which is why this base stays as small as it is.

    • Where it's used: four framework sweeps derive from it: PermissionGrantRefreshService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/PermissionGrantRefreshService.cs:36), RefreshSessionCleanupService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/RefreshSessionCleanupService.cs:53), InternalCommandCleanupService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/InternalCommands/Administration/InternalCommandCleanupService.cs:46) and OutboxCleanupService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Outbox/Administration/OutboxCleanupService.cs:50). ScheduledJobRunner is the closest relative and deliberately is not a subclass: it derives BackgroundService directly and only names this class in a comment (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobRunner.cs).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: nothing in this base coordinates two replicas running the same sweep, so any subclass owns that question itself. Contrast ScheduledJobRunner, which answers it with a database claim lease rather than by inheriting one.

    MessageBusSettings

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/MessageBusSettings.cs:13 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the MessageBus section. It selects the transport, says how to reach the broker, which queue this host receives on and whether the transport may create its own broker entities, how hard to retry a failing consumer, how much work to take on at once, and whether the two store-and-forward guards (the transactional outbox and the consumer-side idempotency inbox) are on (MessageBusSettings.cs:6-12). Despite the name it is the single switch for the whole event delivery posture, not just for the wire protocol.

    • Depends on: MessageBusProviders, the string constants and case-insensitive predicates for the built-in transport names (MessageBusSettings.cs:2), and, in its XML doc only, IBrokerTransport (whose MaxRedeliveryDelay it names, :182-189). Externals: System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations for the [StringLength] and [Range] guards (:1).

    • Concept introduced: a tri-state flag that resolves from the transport. Two of the properties here are bool?, not bool, and each has a computed companion. EnableInbox (:134) is the raw configured value and IsInboxEnabled (:142) is what every framework component actually reads: EnableInbox ?? !MessageBusProviders.IsInProcess(Provider). EnableOutbox (:172) and IsOutboxEnabled (:180) work identically. The point of the third state is that "the host said nothing" and "the host said false" are different facts. Unset means "let the transport decide", which turns both features ON for a broker and OFF in-process, and an explicit value wins (with the one refusal described under EnableOutbox). That is why a settings class that could have been a bag of booleans carries derived properties: the resolution rule lives once, next to the data, instead of being repeated at every read site.

      [Rubric §6, CQRS and Event-Driven] assesses how reliably a state change turns into a delivered event. Both resolved flags default ON for a broker deliberately, and the XML doc argues the case rather than just stating it: broker delivery is at-least-once by contract, so an ack after a network blip, a redelivery after a lease expiry, or an outbox row republished after a crash all hand the same event to the same handlers twice, and with the inbox off every one of those becomes a duplicate side effect (:116-125, ADR-021). Symmetrically, a single-process host dispatches every event inside the process that raised it, so the store-and-forward hop buys it two background services, a table and a poll loop for nothing (:151-156, ADR-100).

      [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity] assesses whether transient failures are absorbed before they become lost messages. This class configures two independent retry tiers, both run by the framework's own receive pipeline rather than by a broker library, so every transport behaves the same. RetryLimit / RetryMinIntervalSeconds / RetryMaxIntervalSeconds drive the in-process tier: BrokerReceivePipeline runs the consumer up to RetryLimit + 1 times, each attempt in a fresh DI scope (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:179-190), waiting the exponential delay BrokerTransportPolicies.RetryDelay computes from the floor and the cap (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:27-33). RedeliveryIntervalsSeconds drives the second tier: once the in-process attempts are spent, the pipeline schedules the next redelivery on the host's queue while one is left, and dead-letters only after the last (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:157-177).

      [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether several services can share infrastructure without colliding. Each host receives on ONE queue of its own, derived from its application name, and every event it consumes is bound to that queue, so two services consuming the same event each get their own copy instead of competing for one (:56-62). Topic names are separately prefixed with ApplicationNamespace, which a broker host must set.

    • Walkthrough: two static members, thirteen init properties, and two computed properties.

      • SectionName = "MessageBus" (MessageBusSettings.cs:16), the bind key.
      • Provider (:25): a string, not an enum, compared case-insensitively, defaulting to MessageBusProviders.InProcess, so the modular monolith is the zero-configuration case. InProcess, RabbitMq and PostgreSql are built in; any other value names an IBrokerTransport an adapter package registers before AddBrokerMessaging (for example AzureServiceBus from MMCA.Common.Azure through AddAzureServiceBusTransport()) (:18-24). When nothing is registered under the name, AddBrokerMessaging fails naming AddBrokerTransport(...) as the fix (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:228). The transport-selection decision is ADR-066, and the move of vendor brokers into adapter packages is ADR-134.
      • ConnectionString (:33): nullable, and only the first of three sources. ResolveBrokerConnectionString prefers it, then falls back to ConnectionStrings:rabbitmq and ConnectionStrings:messaging, which is what Aspire injects via WithReference(broker) (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:287-293).
      • EmulatorAdminEndpoint (:54) with [StringLength(2048)] (:53): the base address of the Azure Service Bus emulator's HTTP management plane. The emulator serves the data plane (AMQP) and the management plane (HTTP) on two different ports, so the administration client that provisions topics, subscriptions and queues cannot be derived from ConnectionString alone (:41-45). It is read only when the connection string carries UseDevelopmentEmulator=true, and then a missing or malformed value fails at registration (:47-51). The reader is the Azure adapter, not this assembly: AzureServiceBusTransport hands it to ServiceBusEmulatorSupport.
      • QueueName (:71) with [StringLength(50)] (:70): the ONE queue this host receives on, or null (the default) to derive it from the host application name in lower kebab case with a trailing -service removed, so MMCA.ADC.Engagement.Service receives on mmca-adc-engagement (:56-62). AddBrokerMessaging hands it with the host's applicationName to BrokerNaming.Queue (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:96). Set it explicitly only to pin a name that must survive a host rename; replicas share the queue as competing consumers anyway, because they run under the same application name (:63-68).
      • ProvisionTopology (:84), default true: whether the transport creates the topic per event, this host's queue and the topic-to-queue bindings, idempotently, when the receiver starts and on the first publish to a missing topic (:73-77). Set it false where the entities are provisioned out of band (infrastructure as code, or an identity that may send and receive but not manage), and the transport then assumes every entity exists (:78-82).
      • RetryLimit (:94) with [Range(0, 20)] (:93), default 5: a message is attempted up to RetryLimit + 1 times per delivery, and 0 disables in-process retries (:86-92).
      • RetryMinIntervalSeconds (:101) with [Range(0, 300)], default 1, and RetryMaxIntervalSeconds (:107) with [Range(0, 3600)], default 30: the floor and the cap of the doubling backoff.
      • EnableInbox (:134) and IsInboxEnabled (:142). AddBrokerMessaging registers EfInboxStore when the resolved value is true and NoOpInboxStore plus a startup InboxDisabledWarningService when it is false, so an opt-out is recorded in the log rather than passing silently (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:134, :142, :147). The InboxMessages table is part of the shared relational model created by the standard migrations (Cosmos hosts skip it), so turning it on for a migrated relational host needs no schema work (:112-115).
      • EnableOutbox (:172) and IsOutboxEnabled (:180). AddInfrastructure reads the resolved value to decide whether to run OutboxProcessor and OutboxCleanupService or the single OutboxDisabledNoticeService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:260-267). Turning it off under a broker is not honored: EnsureOutboxAvailableForProvider throws at registration, because a broker with no outbox has no delivery channel at all (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:248-250, argued at MessageBusSettings.cs:159-164), and AddBrokerMessaging runs that check itself (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:80) so a service host that wires only the broker still fails loudly. The OutboxMessages table stays part of the EF model either way, so flipping the flag is never a migration. With the outbox off, a handler failure is logged at Error and nothing retries it; each event dispatches on its own, so one failing handler does not stop the later events of the save (MessageBusSettings.cs:166-169).
      • DefaultRedeliveryIntervalsSeconds (:190), a static [60, 600, 3600]: one minute, ten minutes and one hour, a spread wide enough to ride out a dependency restart, a failover and a short incident without an operator replaying the dead-letter queue by hand (:182-189).
      • RedeliveryIntervalsSeconds (:213): nullable with no initializer, and that is on purpose: the configuration binder appends a configured list to an existing collection instead of replacing it, so a non-null default would make the defaults impossible to shorten by configuration (:202-206). A configured list REPLACES the default and is never merged with it; non-positive entries are dropped, so [0] turns second-level redelivery off (an empty array cannot be expressed in configuration); an interval longer than the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay is shortened to it, which matters on Amazon SQS with its 15 minute cap (:192-201). BuildRedeliveryIntervals applies all three rules (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:65-71), and AddBrokerMessaging passes the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay into the pipeline that calls it (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:108-115). Every transport honors the result: RabbitMQ through per-interval delay queues (no broker plugin), PostgreSQL through the row's visibility time, Azure Service Bus and Amazon SQS through their native scheduling (MessageBusSettings.cs:207-211).
      • PrefetchCount (:223) and ConcurrentMessageLimit (:232): both nullable int, both unset by default, and both range-guarded in code rather than by [Range], because the binder never validates this section (:215-222, :225-231). ResolvePrefetchCount and ResolveConcurrentMessageLimit return the value only when it is greater than zero, leaving the transport's own default in place otherwise (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:85-89, :98-102). PrefetchCount caps how many messages the transport holds locally ahead of the consumer; a window larger than the work a consumer can finish inside its lock or lease is what turns a slow consumer into redeliveries, while a window of one serializes the queue (:216-219). ConcurrentMessageLimit caps how many messages are consumed at once from the host's queue, the backpressure knob for how many database connections and downstream calls a burst of events can open (:226-229).

    • Why it's built this way: resolving both guards from the transport rather than shipping fixed defaults is what lets one settings class serve the monolith and the extracted-service topology at the same time (ADR-008), while keeping the at-least-once contract intact where it matters (ADR-003, ADR-021). Refusing an outbox-less broker at registration rather than honoring it follows the fail-fast configuration contract (ADR-070): the misconfiguration becomes a startup exception instead of silently dropped events. Keeping the retry, redelivery and backpressure knobs here, applied once by the framework pipeline, is what lets a new transport inherit the whole failure policy instead of re-implementing it.

    • Where it's used: bound with .ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() in AddInfrastructure (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:215), then read eagerly in the same method to gate the outbox hosted services (:260-267). AddBrokerMessaging reads it again, falling back to new MessageBusSettings() when the section is absent (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:70), short-circuits on the in-process provider (:72), and otherwise builds the BrokerTopology (:94-97), registers the receive pipeline with these settings (:109-115), and replaces IMessageBus with BrokerMessageBus (:119) and IEventBus with BrokerEventBus (:125), so OutboxProcessor becomes the only delivery channel. InProcessEventBus reads the resolved outbox flag, and OutboxCleanupService reads IsInboxEnabled to decide whether to purge inbox rows. The vendor receivers (AzureServiceBusTransport, AmazonSqsTransport) read the same instance (for example MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aws/Messaging/AmazonSqsReceiver.cs). StartupConfigurationSummaryService logs the resolved Provider and ProvisionTopology at start. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Settings/MessageBusSettingsTests.cs and MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportPoliciesTests.cs.

    • Caveats: no broker library sits underneath any of these settings: MassTransit is banned from the framework (ADR-118, enforced by MassTransit_MustNotBeReferenced in MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Governance/DependencyVersionTestsBase.cs:13 and the banned-assembly list in MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Layering/ArchitectureRules.Transport.cs:16) and the transports are framework code, so every knob here is honored by MMCA.Common's own receive pipeline and transports rather than translated into a library's API.

    [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] applies: this type sits on the path a message takes once it leaves the process (outbox, bus, consumer, or broker plumbing), which is what section 10 scores.

    SmtpTransportSecurity

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Mail · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Mail/SmtpTransportSecurity.cs:26 · Level 1 · class (static, partial)

    • What it is: the resolver behind SmtpSettings.EnableSsl. It answers whether an SMTP session must negotiate TLS, treating an unset Smtp:EnableSsl key as "secure unless the host is Development" rather than as "off" (SEC-Common-54).

    • Depends on: IConfiguration, IHostEnvironment, ILogger, and SmtpSettings (the second overload's parameter). [LoggerMessage] source generation for the warning.

    • Concept: fail-closed configuration for a security-relevant default. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §22, Compliance & Governance]: leaving Smtp:EnableSsl unset used to mean cleartext, because SmtpSettings.EnableSsl is a plain bool defaulting to false. This type reads the raw configuration key rather than the bound settings object, because the settings object cannot distinguish "configured false" from "never configured" once binding has happened (SmtpTransportSecurity.cs:39-40); only the presence of the key in configuration can. Development is the one carved-out exception, consistent with the workspace's dev-only-relaxations-fail-closed policy (ADR-122).

    • Walkthrough: two overloads of Resolve and one generated log method.

      • Resolve(configuration, environment) (:37-49): reads Smtp:EnableSsl (EnableSslConfigKey = "Smtp:EnableSsl", :29); if it parses as a bool, that value wins; otherwise returns environment?.IsDevelopment() != true, so a null environment is also treated as non-Development (secure by default).
      • Resolve(settings, configuration, environment, logger) (:65-84): calls the first overload, and when the resolved value is false, the host is not Development, settings.Host is set, and a logger was supplied, emits one LogCleartextSmtp warning naming the config key and the SMTP host before returning the same resolved value.
      • LogCleartextSmtp (:686-690): [LoggerMessage(EventId = 5401, Level = Warning)], message text states plainly that credentials and message bodies, "password-reset tokens included," travel in cleartext to the named host.

    • Why it's built this way: a security-relevant default that only reveals itself the first time someone inspects network traffic is exactly the failure mode ADR-122 exists to close off; resolving from the raw configuration key rather than the bound bool is what lets "unset" and "explicitly false" resolve differently at all.

    • Where it's used: SmtpSettings.EnableSsl's XML doc references it as the resolver of record (SmtpSettings.cs:29); called from SmtpEmailSender to decide the SmtpClient's TLS posture, and from SensitiveDataLoggingGate for the analogous decision on a different setting. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Mail/SmtpTransportSecurityTests.cs.

    CloudAdapterTripwire

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Configuration · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:32 · Level 4 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: a startup validator that fails the host when configuration switches on a capability whose implementation lives in a package or registration call that never ran, so the inert core default is still in place (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:12-14). It checks three switches: passkeys, machine clients and native push.

    • Depends on: IValidateOptions<CloudAdapterTripwireOptions> (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:32), with CloudAdapterTripwireOptions as the empty carrier type; the root IServiceProvider as its single primary-constructor parameter; IConfiguration (resolved from that provider); IPasskeyCeremony, IMachineClientService, INativePushSender and its core no-op NullNativePushSender (:4-8).

    • Concept introduced: a tripwire on a quiet default. The core packages are cloud-neutral, so native push resolves to NullNativePushSender until an adapter swaps it, and that default is deliberately quiet: a push is dropped (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:16-18). Quiet is right for a host that never switched push on and wrong for one that did, because a deployment that sets NativePush:Enabled but lost the adapter call would start, pass its health checks and silently stop delivering pushes (:18-21). The opt-in passkeys and machine-client features fail the same quiet way: an enabled section without its registration call leaves every one of their routes answering 404 (:37-41, :44-48). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]: the tripwire turns each silent loss into a boot failure whose message names the missing call. The cloud-neutral core is ADR-134, native push is ADR-044, passkeys are ADR-139 and machine clients are ADR-140.

    • Walkthrough:

      • Three internal key constants, so the tests can name them: NativePushEnabledKey = "NativePush:Enabled" (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:35), PasskeysEnabledKey = "Passkeys:Enabled" (:42) and MachineClientsEnabledKey = "MachineClients:Enabled" (:49).
      • Validate(name, options) (:52-86) resolves IConfiguration and returns ValidateOptionsResult.Skip when there is none (:54-58), then collects failures inside a created scope (:62), so it sees each service the way a request would.
      • Passkeys (:64-69): fails when the switch is on and no IPasskeyCeremony resolves, naming services.AddPasskeys(configuration) from MMCA.Common.Passkeys with Passkeys:RelyingPartyId and Passkeys:Origins.
      • Machine clients (:71-75): fails when the switch is on and IMachineClientService is not registered, naming services.AddMachineClients(configuration) and the app's IServiceAccountProvisioner. A missing provisioner is left to the settings validator that call registers (:47-48).
      • Native push (:77-82): fails when the switch is on and the resolved INativePushSender is absent or still NullNativePushSender. The message lists the three adapter paths with their registration calls and required keys: AddAzureNotificationHubsPush from MMCA.Common.Azure, AddAmazonSnsPush from MMCA.Common.Aws, and AddFirebaseCloudMessagingPush from MMCA.Common.Gcp.
      • It returns Success when no failure was collected, otherwise Fail(failures) (:85), so one boot reports every missing call at once.
      • Two private helpers: IsSwitchedOn (:92-93) is true only when the key parses as true, and IsRegistered<TService> (:99-100) asks IServiceProviderIsService without constructing the service (treating an unanswerable provider as registered).

    • Why it's built this way: a tripwire must fire on a key that declares intent, so file storage deliberately has no check. A FileStorage section is routinely shared configuration (one user-secrets id across every service of a solution), so a host that never stores files sees it too, and a host that does store files and lost its adapter call is not silent anyway: NullFileStorageService fails every upload with FileStorage.NotConfigured (CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:23-29). Running as an options validator under ValidateOnStart places the check with the other startup validators, before any hosted service starts, the fail-fast contract of ADR-070.

    • Where it's used: registered once in AddInfrastructure through TryAddEnumerable (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:246). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwireTests.cs, and the machine-client branch also by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Auth/MachineClients/AddMachineClientsTests.cs.

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Configuration · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:35 · Level 11 · class (internal sealed partial, IHostedService)

    • What it is: a hosted service that writes one Information line at host start naming the posture the host actually resolved: the MMCA.Common version, the database engines it configures, the message bus transport with its ProvisionTopology value, the cache mode and the tenancy mode. A support question ("which version, which bus, which cache?") is then answered by the first lines of the log rather than by reading the deployed configuration (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:14-19).

It calls DataSourceResolver.ResolveConfiguredEngines, and checks for HybridCache, IDistributedCache and MemoryDistributedCache from the Microsoft caching packages (:2-3).

    • Concept introduced: log the resolved posture, never the configuration text. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] scores whether a running system can be understood from outside. Several of the settings it reports resolve from more than one source (a transport name that may be an adapter's, a cache tier picked by registrations, a tenancy mode implied by per-tenant data sources), so the configured values alone do not say what the host is doing; this line does. [Rubric §11, Security]: only names, enum values and flags are logged. Connection strings, keys and every other secret stay out, and the engines are derived from WHETHER a connection string is set, never from its text (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:20-23).

    • Walkthrough:

      • FrameworkVersion (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:49-52): the AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute stamped on the assembly (the release tag on a release build, the 0.0.0-dev placeholder otherwise), or unknown when it is absent, computed once in a static property.
      • StartAsync (:55-77) builds the summary only when Information is enabled (:59), so a host that filters Information pays nothing for the engine and cache probes. It names the engines (none when there are none, :61-62), the cache mode and the tenancy mode, and writes them with the bus Provider and ProvisionTopology through the source-generated LogConfigurationSummary (:66-73, declared at :127-137). It writes nothing else.
      • StopAsync (:80) is a completed task.
      • CacheMode(services) (:95-107) returns hybrid when HybridCache is registered, misconfigured when the resolved IDistributedCache is not the in-memory MemoryDistributedCache (the host wired Redis but not the cache over it, which the AddCaching factory refuses on first use), and memory otherwise. It deliberately repeats the decision the ICacheService registrations make instead of resolving ICacheService, because the two-level cache resolves IConnectionMultiplexer and constructing it here would open a Redis-backed host's connection at startup instead of on first use; HybridCache is checked by registration through IServiceProviderIsService, and resolving IDistributedCache does not connect (:82-94).
      • TenancyMode(settings) (:115-125) returns off when tenancy is disabled, database-per-tenant when at least one tenant routes a data source to its own database, and shared-database otherwise.

    • Why it's built this way: the summary is one line so it sits at the top of every log. Naming a misconfigured cache up front surfaces at boot a state that would otherwise fail only on the first cache use. Registration through TryAddEnumerable means a host whose modules each call AddInfrastructure still writes the summary exactly once (StartupConfigurationSummaryService.cs:24-27).

    • Where it's used: registered in AddInfrastructure with TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IHostedService, Configuration.StartupConfigurationSummaryService>()) (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:238). CacheMode and TenancyMode are internal static so the tests can call them directly. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Configuration/StartupConfigurationSummaryServiceTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: no ADR records this service. The line is written once at start, so a setting changed at runtime through a reloadable provider is not reflected in it.

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerConsumerKind.cs:4 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: says how a host consumes one subscribed integration event: Current = 0 delivers it to the handlers of its own type, Upcasted = 1 treats it as a retired contract that is upcast to its terminal successor first (BrokerConsumerKind.cs:7,10).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party.
    • Concept: a two-value switch carried on every BrokerSubscription; the upcasting idea itself belongs to ADR-090 and is taught at UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>.
    • Walkthrough: explicit numeric values (BrokerConsumerKind.cs:7,10), with Current as the default.
    • Why it's built this way: one subscription list serves both kinds, so the receive pipeline needs only this flag to pick the consumer type: BrokerConsumerBuilder maps Upcasted to UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<> and anything else to IntegrationEventConsumer<> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:40-44).

    BrokerDisposition

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerDisposition.cs:8 · Level 0 · record (abstract)

    • What it is: the closed set of outcomes the framework receive pipeline hands back to a transport for one delivered message: complete it, redeliver it later, or dead-letter it.
    • Depends on: BrokerHeaders (the redelivery-count header the Redeliver case documents, BrokerDisposition.cs:18).
    • Concept introduced, the disposition as a value. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration] assesses whether delivery, retry and poison handling are explicit and consistent across transports; here the decision about a message is made once, in transport-neutral code, and returned as data, so every transport (RabbitMQ, PostgreSQL, Azure Service Bus, Amazon SQS) only has to apply a verdict it did not compute. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns]: an abstract record with nested sealed records is the C# shape of a discriminated union; consumers switch on the three cases.
    • Walkthrough: Complete (BrokerDisposition.cs:11) is a shared singleton Completed instance; the three nested cases are Completed (:14), Redeliver (:24) and DeadLetter (:33). The doc comments define the contract each transport implements: Redeliver enqueues a delayed copy with every other header and the body unchanged, then acknowledges the original (BrokerDisposition.cs:16-21); DeadLetter moves the message to the dead-letter location with reason and detail "where the broker allows", then acknowledges it (BrokerDisposition.cs:26-30).
    • Why it's built this way: retry, redelivery and dead-lettering live once in the framework pipeline and BrokerTransportPolicies, shared by every transport (MMCA.Common/AGENTS.md, Microservices Extraction Boundaries); the poison and redelivery policy is ADR-087, and the native-transport extension point is ADR-118.
    • Where it's used: produced by BrokerReceivePipeline (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:82,100,166,176) and applied by RabbitMqDispositionApplier, PostgreSqlDispositionApplier and the cloud adapters' delivery handlers (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Azure/Messaging/AzureServiceBusDeliveryHandler.cs, MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aws/Messaging/AmazonSqsDeliveryHandler.cs, per the brief's usage sites).

    BrokerHeaders

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerHeaders.cs:8 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the header-name constants that make up the framework's wire contract on every broker.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party.
    • Concept: a shared wire vocabulary. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether a contract is explicit and stable; here the message envelope is a fixed set of named headers independent of any broker SDK, so a publisher on one transport and the receive pipeline agree on names by construction.
    • Walkthrough: EventName = "mmca-event-name" (BrokerHeaders.cs:11, the receiver resolves the subscription and CLR type from it); MessageId = "mmca-message-id" (:14, the key the inbox dedupes on); RedeliveryCount = "mmca-redelivery-count" (:17, absent means none); ContentType = "content-type" (:20) with JsonContentType = "application/json" (:23, the only body type the framework writes); TraceParent = "traceparent" (:26) and TraceState = "tracestate" (:29) for W3C trace context.
    • Why it's built this way: the inbox key and the redelivery counter must survive any broker, so they travel as plain string headers rather than broker-native properties; inbox dedupe is ADR-021.
    • Where it's used: BrokerMessageBus writes EventName, MessageId, ContentType and the trace headers (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/BrokerMessageBus.cs:66-68,113,116); IncomingBrokerMessage reads EventName and RedeliveryCount (IncomingBrokerMessage.cs:17,24); BrokerReceivePipeline names the header in its unknown-event detail (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:126).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the MMCA-* ambient-origin headers restored by the consumer are not declared here; they belong to AmbientOrigin.

    • Concept: the unit of BrokerTopology; a transport binds one topic per subscription to the host's queue.

    • Why it's built this way: name and topic are computed once at registration with BrokerNaming (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:49,60), so the receiver never recomputes them per message.
    • Where it's used: built by BrokerConsumerBuilder (BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:60), held by BrokerTopology, and looked up by BrokerReceivePipeline (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:120).

    • What it is: the BrokerDisposition case for a message that cannot be handled: move it to the dead-letter location with Reason and Detail, then acknowledge it (BrokerDisposition.cs:26-33).
    • Depends on: BrokerDisposition.
    • Concept: see BrokerDisposition; poison handling is ADR-087.
    • Walkthrough: Reason is a short machine-friendly string and Detail a nullable human-readable description (BrokerDisposition.cs:31-32). The pipeline uses three reasons: unknown-event, poison and handler-failed (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:29,32,35). An unknown event or an undeserializable body is dead-lettered immediately, since no retry can fix it (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:124,137,144); a handler failure is dead-lettered only after every redelivery is spent (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:162-176).

    • What it is: the publish half of a broker transport: one method, PublishAsync(OutgoingBrokerMessage, CancellationToken) (IBrokerPublisher.cs:18).
    • Depends on: OutgoingBrokerMessage.
    • Concept: a narrow port per transport. [Rubric §1, SOLID] (interface segregation, dependency inversion): the framework's bus depends on this one-method abstraction, and each transport supplies only an implementation, so adding a broker never touches the publish path.
    • Walkthrough: the contract carries the body and every header unchanged, and when MessageBus:ProvisionTopology is set a missing topic is created first (IBrokerPublisher.cs:12-13). The returned task completes when the broker has accepted the message (IBrokerPublisher.cs:17).
    • Why it's built this way: a transport registers "only its IBrokerPublisher and its hosted receiver"; everything else is shared framework code (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:44-46; MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/IBrokerTransport.cs:38). See ADR-118 and ADR-134.
    • Where it's used: consumed by BrokerMessageBus (BrokerMessageBus.cs:47); implemented by RabbitMqPublisher, PostgreSqlPublisher, and the Azure Service Bus and Amazon SQS publishers in the vendor adapters.

    IncomingBrokerMessage

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IncomingBrokerMessage.cs:11 · Level 1 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: a delivered message as the receive pipeline sees it: Body, Headers, and the broker's own BrokerMessageId (IncomingBrokerMessage.cs:11-14).
    • Depends on: BrokerHeaders.
    • Concept: the receive-side envelope, the twin of OutgoingBrokerMessage.
    • Walkthrough: EventName (IncomingBrokerMessage.cs:17) reads the mmca-event-name header or returns null. RedeliveryCount (IncomingBrokerMessage.cs:23-27) parses the mmca-redelivery-count header with NumberStyles.None and the invariant culture, so an absent or malformed value (including a sign) reads as zero.
    • Why it's built this way: tolerant parsing means a tampered or foreign header degrades to "first attempt" rather than throwing inside the receive loop. BrokerMessageId is kept separate from the event's own MessageId header because it is only used for logging the broker-side delivery (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:123,136).
    • Where it's used: built by each transport receiver (for example RabbitMqReceiver, PostgreSqlReceiver) and the vendor message mappings, then passed to IBrokerReceivePipeline.

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerDisposition.cs:24 · Level 1 · record (sealed, nested in BrokerDisposition)

    • What it is: the BrokerDisposition case for a second-level redelivery: enqueue a copy visible after Delay with the redelivery-count header set to RedeliveryCount, then acknowledge the original (BrokerDisposition.cs:16-24).
    • Depends on: BrokerDisposition, BrokerHeaders.
    • Concept: second-level redelivery per ADR-087: after in-process retries fail, the message leaves the consumer and comes back later, instead of holding the delivery.
    • Walkthrough: BrokerReceivePipeline returns it while redeliveryCount < _redeliveryIntervals.Length, taking the delay from the interval at the current count and incrementing the count (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:162-166); the count read comes from IncomingBrokerMessage.RedeliveryCount (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:104).
    • Where it's used: applied by the transport appliers and vendor delivery handlers, each with its own delay mechanism.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the redelivery interval values come from settings and the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:108-113); the defaults are not shown in these files.

    BrokerNaming

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerNaming.cs:13 · Level 2 · class (static)

    • What it is: the deterministic naming rules for broker entities: event wire names, topics, the host queue name, length fitting, and kebab casing.
    • Depends on: EventNameResolver (BrokerNaming.cs:29, for an EventNameAttribute declared name); BCL SHA256, StringBuilder.
    • Concept: naming as a pure function. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether services can be split and redeployed independently; because every host derives the same names from the same inputs, a publisher and a separately deployed consumer agree on topics without shared configuration.
    • Walkthrough:
      • EventName(Type) (BrokerNaming.cs:25-30): kebab-case of the declared [EventName] when present, otherwise the CLR full name, so equal short names in different modules never share a topic.
      • Topic(applicationNamespace, eventName) (BrokerNaming.cs:36-42): {kebab(namespace)}-{eventName}.
      • Queue(configured, applicationName) (BrokerNaming.cs:53-69): the configured MessageBus:QueueName when set, else the kebab application name with a trailing -service trimmed (only when derived, and only if something remains); throws InvalidOperationException when neither yields a name.
      • Fit(name, maxLength) (BrokerNaming.cs:80-92): returns a name within the limit unchanged; otherwise keeps the prefix and appends - plus the first 8 lowercase hex digits of its SHA-256. maxLength must be at least 16 (:83).
      • Kebab(value) (BrokerNaming.cs:97-130): lowercases ASCII letters and digits, collapses every other run to one -, and also breaks at a lower-to-upper boundary (UserRegistered becomes user-registered, :110-113).
    • Why it's built this way: topics are prefixed with the application namespace so two applications sharing a broker never publish onto each other's topics (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:86-89). The hash suffix in Fit keeps two long names distinct and identical on every host (BrokerNaming.cs:71-75).
    • Where it's used: BrokerConsumerBuilder (BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:49,60), BrokerTopology.TopicFor (BrokerTopology.cs:55), AddBrokerMessaging for the queue (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:96), RabbitMqNames, and the Azure and AWS entity-name helpers; ADC's BrokerTopologyBicepTests checks infrastructure names against it.

    IBrokerConsumerBuilder

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:16 · Level 2 · interface

    • What it is: the fluent registration surface a host uses to declare which integration events it consumes from the broker.
    • Depends on: IIntegrationEvent (the generic constraint).
    • Concept: declarative subscription. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration]: a host lists its consumed events once, and the topology, the per-subscription consumer registration and the broker bindings are all derived from that list.
    • Walkthrough: RegisterIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>() (IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:26-27) delivers each message to every IIntegrationEventHandler<TEvent> in the host through the inbox. RegisterUpcastedIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>() (IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:40-41) drains a retired contract, upcasting it to its terminal successor and delivering to that contract's handlers; pair it with AddEventUpcaster<TEvent, TNew, TUpcaster>() and a plain registration for the current contract, never register both kinds for the same type, and with no upcaster registered it degrades to ordinary dispatch (IBrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:30-35). Both throw InvalidOperationException when the type is already registered (:25,39).
    • Why it's built this way: registering the same event both ways would bind two consumers to one wire name; the builder rejects it by type or by wire name (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:51-58). Upcasting is ADR-090.
    • Where it's used: implemented by BrokerConsumerBuilder, passed to the configureConsumers callback of AddBrokerMessaging (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:91-92); ADC's per-service registrations (MMCA.ADC/Source/Services/MMCA.ADC.Conference.Service/ConferenceBrokerConsumers.cs, EngagementBrokerConsumers.cs, IdentityBrokerConsumers.cs) call it.

    IBrokerReceivePipeline

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/IBrokerReceivePipeline.cs:16 · Level 2 · interface

    • What it is: the transport-neutral handling of one delivered message: ProcessAsync(IncomingBrokerMessage, CancellationToken) returning a BrokerDisposition (IBrokerReceivePipeline.cs:22).
    • Depends on: IncomingBrokerMessage, BrokerDisposition.
    • Concept: the split between "decide" and "apply".
