[Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether behavior can be verified without infrastructure; because the decision is a pure function of message and handler outcome returning a value, the pipeline is unit-tested without a broker and each transport is tested only on how it applies the three dispositions.
    • Walkthrough: one method; the cancellation token fires when the host is stopping (IBrokerReceivePipeline.cs:20).
    • Why it's built this way: the framework pipeline owns trace context, origin restore, inbox, retry and dead-lettering, and a transport only receives and applies (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:44-46; MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/IBrokerTransport.cs:13,38-40).
    • Where it's used: registered as a singleton BrokerReceivePipeline (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:109); called by RabbitMqReceiver, PostgreSqlReceiver, and the Azure and AWS delivery handlers.

    BrokerTopology

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Broker · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Broker/BrokerTopology.cs:10 · Level 3 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a host's complete broker shape: the application namespace topics are prefixed with, the host's queue name, and the subscriptions bound to that queue, with lookup by wire name.
    • Depends on: BrokerSubscription, BrokerNaming, BrokerHeaders (doc reference).
    • Concept: one immutable description that every transport provisions from and the receive pipeline routes by. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] (as configuration safety): a duplicate subscription fails at startup, not as a silently misrouted message.
    • Walkthrough: the constructor (BrokerTopology.cs:19-41) guards its arguments, rejects two subscriptions with the same event name with an InvalidOperationException naming both registration methods (:25-34), and indexes the rest in an ordinal dictionary (:36). ApplicationNamespace, QueueName and Subscriptions (registration order) are read-only properties (:44,47,50). TopicFor(Type) composes BrokerNaming.Topic and .EventName (:55). TryGetSubscription(eventName, out subscription) is the per-message lookup (:61-62).
    • Why it's built this way: BrokerConsumerBuilder already rejects duplicates (BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:51-58); the constructor repeats the check because the topology is public and can be built directly (as tests do).
    • Where it's used: built once and registered as a singleton by AddBrokerMessaging (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:94-99), which also registers one scoped consumer per subscription (:103-106). Read by BrokerReceivePipeline (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:120), BrokerMessageBus, BrokerTransportContext, and every receiver and provisioner.

    MessageBusProviders

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/MessageBusProviders.cs:10 · Level 0 · class (public static)

    • What it is: the vocabulary of MessageBus:Provider. Three public string constants name the transports the core package ships (InProcess, RabbitMq, PostgreSql), three internal predicates compare a configured value against them case-insensitively, and an internal lookup table names the adapter package and registration call for the two cloud transports the framework knows about (MessageBusProviders.cs:10-58).

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. BCL only (StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase, string.Equals).

    • Concept introduced, transport selection as a configuration string. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether the move from one process to many is a deployment change rather than a code change, and this class is where that move is spelled. The same host binary runs as a modular monolith with InProcess (the default when the setting is blank, :12-16), as a development microservice deployment on RabbitMq (:18-19), or on the built-in PostgreSQL transport against any PostgreSQL database with PostgreSql (:21-27). [Rubric §33, Developer Experience] assesses whether a misconfiguration tells the developer how to fix it: KnownAdapterTransports exists only to make the "unknown provider" error actionable, and its doc says it registers nothing (:29-33). The provider switch itself is ADR-066; the cloud-neutral split behind the adapter table is ADR-134.

    • Walkthrough

      • InProcess = "InProcess" (MessageBusProviders.cs:16), RabbitMq = "RabbitMq" (:19), PostgreSql = "PostgreSql" (:27). The PostgreSql doc stresses that the broker is a database, not a cloud service, so any managed or self-hosted PostgreSQL serves (:21-26).
      • KnownAdapterTransports (:34-39) is an OrdinalIgnoreCase dictionary of (Package, Registration) pairs: AzureServiceBus maps to MMCA.Common.Azure and services.AddAzureServiceBusTransport() (:37), AmazonSqs to MMCA.Common.Aws and services.AddAmazonSqsTransport() (:38).
      • IsInProcess(provider) (:44-45) is true for a null, empty or whitespace value as well as for InProcess, which is what makes in-process dispatch the zero-configuration default. IsRabbitMq (:50-51) and IsPostgreSql (:56-57) are plain case-insensitive equality checks.

    • Why it's built this way: keeping the names as constants in one place means the selection logic, the outbox default and the startup summary compare against the same strings. Keeping the adapter table internal and descriptive (a package name plus a call, never a type reference) is what lets the core package name a cloud transport in an error message without referencing its SDK, which ADR-134 forbids.

    • Where it's used: AddBrokerMessaging returns before registering any broker service when IsInProcess holds (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:72). ResolveBrokerTransport (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:199) returns RabbitMqBrokerTransport or PostgreSqlBrokerTransport for the built-in names (:201-208), and otherwise builds its failure from these members: the available list starts with the three constants (:225) and the remedy quotes the KnownAdapterTransports entry when one matches (:226). MessageBusSettings resolves the inbox and outbox defaults from IsInProcess (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/MessageBusSettings.cs:142, :180), and each built-in transport returns its constant as its Name. StartupConfigurationSummaryService also references the type.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: KnownAdapterTransports carries only the Azure and AWS entries; a provider name for any other adapter falls through to the generic "register an IBrokerTransport named ..." remedy (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:228).

    PostgreSqlClaimedMessage

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlClaimedMessage.cs:14 · Level 0 · record (internal sealed)

    • What it is: one row of the PostgreSQL transport's messages table as a receiver holds it after a claim: the row Id, the LockToken that proves the claim, the application MessageId, the headers, the body bytes and the DeliveryCount (PostgreSqlClaimedMessage.cs:14-20).

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. BCL types only.

    • Concept: the claim-under-a-lease model is taught at IPostgreSqlMessageStore. What matters about this record is that Id and LockToken travel together: every settle statement matches on both, so a receiver whose lease passed to another claim changes nothing.

    • Walkthrough

      • Six positional members (PostgreSqlClaimedMessage.cs:15-20). Headers is an IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> (:18) and Body a byte[] (:19).
      • PostgreSqlMessageStore builds one per row the claim statement returns, stamping the one lock token it generated for the whole batch (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:103, :119-125).

    • Why it's built this way: a positional record keeps the claim result immutable, so the receiver can hand the same instance to the pipeline, the lease renewer and the settle call without one of them changing what the others see.

    • Where it's used: returned by IPostgreSqlMessageStore.ClaimAsync and passed back to every settle and renew method (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/IPostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:36-71). PostgreSqlReceiver tracks the in-flight ones by Id (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiver.cs:40), and PostgreSqlDispositionApplier settles them. The test double MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/FakePostgreSqlMessageStore.cs builds them directly.

    PostgreSqlTransportSettings

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlTransportSettings.cs:8 · Level 0 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the MessageBus:PostgreSql sub-section that tunes the built-in PostgreSQL transport: the schema the broker's tables live in, the role the migration creates and makes their owner, and whether this host runs that migration at startup (PostgreSqlTransportSettings.cs:8-43). Everything else (connection string, retry, redelivery, backpressure, topology provisioning) comes from the shared MessageBus section.

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. Plain init properties read through IConfiguration's Get<T>().

    • Concept: the parent section and its options shape are taught at MessageBusSettings. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] applies to the default schema: the broker can share a database with the application's own tables because its tables sit in their own transport schema (:16-20). [Rubric §17, DevOps] applies to MigrateOnStartup: the migration needs rights to create a role and a schema, so a host whose database user has neither turns the switch off and creates the schema out of band, which is safe because the DDL is idempotent (:30-35).

    • Walkthrough

      • SectionPath = "MessageBus:PostgreSql" (PostgreSqlTransportSettings.cs:11) and DefaultName = "transport" (:14), the default for both the schema and the role.
      • Schema (:21) and Role (:28) are nullable; their docs state the identifier rule (a letter or underscore, then letters, digits or underscores, at most 63 characters, :18-19, :27). EffectiveSchema (:39) and EffectiveRole (:42) fall back to DefaultName when the configured value is null or whitespace.
      • Role is the role the migration creates when missing, grants to the connecting user, and makes the owner of the schema and its tables, so every service that connects as a member of it can use the transport (:23-27).
      • MigrateOnStartup (:36) defaults to true.

    • Why it's built this way: the doc on MigrateOnStartup names the constraint directly (PostgreSqlTransportSettings.cs:30-35): creating a role and a schema is a privilege an application user often lacks, so a deployment needs a way to run the migration once from a host that has it. The type is internal because only the transport reads it.

    • Where it's used: PostgreSqlBrokerTransport reads it through ReadSettings, which falls back to a default instance when the section is absent (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:99-101). Register feeds EffectiveSchema and EffectiveRole into PostgreSqlTransportSql (:67-68) and uses MigrateOnStartup to decide whether to register PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator and whether the publisher and receiver ensure the schema first (:69-79, :86). Also read by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.PostgreSQL.Tests/PostgreSqlBrokerTransportTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the section carries no validation attributes and is read with Get<T>(); the identifier rule is enforced later, when PostgreSqlTransportSql is constructed during Register (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlTransportSql.cs:35-36), so a bad name fails at startup rather than at bind time.

    IPostgreSqlMessageStore

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/IPostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:10 · Level 1 · interface (internal)

    • What it is: every database operation the PostgreSQL transport performs, as eleven async methods: create the schema, bind topics to a queue, publish, claim, the four settle outcomes (complete, redeliver, dead-letter, release), renew leases, ask when the next row is due, and listen for publish notifications (IPostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:10-88).

    • Depends on: OutgoingBrokerMessage and PostgreSqlClaimedMessage.

    • Concept introduced, a database table as a queue under leased claims. [Rubric §10, Messaging and Integration] assesses whether delivery semantics are explicit rather than inherited from a vendor. Here they are spelled out in the method contracts: a claim takes up to limit due rows "under a lease" (:30-36), and every settle method returns false "when the lease was lost (another claim holds the row)" (:41, :49, :57, :63). A crashed receiver therefore loses nothing: its lease expires and the row becomes claimable again, which is at-least-once delivery that the inbox then dedupes (ADR-021). [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity] applies to ListenAsync: it throws when the connection fails (:79-81), and the receiver falls back to polling rather than stalling.

    • Walkthrough

      • EnsureSchemaAsync (IPostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:15) runs the migration once per process; a failed attempt is retried on the next call (:12).
      • SubscribeAsync(queue, topics) (:22) and PublishAsync(message) (:28): publish inserts one row per queue subscribed to the message's topic and signals those queues (:24).
      • ClaimAsync(queue, limit, lease) (:36) returns the claimed rows, possibly none.
      • CompleteAsync deletes a handled row (:42); RedeliverAsync(message, delay, headers) hides it for delay with new headers and releases the claim (:50); DeadLetterAsync(message, reason, detail) moves it to dead_letters (:58); ReleaseAsync frees the claim without settling, so the row is claimable at once (:64).
      • RenewAsync(messages, lease) (:71) extends the lease of every row still held; NextDueAsync(queue) (:77) returns the wait until the next claimable row, or null for an empty queue.
      • ListenAsync(queue, notified) (:87) calls notified per notification and once when listening starts (:84).

    • Why it's built this way: putting the SQL behind an interface separates the receiver's concurrency logic from the database, so PostgreSqlReceiver and PostgreSqlDispositionApplier are unit-tested against MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/FakePostgreSqlMessageStore.cs without a server.

    • Where it's used: implemented by PostgreSqlMessageStore. Consumed by PostgreSqlReceiver, PostgreSqlPublisher, PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator and PostgreSqlDispositionApplier.

    BrokerTransportPolicies

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:16 · Level 2 · class (public static)

    • What it is: the receive-side policies every broker transport shares, as pure functions of MessageBusSettings: the exponential in-process retry delay, the second-level redelivery intervals (clamped to a transport's delay cap), and the two backpressure knobs (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:16-104).

    • Depends on: MessageBusSettings only. No transport library.

    • Concept introduced, one failure policy across interchangeable transports. [Rubric §10, Messaging and Integration] assesses whether poison and transient failures are handled deliberately rather than by each transport's defaults, and [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity] assesses whether a transient fault is absorbed before it becomes a dead letter. Because IBrokerTransport lets an adapter package supply the transport, the retry and redelivery numbers would otherwise be re-derived (and drift) per broker. This class is the single definition: the framework receive pipeline reads the retry delay and redelivery intervals from it, and each transport reads its backpressure values from it. In-process retry absorbs a blip measured in seconds; second-level redelivery re-enqueues the message over one minute, ten minutes and one hour by default, so an outage measured in minutes or hours does not dead-letter the event, and every in-process retry is exhausted before a redelivery is asked for (:10-14). Poison-message handling is ADR-087; the library policy that keeps the transports as framework code is ADR-118.

    • Walkthrough

      • RetryDelay(settings, retryNumber) (BrokerTransportPolicies.cs:27-40) rejects a retry number below 1 (:30), doubles RetryMinIntervalSeconds per retry and caps the result at RetryMaxIntervalSeconds (:32-37), with the exponent capped at 30 (:36). With the defaults (1 and 30 seconds) the five retries wait 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds (:19-22); RetryLimit defaults to 5 (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/MessageBusSettings.cs:94).
      • BuildRedeliveryIntervals(settings) (:52-53) delegates to the two-argument overload with no cap.
      • BuildRedeliveryIntervals(settings, maxRedeliveryDelay) (:65-75) falls back to MessageBusSettings.DefaultRedeliveryIntervalsSeconds when nothing is configured, drops non-positive entries (:72), and shortens every interval longer than the cap to the cap (:74). A null or non-positive cap means no cap (:69). A zero interval is dropped because it would redeliver immediately, which is what the in-process retry already does, and an empty result turns second-level redelivery off (:43-48).
      • ResolvePrefetchCount (:85-90) and ResolveConcurrentMessageLimit (:98-103) return the configured value only when it is greater than zero, otherwise null so the transport keeps its own default. The doc explains why the guard is code rather than a [Range] attribute: AddBrokerMessaging binds the section with Get<MessageBusSettings>(), which never runs DataAnnotations (:77-81).

    • Why it's built this way: as pure functions with no transport type in their signatures, the policies can be shared by transports that have nothing else in common (an AMQP channel, a PostgreSQL table, a cloud SDK receiver), and they are trivially unit-tested. Returning null for an unset knob, rather than a framework default, leaves each broker's own sensible default in place.

    • Where it's used: BrokerReceivePipeline builds its intervals with the transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:72) and waits RetryDelay between attempts (:197). PostgreSqlReceiverOptions resolves its concurrency and claim batch from the two backpressure functions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiverOptions.cs:41-42), as do RabbitMqBrokerTransport (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:95, :105), AmazonSqsReceiver (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aws/Messaging/AmazonSqsReceiver.cs:75, :81) and AzureServiceBusReceiver (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Azure/Messaging/AzureServiceBusReceiver.cs:88-89). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportPoliciesTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the cap clamps rather than rejects, so a configured interval longer than a broker allows (Amazon SQS caps a delay at 15 minutes, :59-60) runs at the cap without an error.

    PostgreSqlDispositionApplier

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlDispositionApplier.cs:17 · Level 2 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the one function that turns a BrokerDisposition returned by the receive pipeline into the matching IPostgreSqlMessageStore settle call (PostgreSqlDispositionApplier.cs:17-49).

    • Depends on: IPostgreSqlMessageStore, PostgreSqlClaimedMessage, BrokerDisposition and its Redeliver and DeadLetter cases, BrokerHeaders.

    • Concept: the pipeline-decides, transport-acts split is taught at IBrokerTransport; this is the PostgreSQL transport's half of it.

    • Walkthrough

      • ApplyAsync(store, message, disposition, cancellationToken) (PostgreSqlDispositionApplier.cs:25-48) null-guards its three references (:31-33) and switches on the disposition (:35).
      • Redeliver calls RedeliverAsync with the redelivery delay and a copy of the row's headers in which BrokerHeaders.RedeliveryCount is set to the new count (:37-44).
      • DeadLetter calls DeadLetterAsync with the reason and detail (:45); anything else completes the row (:46).
      • The result is the store's: false means the lease had already been lost and another claim owns the row (:22).

    • Why it's built this way: carrying the redelivery count in the row's headers is what lets the next delivery's pipeline know which redelivery interval comes next, since the row itself is re-used rather than re-published. Keeping the mapping in a static function makes every branch testable without a receiver.

    • Where it's used: PostgreSqlReceiver calls it after each pipeline run (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiver.cs:230). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlDispositionApplierTests.cs.

    PostgreSqlPublisher

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlPublisher.cs:13 · Level 2 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the PostgreSQL transport's IBrokerPublisher: it ensures the schema exists when this host migrates at startup, then hands the message to the store's fan-out insert (PostgreSqlPublisher.cs:13-27).

    • Depends on: IPostgreSqlMessageStore, IBrokerPublisher, OutgoingBrokerMessage.

    • Concept: the publisher contract is taught at IBrokerPublisher.

    • Walkthrough

      • Primary constructor over the store and a migrateOnStartup flag (PostgreSqlPublisher.cs:13).
      • PublishAsync (:16-26) null-guards the message, awaits EnsureSchemaAsync when migrateOnStartup is set (:20-23), then store.PublishAsync (:25).

    • Why it's built this way: the outbox processor can publish before the hosted PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator has finished, and the store's EnsureSchemaAsync runs the migration only once per process (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:54-67), so awaiting it here costs nothing after the first call and closes that startup race.

    • Where it's used: registered as the singleton IBrokerPublisher by PostgreSqlBrokerTransport (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:73). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransportTests.cs and BrokerTransportRegistrationTests.cs in the same test project.

    PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator.cs:12 · Level 2 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: an IHostedService whose StartAsync is the store's EnsureSchemaAsync and whose StopAsync does nothing (PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator.cs:12-19).

    • Depends on: IPostgreSqlMessageStore; Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.IHostedService.

    • Concept: [Rubric §17, DevOps]: the schema is created by the application at startup, with an opt-out at PostgreSqlTransportSettings for a host without the rights.

    • Walkthrough

      • StartAsync (PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator.cs:15) returns store.EnsureSchemaAsync(cancellationToken); StopAsync (:18) returns a completed task.

    • Why it's built this way: hosted services start in registration order, and PostgreSqlBrokerTransport registers this one before the receiver, so the migration finishes before the receiver starts claiming (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:75-79).

    • Where it's used: registered only when MigrateOnStartup is true (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:76-79). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransportTests.cs.

    PostgreSqlReceiverOptions

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiverOptions.cs:11 · Level 3 · record (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the seven values PostgreSqlReceiver runs with: concurrency, claim batch size, whether to migrate and whether to provision topology first, and the lease, renewal and poll intervals (PostgreSqlReceiverOptions.cs:11-53).

    • Depends on: MessageBusSettings, BrokerTransportPolicies.

    • Concept: backpressure is taught at BrokerTransportPolicies; the lease model at IPostgreSqlMessageStore.

    • Walkthrough

      • Positional members (PostgreSqlReceiverOptions.cs:12-18).
      • DefaultLease is 60 seconds, "long enough to ride out a renewal missed to a database blip" (:20-21); DefaultRenewInterval is 20 seconds, a third of the lease, so one missed renewal does not lose the claim (:23-24); DefaultPollInterval is 5 seconds, the fallback when no notification arrives (:26-27).
      • From(settings, migrateOnStartup) (:37-52): concurrency is MessageBus:ConcurrentMessageLimit, else Environment.ProcessorCount, at least 1 (:41); the claim batch is MessageBus:PrefetchCount, else the concurrency, clamped to [1, concurrency] (:42); ProvisionTopology comes from the shared settings (:48), which default it to true (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/MessageBusSettings.cs:84).

    • Why it's built this way: a batch larger than the concurrency would claim rows no worker can start, and their leases would tick while they wait, so the clamp keeps every claimed row immediately runnable. The three timings are not configuration keys; only a test adjusts them, through the internal constructor of PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.

    • Where it's used: built in PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.Register (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:86-87) and passed to PostgreSqlReceiver. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiverTests.cs.

    PostgreSqlTransportSql

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlTransportSql.cs:24 · Level 3 · class (internal sealed partial)

    • What it is: every SQL statement the PostgreSQL transport runs, built once per schema and role: the idempotent migration, subscribe, the fan-out publish, claim, the four settle statements, renew, next-due and LISTEN, plus the identifier validation that makes writing the schema and role names into SQL safe (PostgreSqlTransportSql.cs:24-237).

    • Depends on: BrokerNaming (to fit the notification channel name). BCL GeneratedRegex, SHA256, BinaryPrimitives.

    • Concept: [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] applies to the three-table design: subscriptions binds topics to queues, messages holds one row per queue per publish with visible_after and the lease columns, and dead_letters keeps settled failures with a reason (:206-234). The claim uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (:67), so competing receivers on several replicas take disjoint rows without blocking each other.

    • Walkthrough

      • The constructor (PostgreSqlTransportSql.cs:33-100) validates the schema and role against MessageBus:PostgreSql:Schema and :Role (:35-36), derives NotifyChannel as {schema}_messages fitted to MaxIdentifierLength 63 (:27, :40), and builds each statement.
      • Publish (:50-57) inserts one messages row per subscribed queue in one statement and calls pg_notify once per distinct queue with the queue name as payload (:57).
      • Claim (:59-72) selects due rows (visible_after <= now() and no live lock), oldest first, LIMIT @limit FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then stamps lock_token, locked_until = now() + @lease and increments delivery_count (:69).
      • Complete, Redeliver, DeadLetter and Release (:74-88) all match WHERE id = @id AND lock_token = @lock_token, which is what makes a lost lease a no-op. Redeliver pushes visible_after out by @delay and replaces the headers (:76-79); DeadLetter moves the row in one DELETE ... RETURNING into INSERT (:81-86).
      • Renew (:90-93) extends every (id, lock_token) pair passed as arrays; NextDue (:95-97) returns seconds until the earliest claimable row.
      • ValidateIdentifier (:159-166) throws InvalidOperationException naming the key unless the value matches ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,62}$ (:144); Quote (:150) double-quotes it.
      • BuildMigrate (:185-236) takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed by MigrationLockKey (the first eight bytes of a SHA-256 of mmca-broker-transport: plus the schema, :174-175, :193), creates the role if missing and grants it to the current user (:194-203), creates the schema owned by the role (:204), then SET LOCAL ROLE so the tables and indexes are created as, and owned by, the role (:205-235).

    • Why it's built this way: the schema and role are identifiers, which cannot be passed as parameters, so they are validated to a plain-identifier pattern and quoted, and every value is a parameter; that is the justification the store records on its CA2100 suppressions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:18-19). The advisory lock serializes replicas migrating the same schema at once, and owning the tables through a shared role lets each service's own database user use them once it is a member.

    • Where it's used: constructed by PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.Register (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:68) and handed to PostgreSqlMessageStore. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlTransportSqlTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the migration only creates; nothing in source drops or alters the transport tables, so a later column change would need its own migration step.

    BrokerTransportContext

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportContext.cs:11 · Level 4 · class (public sealed)

    • What it is: the parameter object every IBrokerTransport receives: the bound MessageBus section, the resolved broker connection string (or null), the application configuration for any transport-specific keys, and the BrokerTopology this host consumes (BrokerTransportContext.cs:11-52).

    • Depends on: MessageBusSettings, BrokerTopology and Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.IConfiguration.

    • Concept: [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses whether a contract can grow without breaking its implementers. Bundling the inputs into one class keeps IBrokerTransport.Register at two parameters, so the framework can hand transports more context (as it did with Topology) without changing a signature that adapter packages implement. The transport abstraction itself is taught at IBrokerTransport.

    • Walkthrough

      • The constructor (BrokerTransportContext.cs:18-32) null-guards settings, configuration and topology (:24-26) but deliberately not connectionString, which is nullable.
      • Topology (:38) is the queue this host receives on and the topics bound to it; its doc notes it is also registered as a singleton so a hosted receiver can take it from DI (:34-37).
      • Settings (:41) and Configuration (:51) are get-only.
      • ConnectionString (:48) is resolved, per its doc, from MessageBus:ConnectionString, then ConnectionStrings:rabbitmq, then ConnectionStrings:messaging; null means "none is set", and the transport then keeps its own default host (:43-47).

    • Why it's built this way: the null connection string is a meaningful value, not an error: a transport with a default host can fall back to it, while PostgreSqlBrokerTransport rejects it because a PostgreSQL broker has no default host. The context carries the value and leaves that policy to each transport.

    • Where it's used: built once at the end of AddBrokerMessaging, after the topology and the receive pipeline are registered, with the connection string from ResolveBrokerConnectionString, and passed to the selected transport's Register (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:150-158, :293). Read by both built-in transports and by the adapter transports AzureServiceBusTransport and AmazonSqsTransport; constructed directly in MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportRegistrationTests.cs.

    PostgreSqlMessageStore

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:16 · Level 4 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the Npgsql implementation of IPostgreSqlMessageStore: it runs the PostgreSqlTransportSql statements on an NpgsqlDataSource, serializes headers as jsonb, and owns the once-per-process migration (PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:16-301).

    • Depends on: IPostgreSqlMessageStore, PostgreSqlTransportSql, PostgreSqlClaimedMessage, OutgoingBrokerMessage; Npgsql (NpgsqlDataSource, NpgsqlDbType.Jsonb), System.Text.Json.

    • Concept: the leased-claim contract is taught at IPostgreSqlMessageStore; this is its only production implementation.

    • Walkthrough

      • The constructor (PostgreSqlMessageStore.cs:31-39) takes the data source, whether it owns it, and the statements. DisposeAsync and Dispose dispose the data source only when owned (:247-262).
      • SerializeHeaders and DeserializeHeaders (:44-51) map headers to and from a JSON object, read back with an ordinal comparer.
      • EnsureSchemaAsync (:54-67) starts MigrateAsync under a lock when no attempt exists or the last one faulted or was canceled (:58-63), and returns WaitAsync(cancellationToken) (:65), so a caller that gives up does not cancel the migration another caller awaits. MigrateAsync runs the migration in one transaction (:265-282).
      • PublishAsync (:84-98) binds topic, message id, jsonb headers, body and the notify channel (:91-95).
      • ClaimAsync (:101-133) generates one lock token for the batch (:103), reads each returned row into a PostgreSqlClaimedMessage, and sorts by Id because RETURNING order is unspecified (:130-131).
      • CompleteAsync, RedeliverAsync, DeadLetterAsync and ReleaseAsync (:136-173) share SettleAsync (:284-300), which binds id and lock_token and reports success as "more than zero rows affected" (:298).
      • RenewAsync (:176-192) returns early for an empty set (:179-182) and otherwise renews all rows in one statement.
      • ListenAsync (:208-244) opens a dedicated connection, forwards notifications whose payload equals the queue (:215-221), issues LISTEN, calls notified once because anything published before LISTEN took effect raised no notification (:229-230), then waits on the connection until canceled (:232-243).

    • Why it's built this way: borrowing a shared data source (ownsDataSource: false) lets a host's PostgreSQL authentication customization reach the broker connection, the migration included, while a store that created its own data source still cleans it up.

    • Where it's used: registered as a singleton by PostgreSqlBrokerTransport through CreateStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:72, :103-109) and resolved by the publisher, migrator and receiver. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlMessageStoreTests.cs and, against a real server, MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.PostgreSQL.Tests/PostgreSqlLeaseRenewalTests.cs.

    PostgreSqlReceiver

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiver.cs:23 · Level 4 · class (internal sealed partial)

    • What it is: the PostgreSQL transport's hosted receiver: a BackgroundService that claims due rows of this host's queue up to a concurrency limit, runs each through the framework IBrokerReceivePipeline, applies the returned disposition, renews leases of in-flight rows, and wakes on LISTEN notifications with polling as the fallback (PostgreSqlReceiver.cs:23-372).

    • Depends on: BrokerTopology, IBrokerReceivePipeline, IPostgreSqlMessageStore, PostgreSqlReceiverOptions, PostgreSqlDispositionApplier, IncomingBrokerMessage.

    • Concept: [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity]: every step that touches the database is wrapped so a failure is logged and retried after RetryDelay (5 seconds, PostgreSqlReceiver.cs:26) rather than ending the service, and a row that cannot be settled is released or left for its lease to expire, never lost.

    • Walkthrough

      • State: a SemaphoreSlim sized to Concurrency (:67), an in-flight map by row id (:40), and a one-slot wake channel that drops extra writes (:41).
      • ExecuteAsync (:78-101) runs PrepareAsync, starts the listen and renew loops (:85-86), runs the receive loop, and on stop drains in-flight rows for up to DrainTimeout 10 seconds (:32, :99, :347-356).
      • PrepareAsync (:117-152) ensures the schema when MigrateOnStartup (:123-126) and subscribes the queue to the distinct topics of the topology when ProvisionTopology (:128-134), retrying on failure (:142-150).
      • ReceiveLoopAsync (:154-199) waits for one free slot, takes up to ClaimBatchSize more without waiting (:158-163), claims that many rows (:168), returns unused slots (:183-186), starts one task per row (:188-192), and waits for work when nothing was claimed (:194-197).
      • ProcessAsync (:221-244) builds an IncomingBrokerMessage with the row id as its transport id (:223), runs the pipeline (:226), and applies the disposition with CancellationToken.None so a decided outcome is written even while the host stops (:228-230). A lost lease is logged (:232); a cancellation or settle failure releases the claim (:237, :241-242), and a failed release leaves the lease to expire (:246-257).
      • WaitForWorkAsync (:259-290) sleeps until the sooner of PollInterval and the queue's next due row, never less than 100 ms (:29, :264-277), and wakes early on a notification (:283).
      • ListenLoopAsync (:292-316) keeps a LISTEN open and restarts it after a failure; polling keeps the queue moving meanwhile (:307). RenewLoopAsync (:318-345) renews every in-flight lease each RenewInterval.

    • Why it's built this way: claiming only as many rows as there are free workers keeps every lease running against work that is actually executing, and notification plus polling bounds the latency of a publish to near zero while surviving a dropped listener. Settling outside the host's token avoids reprocessing a message whose handler already succeeded.

    • Where it's used: registered as a hosted service by PostgreSqlBrokerTransport only when the topology has subscriptions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:81-93). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlReceiverTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the drain waits at most 10 seconds (:32); a handler still running after that settles after the receiver is disposed, and its slot release is swallowed (:207-218).

    IBrokerTransport

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/IBrokerTransport.cs:22 · Level 5 · interface

    • What it is: the extension point a broker transport implements: a provider Name that MessageBus:Provider selects it by, the longest redelivery delay its broker can schedule, and one Register call that adds its publisher and hosted receiver (IBrokerTransport.cs:22-52).

    • Depends on: BrokerTransportContext and Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.IServiceCollection.

    • Concept introduced, a pluggable transport behind a name. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses whether a variation point is expressed as a strategy rather than a switch statement, and [Rubric §32, Dependency and Supply-Chain] assesses whether optional vendor dependencies stay out of the core. The boundary is narrow by design: AddBrokerMessaging owns everything that is the same on every broker (topology, wire format, the receive pipeline with origin restore, inbox, retry, redelivery and dead-letter decisions, the outbox-only publish path, tracing), and a transport only moves bytes: it publishes an OutgoingBrokerMessage to a topic, delivers each message on the host's queue to IBrokerReceivePipeline, and carries out the BrokerDisposition the pipeline returns (:8-14). The core ships RabbitMQ and PostgreSQL; a cloud broker is an adapter package with one registration method, so the core packages never reference a vendor SDK (:17-19). Application code never sees which transport won: it publishes through IMessageBus (ADR-066, ADR-118, ADR-134).

    • Walkthrough

      • Name (IBrokerTransport.cs:28) is compared case-insensitively against MessageBus:Provider and is meant to be stable and vendor-shaped, for example AzureServiceBus (:24-27).
      • MaxRedeliveryDelay (:35) is the broker's delay cap, or null for none; the receive pipeline clamps every redelivery interval to it (Amazon SQS caps a delay at 15 minutes, :30-34).
      • Register(services, context) (:51) adds a singleton IBrokerPublisher and a hosted receiver for context.Topology's queue; with ProvisionTopology set, the receiver creates topics, queue and bindings idempotently before receiving and the publisher creates a missing topic on first publish (:37-43). It runs while AddBrokerMessaging runs, so a missing namespace or connection string throws at startup rather than at the first publish (:44-47).

    • Why it's built this way: making the transport an instance with a name, rather than an enum the core switches on, is what lets a new broker ship without a core release, and what keeps the core free of every cloud SDK. Keeping retry and dead-letter decisions in the shared pipeline means a new transport cannot get them wrong.

    • Where it's used: AddBrokerTransport rejects a blank Name and registers the instance with TryAddEnumerable (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:174-183). ResolveBrokerTransport (:199) returns a built-in for RabbitMq or PostgreSql (:201-208), otherwise a registered instance whose name matches, read off the service collection because the choice is made before any provider exists (:213); with no match it throws an InvalidOperationException naming the available providers and the remedy (:225-230). AddBrokerMessaging resolves the transport before registering anything (:82-84), passes its MaxRedeliveryDelay to BrokerReceivePipeline (:108-115), and calls Register last (:150-158). Implemented by RabbitMqBrokerTransport, PostgreSqlBrokerTransport, AzureServiceBusTransport and AmazonSqsTransport; registration behavior covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/BrokerTransportRegistrationTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: only ImplementationInstance registrations are seen (DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:213), so a transport registered by type or factory rather than through AddBrokerTransport is not found.

    PostgreSqlBrokerTransport

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.PostgreSql · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:36 · Level 6 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the built-in IBrokerTransport for MessageBus:Provider = PostgreSql: topics, queues and delayed redeliveries kept in three tables of one PostgreSQL database, written on Npgsql, so any PostgreSQL (Cloud SQL, Amazon RDS, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, a container) is the broker (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:10-36).

    • Depends on: IBrokerTransport, BrokerTransportContext, PostgreSqlTransportSettings, PostgreSqlTransportSql, PostgreSqlMessageStore, PostgreSqlPublisher, PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator, PostgreSqlReceiver, PostgreSqlReceiverOptions, MessageBusProviders, NpgsqlDataSources; Npgsql.

    • Concept: the transport strategy is taught at IBrokerTransport. What is particular here is [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] without a broker service: a database is the broker, which is why this transport is core rather than an adapter (ADR-113, ADR-134). A publish inserts one row per subscribed queue and wakes receivers with pg_notify; a receiver claims with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED under a renewed lease; a redelivery pushes visible_after out, so there is no delay cap; a dead letter moves the row to {schema}.dead_letters (:16-22). [Rubric §17, DevOps] applies to the hosted-service ordering below.

    • Walkthrough

      • Name returns MessageBusProviders.PostgreSql (PostgreSqlBrokerTransport.cs:55); MaxRedeliveryDelay is null (:58).
      • A public parameterless constructor (:41-43) and an internal one taking a function that adjusts the resolved PostgreSqlReceiverOptions, which exists only so a test can shorten the lease, renewal and poll interval (:45-52).
      • Register(services, context) (:61-94) fails a missing connection string first (:66), reads PostgreSqlTransportSettings (:67), builds PostgreSqlTransportSql from the effective schema and role (:68), and registers the store singleton (:72) and the PostgreSqlPublisher as IBrokerPublisher (:73). When MigrateOnStartup holds it adds PostgreSqlSchemaMigrator (:76-79). With no subscriptions it stops there, a publish-only host (:81-84); otherwise it resolves the receiver options (:86-87) and adds the PostgreSqlReceiver hosted service (:88-93).
      • ReadSettings (:99-101) binds MessageBus:PostgreSql, defaulting when the section is absent.
      • CreateStore (:103-109) asks NpgsqlDataSources.Resolve for a shared data source for the connection string; with one the store borrows it (:107), without one it creates and owns its own (:108).
      • RequireConnectionString (:111-117) throws an InvalidOperationException telling the operator to set MessageBus:ConnectionString (or ConnectionStrings:messaging), because unlike RabbitMQ there is no default host (:113-116).

    • Why it's built this way: hosted services start in registration order, so registering the migrator before the receiver guarantees the schema exists before the first claim (:75). Resolving a shared data source means a host that registers an INpgsqlDataSourceConfigurator (an RDS, Cloud SQL or Entra token provider) runs the transport, migration included, on the same authenticated NpgsqlDataSource its PostgreSQL contexts use (:30-33).

    • Where it's used: instantiated by ResolveBrokerTransport when the provider is PostgreSql (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:206-208). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/PostgreSql/PostgreSqlBrokerTransportTests.cs and, against a real server, MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.PostgreSQL.Tests/PostgreSqlBrokerTransportTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the startup migration needs rights to create a role and a schema; a host without them sets MigrateOnStartup to false and relies on another host or a deployment step to run the idempotent DDL (see PostgreSqlTransportSettings). Because MaxRedeliveryDelay is null (:58), every configured redelivery interval runs unclamped.

    IRabbitMqOperations

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/IRabbitMqOperations.cs:9 · Level 0 · interface (internal)

    • What it is: the five broker calls the RabbitMQ transport makes outside its consume loop: declare a fanout exchange, declare a queue, check a queue exists, bind a queue to an exchange, and publish a confirmed message (IRabbitMqOperations.cs:9-55). The interface doc names RabbitMqChannelOperations as its one real implementation (IRabbitMqOperations.cs:3-8).

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. The signatures use BCL types only (IDictionary<string, object?> for declaration arguments, ReadOnlyMemory<byte> for the body, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> for headers), so the RabbitMQ.Client types stay behind the implementation.

    • Concept introduced, a test boundary around a broker client. [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether the logic worth testing can run without its infrastructure. The naming, provisioning and disposition rules of this transport are pure decisions about which entity to declare and which queue a copy goes to; the interface doc says it exists so those rules are "testable without a broker" (IRabbitMqOperations.cs:4-6). RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqDispositionApplier and RabbitMqPublisher take this interface rather than a channel, and the test project supplies a recording fake (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RecordingRabbitMqOperations.cs). The consume loop itself is not behind it: RabbitMqReceiver talks to its consume channel directly.

    • Walkthrough

      • DeclareFanoutExchangeAsync(exchange) (IRabbitMqOperations.cs:15): durable fanout exchange, idempotent.
      • DeclareQueueAsync(queue, arguments) (:22): durable queue, idempotent for identical arguments.
      • EnsureQueueExistsAsync(queue) (:28): a passive declaration that throws when the queue is missing.
      • BindQueueAsync(queue, exchange) (:35): binds a queue to a fanout exchange.
      • PublishAsync(exchange, routingKey, mandatory, body, headers) (:48-54): a persistent publish that completes only on the broker's confirm, throwing on a nack or, with mandatory, on an unroutable message (:37-39). "" is the default exchange, where the routing key is a queue name (:41-42).

    • Why it's built this way: every operation the transport needs before acknowledging a delivery is a confirmed, awaited call, so a fake that records the calls is enough to prove the ordering and the arguments.

    • Where it's used: implemented by RabbitMqChannelOperations; consumed by RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqPublisher and RabbitMqDispositionApplier.

    NativePushPayloads

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Notifications.Push · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/NativePushPayloads.cs:13 · Level 0 · class (public static)

    • What it is: the pure helper that builds the two platform-native JSON payloads for OS-level push: the FCM v1 message for Android and the APNs alert for iOS (NativePushPayloads.cs:13-68). It holds no state and references no vendor SDK, which is why the payload shapes can be asserted in a unit test and shared by every cloud adapter.

    • Depends on: System.Text.Json for serialization. No first-party service types at all.

    • Concept introduced, the third notification channel's wire contract. [Rubric §9, API and Contract Design] assesses whether the shape of a message crossing a boundary is defined in one place rather than assembled ad hoc at each call site, and [Rubric §14, Testability] assesses whether the parts worth testing can be tested without their infrastructure. The framework already carries a durable per-user notification inbox and a transient SignalR push; native OS-level delivery (ADR-044) is the third, and it is the only one whose payload is dictated by an external vendor. FCM v1 wants a message envelope with a notification block; APNs wants a reserved aps block with an alert inside it and any application data as sibling top-level keys. The class doc (NativePushPayloads.cs:5-12) records how the adapters share that contract: Azure Notification Hubs forwards these payloads verbatim, SNS mobile push wraps them in its per-platform message structure, and the FCM adapter maps the same fields onto FirebaseAdmin's typed message with a test pinning the equivalence, so one notification looks the same on a device whichever cloud delivered it. [Rubric §32, Dependency and Supply-Chain] applies through the same doc: the helper is pure System.Text.Json, so the core package stays free of any push vendor SDK (ADR-134).

    • Walkthrough

      • BuildFcmV1Payload(title, body, metadata) (NativePushPayloads.cs:20-35) guards title and body against null (:22-23), builds notification from them (:25-28), attaches data only when the metadata dictionary is non-empty (:29-32), and serializes the whole thing under a message root (:34).
      • BuildApnsPayload(title, body, metadata) (NativePushPayloads.cs:42-67) applies the same null guards (:44-45), builds the aps.alert block (:47-53), then lifts each metadata pair to a top-level custom key, which is where APNs expects application data. The guard at :58-62 is the interesting line: a metadata key literally named aps is skipped, because writing it would clobber the alert block and produce a notification the device shows as nothing.
      • User tags and audience chunking are not here. Those are Azure Notification Hubs concepts and live in the Azure adapter's NativePushUserTags.

    • Why it's built this way: keeping this pure and public means the vendor payload shapes are covered by fast tests that need no notification hub, no credentials and no network, and every adapter package composes against one definition instead of carrying its own copy.

    • Where it's used: AzureNotificationHubNativePushSender calls both builders for user-targeted sends (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Azure/Notifications/AzureNotificationHubNativePushSender.cs:35-36) and for broadcasts (:37-38); SnsPushMessage calls both to fill its per-platform structure (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aws/Notifications/SnsPushMessage.cs:29-30). FcmPushMessage references the type without calling it, as the class doc describes. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Notifications/Push/NativePushPayloadsTests.cs, with the FCM equivalence in MMCA.Common/Tests/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Gcp.Tests/Notifications/FcmNativePushSenderTests.cs.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the helper takes no options, so a host wanting a different payload shape replaces INativePushSender rather than configuring this.

    RabbitMqConnectionSource

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqConnectionSource.cs:11 · Level 0 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: one lazily opened RabbitMQ connection with automatic recovery (RabbitMqConnectionSource.cs:11-115). The publisher and the receiver each own one, so a publisher held up by broker flow control never stalls the consumer's acknowledgements (RabbitMqConnectionSource.cs:5-9).

    • Depends on: RabbitMQ.Client's ConnectionFactory and IConnection; a SemaphoreSlim (:14).

    • Concept introduced, deferred connection opening. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses how a service behaves when a dependency is down. Opening is deferred to the first use, so a host whose broker is unreachable still starts and the outbox keeps what it cannot publish; a failed open is not cached, so the next call tries again (RabbitMqConnectionSource.cs:5-7). Recovery after the connection exists is delegated to the client.

    • Walkthrough

      • The constructor (RabbitMqConnectionSource.cs:21-22) only builds the factory; nothing touches the network.
      • CreateFactory (:31-47) turns on AutomaticRecoveryEnabled and TopologyRecoveryEnabled with a 5-second NetworkRecoveryInterval (:35-37), sets the ClientProvidedName shown in the management UI, and applies the URI only when one is given (:41-44); with none the client's default amqp://guest:guest@localhost:5672 applies (:19).
      • GetConnectionAsync (:52-72) returns the cached connection without locking (:56-59), otherwise takes the gate (:61) and opens with ??= (:65), so concurrent first callers share one open. An exception escapes before assignment, which is why a failed open is retried.
      • DisposeAsync (:75-98) closes with a handshake and swallows a close failure on a connection the broker already dropped (:87-92); the synchronous Dispose (:104-114) drops the connection without the handshake. Both are idempotent through _disposed.

    • Why it's built this way: one connection per role isolates publishing from consuming, and automatic topology recovery means a broker restart re-opens the connection, its channels and the consumer without transport code (:24-26).

    • Where it's used: RabbitMqBrokerTransport creates one named {queue} (publish) for the publisher and one named {queue} (receive) for the receiver (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:43, :56); RabbitMqChannelOperations and RabbitMqReceiver open channels on it.

    RabbitMqHeaders

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqHeaders.cs:11 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the converter between the framework's string-to-string headers and AMQP header tables (RabbitMqHeaders.cs:11-72).

    • Depends on: BCL only (Encoding.UTF8, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture). The keys it carries are defined by BrokerHeaders.

    • Concept: the transport-neutral header contract is taught at BrokerHeaders; this is the RabbitMQ encoding of it.

    • Walkthrough

      • Encode (RabbitMqHeaders.cs:19-30) copies every pair into an ordinal dictionary as a string value (:24-27). Every value goes over the wire as an AMQP long string (:5-8).
      • Decode (:40-71) is the reverse, and is wider because the client hands a long string back as UTF-8 bytes. Byte arrays decode as UTF-8, strings pass through, booleans become "true"/"false", other IFormattable values format invariantly, and anything else is dropped (:55-62). A key with the x- prefix (:14) is skipped (:50-53): those are headers RabbitMQ stamps itself, such as the x-death table a delay queue adds, so a redelivered copy never accumulates them (:33-36).

    • Why it's built this way: dropping broker headers on read matters because RabbitMqDispositionApplier republishes a copy built from the decoded headers; without the filter each trip through a delay queue would carry a growing x-death history.

    • Where it's used: Encode by RabbitMqChannelOperations (RabbitMqChannelOperations.cs:67); Decode by RabbitMqReceiver (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:209). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqHeadersTests.cs.

    PushNotificationSettings

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Notifications.Push · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/PushNotificationSettings.cs:8 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the PushNotifications section: the on switch, the SignalR hub path, the regular expression a channel key must match before a client may join or leave a channel, and the per-user cap on simultaneous hub connections (PushNotificationSettings.cs:8-66).

    • Depends on: NotificationScopeKey from MMCA.Common.Shared.Notifications (:1), for the Pattern constant that supplies the default. See NotificationScopeKey. No externals beyond a single [Range(0, 10_000)] data annotation on MaxConnectionsPerUser (PushNotificationSettings.cs:49), which is what ValidateDataAnnotations() checks at startup.

    • Concept introduced: allow-listing client-supplied group names. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §26, Front-End Security] both apply. A hub method that takes a channel key and calls Groups.AddToGroupAsync is joining a SignalR group named by the CLIENT. With no constraint, a caller could join any group the server publishes to and receive another event's or another session's traffic. ChannelKeyPattern is that constraint (PushNotificationSettings.cs:27-37).

      [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] shows up in where the default comes from. The property does not hard-code a regex: it defaults to NotificationScopeKey.Pattern (PushNotificationSettings.cs:37, the constant "^(event|session):[0-9]+$" at NotificationScopeKey.cs:32), the SAME constant the producers NotificationScopeKey.ForEvent and ForSession format against (NotificationScopeKey.cs:44, :43). Producer and guard therefore cannot drift apart by editing one of them; a host that overrides the pattern from configuration takes that alignment on itself, which the doc says outright (PushNotificationSettings.cs:33-34).

      [Rubric §11, Security] also covers MaxConnectionsPerUser: an [Authorize] hub without a connection cap lets one authenticated user open unbounded WebSockets and exhaust the replica, denying live notifications to everyone else (PushNotificationSettings.cs:39-50). 0 opts a host back out of the cap entirely.

    • Walkthrough: one static field and five init properties.

      • SectionName = "PushNotifications" (PushNotificationSettings.cs:11).
      • Enabled (:14): plain bool, default false.
      • HubPath (:25): defaults to "/hubs/notifications". Its doc comment (:16-24) carries two couplings. The JWT bearer handlers accept the query-string access_token on this path (and under /hubs), and a host that moves the hub elsewhere must also set RateLimiting:HubPathPrefixes, which the rate limiter reads separately. And the shipped client, NotificationHubService in MMCA.Common.UI, connects at the default /hubs/notifications with no setting to follow a move, so changing this path also means changing the client, the gateway route, RateLimiting:HubPathPrefixes and the same-origin proxy exemption.
      • ChannelKeyPattern (:37). Enforcement lives in NotificationHub: EnsureValidChannelKey (NotificationHub.cs:174-184) pulls a Regex out of a static ConcurrentDictionary cache keyed on the pattern string (:176-178, the cache declared at :47) and throws HubException("Invalid channel key.") on an empty or non-matching key (:180-183); both JoinChannelAsync (:130) and LeaveChannelAsync (:147) call it before touching Groups. The compiled regex carries a one-second match timeout (NotificationHub.cs:44, :178), so a pathological configured pattern cannot hang the connection, and the cache means join and leave do not recompile per call (:46).
      • MaxConnectionsPerUser (:50): [Range(0, 10_000)] (:49), default 20; 0 disables the cap (PushNotificationSettings.cs:39-42). Tagged SEC-ADC-25 in the remarks: the hub is [Authorize] but had no OnConnectedAsync override, so a single valid user token could open unbounded WebSockets and exhaust the replica, stopping live notifications for everyone (:43-48).
      • CloseConnectionsOnTokenExpiry (:65): plain bool, default false (:51-54). A hub connection is authenticated once, when it opens, so without this a user who is locked, loses a role or signs out everywhere keeps receiving pushes until the connection drops. With it on, the connection ends with its access token; the shipped client reconnects with a fresh token, so a signed-in user sees one reconnect per token lifetime and a revoked user is refused. The cut-off is bounded by Jwt:AccessTokenExpirationMinutes, not immediate, and it needs no sticky ingress because each replica enforces it on the connections it holds (:55-64). [Rubric §11, Security] applies: this is the setting that bounds how long a revoked identity keeps a live channel.

    • Why it's built this way: a configurable pattern rather than a hard-coded one lets each application define its own channel taxonomy without forking the hub, while the shipped default is restrictive rather than permissive. Sourcing that default from the producer's own constant is the cheaper half of the same idea: the safe configuration is also the zero-configuration one.

    • Where it's used: bound with .ValidateDataAnnotations().ValidateOnStart() in AddPushNotifications (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:43-46), which then registers SignalR (:45), adds the Redis backplane when a redis connection string is present (:47-48, :57), and replaces the null implementations with SignalRPushNotificationSender and SignalRLiveChannelPublisher (:62-63). The settings object itself is injected as IOptions<PushNotificationSettings> (NotificationHub.cs:26) and read by NotificationHub in two places: EnsureValidChannelKey (:177) and OnConnectedAsync (:61-81), which reads MaxConnectionsPerUser into cap (:63), tracks a static ConnectionsPerUser count keyed by Context.UserIdentifier (:58), and throws HubException("Too many concurrent connections for this account.") when a new connection would push the count over cap (:68-75); the rejected connection's slot is given back immediately so an aborted connection cannot lock the user out once it drains (:71-73). The cap is skipped when cap <= 0 or the identifier is empty (:66). MapNotificationHub reads the settings to map the hub at HubPath only when Enabled is true, and passes CloseConnectionsOnTokenExpiry to SignalR's CloseOnAuthenticationExpiration (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/SignalRExtensions.cs:24-34). The default pattern is pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Settings/PushNotificationSettingsTests.cs:15-17 and an override by :26, :31; the connection cap itself is covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Hubs/NotificationHubConnectionCapTests.cs.

    • Caveats: this class stands alone. There is no IPushNotificationSettings abstraction in the current source, so a consumer that wants the values takes the concrete options type.

    RabbitMqChannelOperations

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqChannelOperations.cs:12 · Level 1 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the real IRabbitMqOperations: one channel with publisher confirms on a RabbitMqConnectionSource, with every call serialized on that channel (RabbitMqChannelOperations.cs:12-171).

    • Depends on: IRabbitMqOperations, RabbitMqConnectionSource, RabbitMqHeaders, BrokerHeaders; RabbitMQ.Client's IChannel, BasicProperties and CreateChannelOptions.

    • Concept introduced, publisher confirms. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration] assesses whether a message is known to be durable before the sender forgets it. A plain AMQP publish returns as soon as the bytes leave the client; a confirmed publish completes only when the broker has taken responsibility for the message. The channel is created with both publisherConfirmationsEnabled and publisherConfirmationTrackingEnabled (RabbitMqChannelOperations.cs:166-168), which makes BasicPublishAsync await the broker's ack and throw on a nack or a mandatory return (:5-10). That is what lets the outbox delete a row and the receiver acknowledge an original only after its copy is safe.

    • Walkthrough

      • Fields (RabbitMqChannelOperations.cs:14-18): the connection source, whether this instance owns it, a SemaphoreSlim(1, 1) gate and the current channel. The constructor (:23-29) takes ownsConnections, which decides whether disposal cascades to the connection.
      • The four declaration methods (:32-50) map one-to-one onto the client: a durable, non-auto-delete fanout exchange (:34), a durable, non-exclusive queue with the caller's arguments (:40), QueueDeclarePassiveAsync for the existence check (:45) and a binding with an empty routing key (:50).
      • PublishAsync (:54-75) builds BasicProperties with Persistent = true, the encoded header table, and ContentType and MessageId lifted from the framework headers when present (:64-70).
      • RunAsync (:134-148) takes the gate, gets a channel and runs the operation, so calls never interleave on one channel. GetChannelAsync (:150-170) reuses an open channel (:152-155); a channel that exists but is closed was closed by the broker (a failed passive declaration or conflicting arguments does that), which automatic recovery does not repair, so it is discarded and replaced (:157-163).
      • DisposeAsync (:78-97) closes the channel quietly (CloseQuietlyAsync, :117-132) and disposes the connection only when owned (:91-94); Dispose (:100-115) is the synchronous twin.

    • Why it's built this way: serializing calls on one confirmed channel keeps the confirm bookkeeping simple and the ordering of declarations deterministic; replacing a broker-closed channel on the next call turns a channel-level error into one failed operation rather than a dead publisher.

    • Where it's used: RabbitMqBrokerTransport wraps the publisher's connection in one that owns it (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:43); RabbitMqReceiver creates one that does not own its connection, for declarations and disposition copies (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:69).

    NullNativePushSender

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Notifications.Push · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/NullNativePushSender.cs:12 · Level 3 · class (public sealed)

    • What it is: the inert default for INativePushSender. Its one member, SendToUsersAsync, returns NativePushOutcome.None and does nothing else (NullNativePushSender.cs:12-17).

    • Depends on: INativePushSender and NativePushOutcome.

    • Concept introduced, the null-object default for an optional channel. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses whether callers depend on abstractions rather than on the presence of a configured backend, and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether the "not configured" case costs conditional code at every call site. The alternative to this class is an INativePushSender? that every handler null-checks, or a host that throws at resolution time when no hub is configured. Both push a deployment concern into application code. Registering a do-nothing implementation as the default means the third channel always resolves, the send handler is written once with no branch, and enabling native push in an environment is purely a configuration change. The same posture appears in NullFileStorageService, NullPushDeviceRegistrar, and, outside this group, NullPushNotificationSender.

    • Walkthrough: SendToUsersAsync (NullNativePushSender.cs:15-16) is an expression-bodied Task.FromResult(NativePushOutcome.None), the outcome of a call that attempted nothing (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Notifications/NativePushOutcome.cs:11-12). Returning an outcome rather than Task.CompletedTask keeps the caller's bookkeeping uniform: SendPushNotificationHandler records the per-platform outcome on the notification row, and null counts there mean "not attempted" (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Notifications/PushNotifications/UseCases/Send/SendPushNotificationHandler.cs:136-141). There is no logging, deliberately: a per-notification "push was skipped" line in a host that never intends to enable the channel is noise, not signal.

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-044 records that the framework pipeline ships inert by default and each consumer switches it on through a vendor adapter. This class is that decision expressed in code, and the DI comment above its registration names the three adapters that replace it (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:373-376).

    • Where it's used: registered by AddInfrastructure through TryAddTransient (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:377), immediately alongside NullPushDeviceRegistrar (:378). Each adapter uses plain AddTransient for its pair, so the later registration wins: AddAzureNotificationHubsPush (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Azure/AzureServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:133-134), AddAmazonSnsPush (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aws/AwsServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:194-195) and AddFirebaseCloudMessagingPush (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Gcp/GcpServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:166-167). CloudAdapterTripwire also tests for this type: it treats a resolved NullNativePushSender as "no push adapter registered" (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration/CloudAdapterTripwire.cs:78).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: because the swap is "last registration wins" rather than a removal, both descriptors remain in the collection when native push is enabled. Anything resolving IEnumerable<INativePushSender> would see the no-op as well as the real sender; no first-party code does.

    RabbitMqNames

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqNames.cs:19 · Level 3 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the RabbitMQ entity names and declaration arguments derived from the BrokerTopology (RabbitMqNames.cs:19-76): one durable fanout exchange per topic, the host's durable queue, {queue}-error for dead letters and {queue}-delay-{seconds}s per redelivery interval (RabbitMqNames.cs:5-17).

    • Depends on: BrokerNaming (Fit), BrokerTopology; BCL only otherwise.

    • Concept introduced, delayed redelivery without a plugin. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration] assesses whether retry and poison handling are designed rather than left to the broker's defaults. RabbitMQ has no native delayed delivery; the usual answer is the rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange plugin. This transport instead declares one queue per delay interval whose x-message-ttl expires every message after the interval and dead-letters it through the default exchange ("") back to the host queue (RabbitMqNames.cs:70-75). Because every message in one delay queue has the same time to live, expiry at the head keeps them in order, and because the arguments are a pure function of the name, every host declares the queue identically and a repeated declaration is a no-op (:60-66).

    • Walkthrough

      • MaxNameLength = 255 (RabbitMqNames.cs:22), RabbitMQ's short-string limit; every name passes through BrokerNaming.Fit with it, so a publisher and a consumer in different hosts compute the same entity (:5-7).
      • DeadLetterReasonHeader and DeadLetterDetailHeader (:25, :28): x-mmca-dead-letter-reason and x-mmca-dead-letter-detail.
      • Exchange(topic), Queue(queueName) and ErrorQueue(queueName) (:33, :38, :43).
      • DelaySeconds(delay) (:51) rounds up to whole seconds with a floor of one, so a sub-second delay still goes through a delay queue rather than straight back to the host queue.
      • DelayQueue(queueName, delaySeconds) (:57-58) and DelayQueueArguments (:70-75): TTL delaySeconds * 1000, dead-letter exchange "", dead-letter routing key the fitted host queue name.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the dead-letter headers start with x-, the prefix RabbitMqHeaders drops on read, so a dead-lettered copy read back by a receiver would not surface them as framework headers; they are meant for an operator inspecting the error queue.

    • Where it's used: RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqDispositionApplier, RabbitMqPublisher and RabbitMqReceiver. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqNamesTests.cs.

    NullPushDeviceRegistrar

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Notifications.Push · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/Push/NullPushDeviceRegistrar.cs:14 · Level 4 · class (public sealed)

    • What it is: the inert default for IPushDeviceRegistrar. It accepts and discards registrations so a client can call the Devices endpoints unconditionally; nothing is stored until a host enables native push (NullPushDeviceRegistrar.cs:14-27).

    • Depends on: IPushDeviceRegistrar, DeviceInstallationRequest, and Result.

    • Concept: the null-object default introduced at NullNativePushSender. Here all three operations return success (NullPushDeviceRegistrar.cs:17-18, :21-22, :25-26), which is the right choice for this contract specifically: a mobile client registers its device at startup as a matter of course, and failing that call in a host without a hub would surface as an error in an app whose user did nothing wrong. [Rubric §9, API and Contract Design] applies: the Devices endpoints keep the same response shape whether or not the channel is enabled, so no client needs a capability check.

    • Walkthrough: UpsertAsync (NullPushDeviceRegistrar.cs:17-18), DeleteAsync (:21-22) and DeleteAllForUserAsync (:25-26) are all expression-bodied Task.FromResult(Result.Success()). DeleteAllForUserAsync is the account-deletion path: DeleteUserPushInstallationsInternalCommandHandler calls it (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserPushInstallationsInternalCommandHandler.cs:31), and with no adapter there is nothing stored to remove, so success is the truthful answer. There is no validation of the platform string here, unlike AzureNotificationHubDeviceRegistrar, so a request that the real registrar would reject as an unsupported platform is accepted by this one.

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-044 ships the pipeline inert, and both halves of the channel (the sender and the registrar) have to be inert together, which is why they are registered as a pair (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:377-378) and replaced as a pair by each vendor adapter (for example MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Azure/AzureServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:133-134).
