    • Where it's used: registered by AddInfrastructure (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:378) and resolved by DevicesController (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Notifications/DevicesController.cs:27) in any host that has not registered a push adapter (AddAzureNotificationHubsPush, AddAmazonSnsPush or AddFirebaseCloudMessagingPush) with an enabled section.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the divergence in validation strictness between this and the real registrar means a test running against the default registration cannot catch an invalid Platform value. That behavior is only exercised through AzureNotificationHubDeviceRegistrar.

    RabbitMqProvisioner

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqProvisioner.cs:16 · Level 4 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the part of the transport that creates RabbitMQ entities, once per process and idempotently, honoring MessageBusSettings.ProvisionTopology (RabbitMqProvisioner.cs:16-136).

    • Depends on: IRabbitMqOperations, RabbitMqNames, BrokerTopology, MessageBusSettings; ConcurrentDictionary.

    • Concept introduced, provisioning on or off. [Rubric §17, DevOps] assesses whether infrastructure ownership is explicit. With provisioning on, every entity is declared, and a repeated declaration with the same arguments is a no-op on the broker. With it off, nothing is declared: the host queue, its error queue and every delay queue must already exist, and the receive side checks the queue it is about to publish a copy to passively, so a missing one fails the disposition (and the message is redelivered) instead of the copy being silently dropped as unroutable (RabbitMqProvisioner.cs:5-12).

    • Walkthrough

      • Two ordinal ConcurrentDictionary sets remember declared exchanges and queues (RabbitMqProvisioner.cs:18-19); ProvisionTopology (:22) comes from the primary constructor.
      • ProvisionReceiveAsync (:32-56) returns at once when provisioning is off (:37-40), otherwise declares the host queue (:42-43), its error queue (:45-47), and for each subscription the topic's fanout exchange plus the binding to the queue (:49-55).
      • EnsureExchangeAsync (:63-74) declares a topic's exchange before its first publish, skipping it when provisioning is off or already declared (:67); ForgetExchange (:81) drops it from the set after a failed publish, so the next publish declares it again in case it was deleted out of band.
      • EnsureErrorQueueAsync (:88-93) and EnsureDelayQueueAsync (:104-110) funnel into EnsureQueueAsync (:112-135), which declares with arguments when provisioning and otherwise calls the passive EnsureQueueExistsAsync (:125-132), then caches the name (:134). Delay queues are therefore declared lazily, the first time an interval is used.

    • Why it's built this way: a host that runs with least-privilege broker credentials cannot declare entities, so provisioning has to be switchable; the passive check is what keeps that mode from losing messages.

    • Where it's used: RabbitMqBrokerTransport creates one for the publisher and one for the receiver (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:44, :57); consumed by RabbitMqPublisher, RabbitMqReceiver and RabbitMqDispositionApplier. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqProvisionerTests.cs.

    RabbitMqDispositionApplier

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqDispositionApplier.cs:21 · Level 5 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the step that carries out a BrokerDisposition for a delivered message, up to but not including the acknowledgement of the original, which the receiver sends once this returns (RabbitMqDispositionApplier.cs:21-74).

    • Depends on: IRabbitMqOperations, RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqNames, IncomingBrokerMessage, BrokerDisposition with Redeliver, DeadLetter and Completed, BrokerHeaders.

    • Concept: the disposition model is taught at BrokerDisposition; this is how RabbitMQ realizes it. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration] applies to the ordering: both copies are published mandatory and confirmed, so the original is acknowledged only once its copy is safely in a queue, and a failure here throws so the receiver returns the original to the queue (RabbitMqDispositionApplier.cs:16-17).

    • Walkthrough: ApplyAsync (RabbitMqDispositionApplier.cs:31-73).

      • Redeliver (:44-54): ensure the delay queue for RabbitMqNames.DelaySeconds(redeliver.Delay) (:46-48), copy the headers with the new BrokerHeaders.RedeliveryCount (:49-52), and publish to the delay queue through the default exchange, mandatory (:53).
      • DeadLetter (:56-69): ensure the error queue (:58), add the reason header and, when present, the detail header (:59-66), and publish to {queue}-error, mandatory (:68).
      • Completed: nothing to publish; the acknowledgement is all there is (:72).

    • Where it's used: called by RabbitMqReceiver for every processed delivery (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:215). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqDispositionApplierTests.cs.

    RabbitMqPublisher

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqPublisher.cs:10 · Level 5 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the RabbitMQ IBrokerPublisher: it publishes each message, persistent and confirmed, to its topic's fanout exchange, declaring the exchange first when provisioning. A publish the broker did not confirm throws, so the outbox keeps the row and retries it (RabbitMqPublisher.cs:3-8).

    • Depends on: IBrokerPublisher, OutgoingBrokerMessage, IRabbitMqOperations, RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqNames.

    • Concept: the publisher contract is taught at IBrokerPublisher.

    • Walkthrough

      • The constructor (RabbitMqPublisher.cs:18-25) takes the operations and the provisioner.
      • PublishAsync (:28-47) maps the topic to its exchange (:32), ensures the exchange (:35), and publishes with mandatory: false and an empty routing key (:39-40): a fanout exchange with no queue bound yet means no host consumes the event, which is not an error for the publisher (:37-38). Any failure makes the provisioner forget the exchange before rethrowing (:42-46).
      • DisposeAsync and Dispose (:50-51, :54) forward to the operations when they are disposable.

    • Where it's used: registered as the singleton IBrokerPublisher by RabbitMqBrokerTransport (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:42-44). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqPublisherTests.cs.

    RabbitMqReceiver

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqReceiver.cs:21 · Level 6 · class (internal sealed partial)

    • What it is: the hosted service that consumes the host queue with manual acknowledgements, hands every delivery to IBrokerReceivePipeline and applies the resulting disposition before acknowledging (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:21-263).

    • Depends on: BackgroundService, BrokerTopology, IBrokerReceivePipeline, RabbitMqConnectionSource, RabbitMqChannelOperations, RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqDispositionApplier, RabbitMqHeaders, RabbitMqNames, IncomingBrokerMessage; RabbitMQ.Client's AsyncEventingBasicConsumer; source-generated [LoggerMessage] logging.

    • Concept introduced, a receiver that never stops the host. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether a service degrades and recovers rather than crashes. When the broker is unreachable at startup, or a channel is lost and not recovered, the receiver logs a Warning and tries again every ReconnectDelay; the client's automatic recovery repairs an ordinary connection loss on its own (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:13-17). [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration] covers the delivery guarantee: a delivery is acknowledged only after its disposition copy is confirmed, and anything that fails is negatively acknowledged with requeue.

    • Walkthrough

      • Timings: ReconnectDelay 5 seconds (RabbitMqReceiver.cs:24), ChannelCheckInterval 10 seconds (:27), DrainTimeout 10 seconds (:30). An _inFlight counter tracks deliveries being processed (:41).
      • The constructor (:51-75) creates its own RabbitMqChannelOperations over the receiver's connection without owning it (:69) and fixes the fitted queue name (:74).
      • ExecuteAsync (:101-127) loops RunSessionAsync (:107), returns on cancellation (:109-112), logs any other failure (:113-116) and waits ReconnectDelay before the next session (:120).
      • RunSessionAsync (:146-189) opens the connection, provisions the receive topology (:148-149), and when provisioning is off checks the queue passively (:150-153). It opens a consume channel with confirms off and consumerDispatchConcurrency set to the configured concurrency (:155-160), applies the prefetch window with BasicQosAsync (:163), and starts a consumer with autoAck: false (:165-167). It then polls every ChannelCheckInterval: a channel closed while the connection is open was closed by the broker, which recovery never repairs, so the session ends and a new one starts (:170-181). The finally drains and closes the channel (:186-187).
      • DrainAsync (:191-200) waits in 50 ms steps, up to DrainTimeout, for in-flight deliveries to settle.
      • HandleAsync (:202-234) builds an IncomingBrokerMessage from the body, the decoded headers and the AMQP MessageId, falling back to the delivery tag (:207-210); runs the pipeline (:214); applies the disposition (:215-216); then acknowledges (:217). A cancellation during shutdown (:219-223) and any other failure (:224-228, logged at Error) both requeue the delivery. RequeueQuietlyAsync (:236-247) tolerates a closed channel, which returns unacknowledged deliveries to the queue by itself.
      • StopAsync and Dispose (:78-89, :92-98) dispose the operations and the connection; the second disposal is a no-op.
      • Five [LoggerMessage] methods (:249-262) cover consuming, session failure, channel loss, disposition failure and requeue failure.

    • Why it's built this way: separate connections for publishing and consuming, plus prefetch equal to twice the concurrency by default, keep acknowledgements flowing while the publisher is throttled; acknowledging after the confirmed copy makes a crash between the two produce a duplicate, never a loss, which the inbox absorbs.

    • Where it's used: registered as a hosted service by RabbitMqBrokerTransport only when the topology has subscriptions (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:46-60).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the drain waits at most 10 seconds and then closes the channel anyway; deliveries still in flight at that point are returned to the queue by the broker and processed again.

    RabbitMqBrokerTransport

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Transports.RabbitMq · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:24 · Level 7 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the built-in IBrokerTransport for MessageBus:Provider=RabbitMq, the broker the Aspire development stack and the cross-service test tier run, written directly on RabbitMQ.Client against the same contract an adapter package implements (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:7-10).

    • Depends on: IBrokerTransport, BrokerTransportContext, BrokerTransportPolicies, MessageBusProviders, MessageBusSettings, IBrokerPublisher, IBrokerReceivePipeline, and the RabbitMQ types of this part: RabbitMqPublisher, RabbitMqChannelOperations, RabbitMqConnectionSource, RabbitMqProvisioner, RabbitMqReceiver, RabbitMqNames.

    • Concept: the transport strategy is taught at IBrokerTransport; this is its composition root for RabbitMQ. The topology it produces (fanout exchange per topic, one queue per host, {queue}-error, TTL delay queues so delayed redelivery needs no plugin, persistent confirmed publishes, automatic recovery) is summarized in the class doc (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:11-17) and taught at RabbitMqNames. See ADR-066 and ADR-118.

    • Walkthrough

      • Name returns MessageBusProviders.RabbitMq (RabbitMqBrokerTransport.cs:27); MaxRedeliveryDelay is null (:30), since a delay queue can hold any interval.
      • Register (:33-61) parses the URI and reads the topology and ProvisionTopology (:38-40), then registers a singleton IBrokerPublisher: a RabbitMqPublisher over owning RabbitMqChannelOperations on a connection named {queue} (publish) (:42-44). A host with no subscriptions stops there (:46-49). Otherwise it resolves concurrency and prefetch (:51-52) and adds a RabbitMqReceiver hosted service on its own {queue} (receive) connection with its own provisioner (:53-60).
      • ParseConnectionUri (:70-86) returns null for a blank string, so the client default localhost:5672 applies (:72-75), accepts an absolute amqp or amqps URI (:77-81), and otherwise throws an InvalidOperationException naming MessageBus:ConnectionString and ConnectionStrings:rabbitmq (:83-85). The connection string resolution order is in the class doc (:18-22).
      • ResolveConcurrency (:94-95): MessageBus:ConcurrentMessageLimit, else Environment.ProcessorCount, clamped to 1..65535.
      • ResolvePrefetchCount (:104-105): MessageBus:PrefetchCount, else twice the concurrency, so a finished delivery's slot is refilled without a broker round trip (:97-98).

    • Why it's built this way: a bad connection string fails at registration with an actionable message rather than as a runtime connection error, and separate publish and receive connections keep a throttled publisher from stalling consumer acknowledgements.

    • Where it's used: instantiated by ResolveBrokerTransport when the provider is RabbitMq (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:201-204). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Transports/RabbitMq/RabbitMqBrokerTransportTests.cs and, against a live broker, MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.RabbitMq.Tests/RabbitMqBrokerTransportTests.cs.

    JobClaim

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Scheduling · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobRunner.cs:458 · Level 0 · record (private nested, sealed)

    • What it is: the result of one attempt to claim a due job row: which row was due, the occurrence it was due at, the cron expression to compute the next occurrence from, and the claim token, which is null when a different replica won the row.

    • Depends on: nothing first-party. BCL only (string, DateTime, Guid?). It exists solely as the return shape of ScheduledJobRunner.TryClaimNextDueAsync.

    • Concept introduced, three answers in one return value. A claim attempt has three outcomes, not two: nothing was due, something was due and this replica took it, or something was due and another replica took it first. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether the code makes illegal states hard to express: the method returns JobClaim?, so null is "nothing due" and a non-null instance with a null LockToken is "lost the race" (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:409-412). Collapsing the latter two into one null would have cost the caller the ability to mark that name as attempted for this cycle and move on, which is exactly what stops the loop spinning on a row this replica will never own (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:393-402). A positional record gets that shape in one line with value equality and no mutable state.

    • Walkthrough: four positional members, each documented (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:453-458): JobName, DueOn (the occurrence the row was due at, used for the lag metric), CronExpression (what the next occurrence is computed from, read from the row rather than recomputed from settings so an in-flight schedule change cannot retarget a run in progress), and Guid? LockToken. It is constructed once, at ScheduledJobRunner.cs:450, where the token is passed as claimed == 0 ? null : lockToken: the count of rows the claiming ExecuteUpdateAsync actually matched IS the race result.

    • Why it's built this way: private sealed record keeps a purely internal carrier invisible to the package's public surface, so it costs nothing in API compatibility terms while still giving the claim path a named, immutable shape (ADR-074).

    • Where it's used: returned by TryClaimNextDueAsync (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:413-451) and consumed by RunDueJobsAsync (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:376-404).

    ScheduledJobEntry

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Scheduling · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobEntry.cs:20 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the persisted schedule and last-run record for one registered IScheduledJob: one row per job name, upserted by ScheduledJobRunner on every cycle. It carries both the schedule (expression, next occurrence) and the claim lease that makes a multi-replica host safe.

    • Depends on: nothing first-party and nothing beyond string, DateTime and Guid from the BCL, which is why it is Level 0.

    • Concept introduced, the framework bookkeeping entity. [Rubric §4, DDD] assesses whether the domain model stays a model of the business: this class is deliberately not an IAuditableEntity and not an aggregate root, exactly like OutboxMessage, because it is framework bookkeeping rather than domain state (ScheduledJobEntry.cs:8-14). The consequences are concrete: no soft-delete flag, so no global query filter applies to it; no audit stamps, so the save interceptors have nothing to write (which is why the runner can call a plain SaveChangesAsync with no user id, ScheduledJobRunner.cs:325-330); and no concurrency token, because its concurrency control is the explicit claim lease instead. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]: the table is host-scoped and lives in the Default data source only, unlike the outbox, which exists once per physical source (ScheduledJobEntry.cs:15-18). Jobs belong to a host, not to a database. [Rubric §11, Security] by omission: it also carries no user data, which is what keeps it in the audit trail's framework-entity exclusion set alongside the outbox and inbox rows (Persistence/AuditTrail/AuditTrailSaveChangesInterceptor.cs:113-119, this type at :118).

    • Walkthrough, in the order the runner touches them:

      • JobName (ScheduledJobEntry.cs:26), required and init-only: the primary key, matching IScheduledJob.Name, so a job has exactly one schedule row per host.
      • CronExpression (ScheduledJobEntry.cs:34), required with a setter: the five-field UTC expression currently in force, which is either the job's code default or the Scheduler:Jobs:{Name}:Cron override. The runner compares it against the resolved expression every cycle and recomputes the next occurrence only when it changed.
      • NextRunOn (ScheduledJobEntry.cs:40): the UTC instant the job next becomes due. A row whose expression cannot be parsed is parked at DateTime.MaxValue so it is never claimed, which is how one bad cron string in configuration fails just that job.
      • LastRunOn (:43), LastOutcome (:50, one of Succeeded, Failed, Skipped), LastError (:57, truncated to the column width and cleared on success so the column always describes the LAST outcome rather than the last failure ever seen), and LastDurationMs (:60): the operator-facing run record.
      • LockedUntil (:67) and LockToken (:74): the claim lease. Other replicas skip a row with an unexpired lease, so an occurrence runs once even with several replicas polling; the claiming replica stamps its outcome only on a row still carrying its own token, so a replica whose lease expired mid-execution cannot overwrite the record of the replica that took over.

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-074 chose to apply the outbox's proven claim-lease idiom to cron rather than adopt Hangfire or Quartz.NET, so the row shape is deliberately the minimum that idiom needs: a due time, a lease, and a token.

    • Where it's used: mapped by ApplicationDbContext.ConfigureScheduler (Persistence/DbContexts/ApplicationDbContext.cs:594-619), which is gated: the entity is mapped only when the host set Scheduler:Enabled and this context targets the Default source (ApplicationDbContext.cs:586-599, the guard itself at :596-599), so a host that never opted in keeps exactly the model, and the migrations, it had before the scheduler shipped, and Cosmos DB never reaches the method at all (ApplicationDbContext.cs:591-592). The mapping sets ToTable("ScheduledJobs", "dbo") (:603), the JobName key (:604), column widths matching the entity's documented truncation (:605-608), and one index on NextRunOn with the two lease columns as included columns (:615-617), deliberately NOT filtered to unlocked rows, because the poll must also find rows whose lease has expired (that is how a dead replica's work is reclaimed, ApplicationDbContext.cs:610-614). Every read and write of the row lives in ScheduledJobRunner.

    ScheduledJobOverrideSettings

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Scheduling · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/SchedulerSettings.cs:69 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: one entry under Scheduler:Jobs:{Name}, the per-job override that lets a deployment retime a recurring job without touching code. Today it carries exactly one member, the cron expression.

    • Depends on: nothing. It is the value type of SchedulerSettings.Jobs (SchedulerSettings.cs:63) and is read by ScheduledJobRunner.

    • Concept introduced, code default plus configuration override. An IScheduledJob ships with a CronExpression compiled into it, which is the right default because the job's author knows what cadence the work needs. An operator who has to change that cadence for one environment should not need a release. [Rubric §17, DevOps] assesses whether operational behavior can be changed without a code change; this pair is the minimal answer: an absent entry leaves the compiled-in schedule in force, and a present, non-blank Cron replaces it (SchedulerSettings.cs:57-62, :71-77). The change needs a configuration edit and a host restart, not a release. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]: the override is keyed by IScheduledJob.Name, the job's own stable identity, so configuration and code agree on one name rather than on a class name that refactoring would break.

    • Walkthrough: a single string? Cron { get; init; } (SchedulerSettings.cs:78). The whole mechanism lives in the reader, not in this type: ScheduledJobRunner.ResolveCronExpression looks the job up by name and takes the override only when it is present AND non-blank, otherwise the job's own expression (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:173-177). Blank-means-absent matters, because a JSON key set to "" is a common way to try to clear a value and would otherwise produce an unparseable schedule.

    • Why it's built this way: the runner treats a changed expression as a schedule rewrite. On each cycle it reads the stored expressions (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:278-282), leaves a row untouched when the resolved expression matches (recomputing every cycle would push the next occurrence forward forever and nothing would ever fire, :290-296), and otherwise recomputes the next occurrence from the current instant and either updates the row with a schedule-changed log (:304-309) or inserts a new one (:310-322). The settings themselves are read once: the runner snapshots IOptions<SchedulerSettings>.Value at construction (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:47), so an operator edit applies when the host restarts, and the first cycle after that restart performs the rewrite (SchedulerSettings.cs:73-76, ADR-074).

    • Where it's used: ScheduledJobRunner only, through SchedulerSettings.Jobs.

    • Caveats: an override that does not parse is not rejected at startup, unlike the range-checked scalar settings in this namespace. The runner logs the parse failure (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:298-302, message at :670-671) and records the job with the skipped outcome and a DateTime.MaxValue next run (insert at :316-317, update at :359-368), so a bad cron string is an observable non-run rather than a failed boot. Editing the value on a running host changes nothing until the restart.

    SchedulerMetrics

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Scheduling · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/SchedulerMetrics.cs:16 · Level 0 · class (internal, static)

    • What it is: the OpenTelemetry instrument set for the recurring job scheduler: one meter carrying a run counter, an execution-duration histogram, and a schedule-lag histogram, all emitted by ScheduledJobRunner.

    • Depends on: System.Diagnostics.Metrics (BCL) only (SchedulerMetrics.cs:1). Nothing first-party.

    • Concept introduced, the one-meter-per-feature instrument holder. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether a running system can be understood from outside: a background loop is invisible by construction (no request, no response code), so the only evidence that a schedule is healthy is telemetry. The three instruments here are chosen to answer the three operator questions: is it running, how long does it take, and is it on time. [Rubric §31, Cost/FinOps] shows up in the same design: the per-occurrence start and finish lines are logged at Debug rather than Information precisely because a busy schedule would otherwise double the runner's steady-state log volume (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:679-686), and the numbers an operator alerts on come from these metrics instead. A host exports them by registering the MeterName meter; the Aspire service defaults (ConfigureOpenTelemetry) already do (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Aspire/Extensions.Telemetry.cs:313), and the doc records that the name is duplicated as a literal there because that package has no reference to Infrastructure (SchedulerMetrics.cs:5-14).

    • Walkthrough:

      • MeterName = "MMCA.Common.Scheduler" (SchedulerMetrics.cs:19) and the single static Meter built from it (:21). The class doc is explicit that one meter serves every scheduler instrument and that a second Meter with this name must never be created (SchedulerMetrics.cs:11-14), since duplicate meters are a classic source of double-counted telemetry. BrokerMetrics repeats the same shape for the broker transport.
      • RunCounter (SchedulerMetrics.cs:28-31), scheduler.job.runs, unit runs, tagged by job and outcome: the failure rate of a schedule is this counter split by outcome.
      • DurationHistogram (:39-42), scheduler.job.duration in seconds, tagged by job, measured around the job's own ExecuteAsync only so it excludes claim and bookkeeping cost. Its stated purpose is the lease relationship: a job whose duration approaches Scheduler:LeaseSeconds is about to lose its claim mid-run (SchedulerMetrics.cs:33-38).
      • LagHistogram (:50-53), scheduler.job.lag in seconds, the interval between an occurrence becoming due and actually starting. It is floored at zero, and a value near the polling interval is normal for an occurrence that landed just after a cycle (SchedulerMetrics.cs:44-49).

    • Why it's built this way: internal static readonly instruments created once at type initialization means the runner records without resolving anything from DI, and keeping the meter name a constant on the same type is what lets a test assert against it. SchedulerMetricsTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/SchedulerMetricsTests.cs:13) pins the instrument surface.

    • Where it's used: ScheduledJobRunner.ExecuteClaimedJobAsync records the lag before invoking the job (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:476-479) and the duration plus the outcome-tagged count after it returns (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:512-515).

    SchedulerSettings

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Scheduling · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/SchedulerSettings.cs:16 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the Scheduler section for the recurring-job runner: the on switch, the fallback poll interval, the row-claim lease, which engine holds the ScheduledJobs table, and a per-job cron override map. Every property has a default, so a host that opts in needs only Scheduler:Enabled (SchedulerSettings.cs:6-9).

    • Depends on: DataSource, the engine enum, imported from MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces.Infrastructure (SchedulerSettings.cs:2, :52), and ScheduledJobOverrideSettings, the one-property class declared at the bottom of the same file (:69-79). Externals: System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations for [Range] (:1).

    • Concept introduced: one setting that gates both the behavior and the schema. Most feature flags gate behavior. Enabled also decides whether the ScheduledJobs table is mapped into the EF model at all: ApplicationDbContext reads IOptions<SchedulerSettings> with GetService (not GetRequiredService) so an absent registration reads as disabled rather than failing every context construction, then additionally requires the physical source to be the default one (ApplicationDbContext.cs:412-417). The consequence is the one worth learning: a host that leaves the flag false has exactly the model it had before the scheduler shipped, so its migrations never see the table (SchedulerSettings.cs:10-15).

      [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether adopting a framework feature is additive. Because registration and activation are separate (AddScheduledJobs binds and registers the runner, but the runner returns immediately unless Enabled is true, ScheduledJobRunner.cs:86-92), a host can ship the registration and turn the scheduler on per environment (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:31-33).

      [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity] assesses safe behavior under replication. LeaseSeconds is what makes multiple replicas safe: a replica claims a job row for that many seconds and other replicas skip claimed rows, so no occurrence runs twice; if the claiming replica dies mid-execution, the row becomes claimable again once the lease expires (SchedulerSettings.cs:36-46, applied at ScheduledJobRunner.cs:435). While a job runs, the holder renews its lease every half of this value (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:575, :585-589), so the lease no longer has to outlast the longest job; the trade-off is that a shorter lease frees a dead replica's row sooner at the cost of more writes and less time to retry a failed renewal before another replica can claim a job that is still running (SchedulerSettings.cs:39-43).

      [Rubric §31, Cost and FinOps] assesses idle-cost defaults. PollingIntervalSeconds is a BOUND on the smart wait, not a hot loop: the runner normally sleeps until the earliest due job and uses this value only to cap that sleep (SchedulerSettings.cs:28-34, ScheduledJobRunner.cs:124-127). The doc also names it as how quickly a configuration-driven schedule change is noticed, but the runner reads these settings once at construction (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:47), so in practice a changed setting takes effect after a host restart.

    • Walkthrough: one static field, four init properties and one get-only dictionary.

      • SectionName = "Scheduler" (SchedulerSettings.cs:19).
      • Enabled (:26): default false, documented as the deliberate posture that adopting the framework must never add a table or a background loop to a host that did not ask for one.
      • PollingIntervalSeconds (:34): [Range(1, 3600)] (:33), default 30.
      • LeaseSeconds (:46): [Range(10, 3600)] (:45), default 300. The holder renews it every half lease while its job runs, so it does not need to exceed the longest job (:36-44).
      • DataSource (:55): default DataSource.SQLServer. Jobs are host-scoped, so there is exactly one ScheduledJobs table per host rather than one per source, and this only names the relational engine that table lives on; Cosmos DB is not a valid value (:48-54). The runner resolves it against DataSourceKey.DefaultName (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:226-227).
      • Jobs (:63): a get-only Dictionary<string, ScheduledJobOverrideSettings> keyed by IScheduledJob.Name and bound from Scheduler:Jobs:{Name}. ResolveCronExpression takes the override only when the entry exists AND its Cron is non-blank, otherwise the job's compiled-in expression stands (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:173-177). A changed expression applies after a host restart (the runner snapshots the settings at construction, ScheduledJobRunner.cs:47): the first cycle compares the resolved expression against the stored one, leaves an unchanged row alone (recomputing it every cycle would push every schedule forward and nothing would ever fire), and otherwise rewrites the stored value and recomputes the next occurrence from the current instant (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:289-322).

    • Why it's built this way: a persistent, database-backed cron scheduler with per-row leases is the decision recorded in ADR-074; everything in this class is the operator-facing surface of it. Defaulting every property makes the section optional, which is the same fail-soft-on-absence, fail-fast-on-bad-value posture ADR-070 describes: the [Range] guards run under ValidateOnStart, so a bad value fails the boot rather than the first cycle.

    • Where it's used: bound with validation in AddScheduledJobs (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:38-41), which registers the runner through TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IHostedService, ScheduledJobRunner>()) rather than AddHostedService, precisely so two calls cannot start two runners racing for the same rows (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:43-47). Read by ScheduledJobRunner (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:43, :47) and by ApplicationDbContext for the table gate (ApplicationDbContext.cs:415-417); the design-time helper supplies a default instance so dotnet ef can build a model without a host (DesignTimeDbContextHelper, DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs:161-162).

    ChannelJoinAuthorizerMissingWarningService

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Notifications · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Notifications/ChannelJoinAuthorizerMissingWarningService.cs:16 · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed, partial, IHostedService)

    • What it is: a one-shot startup check. When push notifications are registered and no IChannelJoinAuthorizer is, it logs one Warning saying that any authenticated caller can join any well-formed channel on the hub (ChannelJoinAuthorizerMissingWarningService.cs:8-13). It changes no join behavior.

    • Depends on: IServiceProviderIsService and ILogger<ChannelJoinAuthorizerMissingWarningService> as primary-constructor parameters, implementing IHostedService (:16-18). The check names IChannelJoinAuthorizer, and the posture it describes is enforced (or not) by NotificationHub. Externals: Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, .Hosting, .Logging (:1-3).

    • Concept introduced: make an open default visible instead of closing it. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether insecure postures are explicit. Channel joins stay open without an authorizer, which is a legitimate choice when every channel is meant for every signed-in user, so the framework does not refuse to boot; it states the consequence once, at startup, in a message that names the interface to register (:36-39). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: the warning lands in the startup log where an operator reviewing a new deployment sees it, rather than being discoverable only by reading the hub.

    • Walkthrough:

      • StartAsync (:21-31): asks IServiceProviderIsService.IsService(typeof(IChannelJoinAuthorizer)) (:25), which answers without resolving an instance, and logs LogNoChannelJoinAuthorizer when the answer is no (:27). The check runs at start, not at registration, because a host may register its authorizer after calling AddPushNotifications (:23-24).
      • StopAsync (:34): a no-op.
      • LogNoChannelJoinAuthorizer (:36-39): a source-generated [LoggerMessage] at Warning.

    • Why it's built this way: a hosted service is the one place that runs after the whole container is built, so it sees every registration regardless of call order. Push notifications and their channel model are described in ADR-024.

    • Where it's used: registered by AddPushNotifications with AddHostedService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Notifications.cs:86); the comment there notes that AddHostedService is a TryAddEnumerable, so a second call adds no second warning (:83-85).

    GetUserPreferencesQuery

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.GetPreferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/GetPreferences/GetUserPreferencesQuery.cs:5 · Level 1 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the one-line query that asks for a single account's stored UI preferences. It is a positional record with exactly one member, UserId, and it implements IUserScopedRequest (GetUserPreferencesQuery.cs:5).

    • Depends on: IUserScopedRequest (IUserScopedRequest.cs:8), and the UserIdentifierType alias, which resolves to int through the solution-wide global using (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/GlobalUsings.IdentifierType.cs:1; see primer §4 for the alias convention). No externals.

    • Concept introduced: the one request record in this family that could be shared. Almost everything else in the shared Users use cases keeps its command record app-side, because ADC and Store disagree on the pipeline markers those records carry: both DeleteUserCommand records, for instance, implement ICacheInvalidating with a CachePrefix built from their own User type (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserCommand.cs:14, :17; MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserCommand.cs:17, :20), which is a value no shared record could produce. This query carries no markers at all: it is not ICacheInvalidating, not IQueryCacheable, not ICommandWithRequest<out TRequest>. That absence is precisely what made it hoistable, and it is the rule worth taking away: a type moves into the framework when it has no app-specific policy attached to it.

      [Rubric §9: API & Contract Design] assesses whether the contract between layers is explicit and minimal. The query is the entire input contract for the read: one identifier, supplied by the controller from the authenticated principal rather than by the caller, so there is no way to ask for another account's preferences through this shape (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/UserAccountAuthControllerBase.cs:146-151).

      [Rubric §6: CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses the separation of reads from writes. This is the read half of the culture/theme pair; its write counterpart is the app-side ChangePreferencesCommand handled by ChangePreferencesHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>. Because it is a query, it flows through the shorter query pipeline (FeatureGate, Logging, Caching, handler) with no Validating and no Transactional decorator, per ADR-014.

    • Walkthrough: one positional parameter.

      • UserId (GetUserPreferencesQuery.cs:5): the account to read. Implementing IUserScopedRequest is satisfied by the record's generated property, so the shared handler base can read the target through the interface without knowing the record type (IUserScopedRequest.cs:11).

    • Why it's built this way: the query and its UserPreferencesResponse reply were byte-identical in both app Identity modules, so the handler base could be made generic in the User aggregate alone rather than also in the query type (GetUserPreferencesHandlerBase.cs:10-13). Preferences themselves are the persistence side of ADR-027 (culture) and ADR-028 (theme).

    • Where it's used: constructed by UserAccountAuthControllerBase<TChangePasswordCommand, TChangePreferencesCommand> in its GET preferences action (UserAccountAuthControllerBase.cs:151) and handled by GetUserPreferencesHandlerBase<TUser> (GetUserPreferencesHandlerBase.cs:31-33). Both apps' AuthController take the closed handler interface as a constructor dependency (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/Controllers/AuthController.cs:36, MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.API/Controllers/AuthController.cs:32), and both architecture suites use it as the query specimen when asserting decorator ordering (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:30, MMCA.Store/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Store.Architecture.Tests/Cqrs/DecoratorPipelineOrderTests.cs:30).

    GetUserPreferencesHandlerBase<TUser>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.GetPreferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/GetPreferences/GetUserPreferencesHandlerBase.cs:19 · Level 8 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared preference-read workflow, and the only query handler among the Users bases. Load the account through the read repository and project its two preference fields into a UserPreferencesResponse (GetUserPreferencesHandlerBase.cs:19, :31-43).

    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork as its single primary-constructor parameter (:19); implements IQueryHandler<in TQuery, TResult> closed over GetUserPreferencesQuery and Result<UserPreferencesResponse> (:20). One constraint: TUser is an AuditableBaseEntity<TIdentifierType> implementing IUserPreferences (:21). Also uses Error. No logger, and no externals beyond the BCL.

    • Concept introduced: one generic parameter is enough when nothing app-specific rides on the request. This is the contrast case for the command bases above. Because GetUserPreferencesQuery carries no pipeline markers, it could be shared outright, so the base is generic in the User aggregate only (:10-13). Note also the weaker entity constraint: AuditableBaseEntity<UserIdentifierType> rather than AuditableAggregateRootEntity<...> (:21), because a read needs no domain events and no aggregate behavior. Constraining to the least the workflow actually uses is the pattern worth copying.

      [Rubric §6: CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses read/write separation. The handler takes the read repository via GetReadRepository (:37) rather than GetRepository, and never calls SaveChangesAsync. The class remarks state that the read repository is the correct choice for a query handler, which never saves (:14-17).

      [Rubric §12: Performance & Scalability] assesses avoidable work. The read repository is the no-tracking path, so this query does not materialize an EF change-tracker entry for a preference lookup; the class remarks state it plainly: the read is no-tracking (:15-16). Note the related trap the workspace has hit elsewhere: a no-tracking source poisons a whole composed query, which is precisely why mutation handlers such as ChangePreferencesHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> keep using GetRepository instead.

      [Rubric §15: Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses consistency of error shape. The not-found path produces the identical Error.NotFound.WithSource(HandlerName).WithTarget(typeof(TUser).Name) construction the command bases use (:40-41), so every account use case reports a missing user the same way.

    • Walkthrough: one protected member and one method.

      • Primary constructor (:19): unitOfWork only.
      • HandlerName (:28): the same GetType().Name default, so an app subclass named GetUserPreferencesHandler reports that name as the error source (:23-27).
      • HandleAsync(GetUserPreferencesQuery, CancellationToken) (:31-43): null-guards the query (:35); resolves GetReadRepository<TUser, UserIdentifierType>() (:37); loads by query.UserId (:38); and returns either the stamped Error.NotFound failure (:40-41) or a success wrapping new UserPreferencesResponse(user.PreferredCulture, user.PreferredTheme) (:42). A ternary, not a branch chain: the whole method is a load and a projection.

    • Why it's built this way: the query and the response are shared types, so the only decision the base has to make is which repository is correct for a read, and it uses the no-tracking one (:10-17). Preferences are read at login to reapply a returning user's culture and theme across devices (ADR-027, ADR-028), which is why the read path is worth keeping cheap.

    • Where it's used: subclassed as an empty, name-preserving class in both apps (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/GetPreferences/GetUserPreferencesHandler.cs:13-14, MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/GetPreferences/GetUserPreferencesHandler.cs:12-13). Consumed through the closed IQueryHandler<GetUserPreferencesQuery, Result<UserPreferencesResponse>> interface by UserAccountAuthControllerBase<TChangePasswordCommand, TChangePreferencesCommand> (UserAccountAuthControllerBase.cs:46, :58, :150-151). Pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/GetUserPreferencesHandlerBaseTests.cs:14 through a test subclass (:87), and by each app's own handler tests.

    • Caveats: the soft-delete global query filter applies to this read like any other, so a soft-deleted account resolves to null and returns NotFound rather than its stored preferences. That behavior comes from the persistence layer, not from anything in this class.

Constraints: TUser is an AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> over UserIdentifierType (:64) and TCommand is an IRedeemSignInLinkCommand (:65). Also uses Email, SignInLinkGrant, SignInLinkProfile, SignInLinkErrors, IEmailConfirmableUser, IAuthUser, PasswordCredential and IPasswordClearableUser. Externals: Microsoft.Extensions.Options and Microsoft.Extensions.Logging (source-generated [LoggerMessage], :302-317).

    • Concept introduced: spend the proof before you look anything up. The token is validated and consumed (:96-102) before the account is resolved (:104), so a caller with no valid token learns nothing about whether an address holds an account; every rejection up to and including the spend collapses to one invalid-link error through Rejected (:296-300, class remarks :24-27). [Rubric §11: Security] assesses account-enumeration and credential-handling exposure. Beyond the token-first order, the audit lines carry no address (:315-317), and an unconfirmed account that holds password material has its refresh sessions revoked and its password removed when a link confirms it, because the link proves the mailbox, not the password set on that account (:238-273, remarks :41-48). [Rubric §15: Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether shared behavior has one owner. The app supplies only the lookup and the optional extension points; the order of spend, resolve, confirm and sign-in lives once here.

    • Walkthrough: three protected members, four extension points, one public method.

      • UnitOfWork (:68), Settings (:71) and HandlerName (:77, the GetType().Name default reported as the error source).
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:80-122): null-guards the command; rejects when Settings.Enabled is false (:86-89) or the address is malformed (:91-94); calls ValidateAndConsumeAsync and rejects a refused token (:96-102); resolves the account (:104-108); runs OnEmailOwnershipProvedAsync (:110); then opens the session with SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync(user.Id, command.IpAddress, command.UserAgent, ...) (:112-114) and logs the purpose on success (:116-119).
      • FindUntrackedByEmailAsync (:131, abstract): the app's own no-tracking lookup.
      • ProvisionUser (:147-148, virtual): default returns the invalid-link failure, so account creation through a link is opt-in per app (remarks :30-34).
      • OnUserProvisionedAsync (:157-158) and OnEmailOwnershipProvedAsync (:169-170): virtual no-op post-save extension points.
      • ResolveAccountAsync (:172-226, private): with no account, refuses unless the grant carries a profile (:183-187), else provisions, confirms, adds, saves and calls OnUserProvisionedAsync (:189-206); with an account, reloads it tracked through GetRepository (:209) and confirms it when it is an unconfirmed IEmailConfirmableUser (:216-223).
      • ConfirmExistingAccountAsync (:238-273, private): an account with no stored password is just confirmed and saved (:240-243); a password account whose type is not IPasswordClearableUser is refused before any mutation (:246-250); otherwise sessions are revoked first (:254-258), then ClearPassword (:260) and the confirming save (:266).
      • ConfirmAndSaveAsync (:279-289) and ConfirmIfNeeded (:291-294): confirm then save, or a no-op success for a type that is not confirmable.

    • Why it's built this way: the redeem path is the one that turns a mailbox proof into a session, so the ordering decisions (spend first, revoke before mutate, refuse before mutate) are the part worth not re-deriving per app; the comments at :248 and :252-253 state why each step precedes the next. Sign-in links are part of the opt-in identity completions (ADR-116), and the Enabled gate keeps a host that has not turned them on answering the generic refusal.

    • Where it's used: subclassed by ADC's RedeemSignInLinkHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/RedeemSignInLink/RedeemSignInLinkHandler.cs:46), which overrides FindUntrackedByEmailAsync (:63), ProvisionUser (:83), OnUserProvisionedAsync (:109) and OnEmailOwnershipProvedAsync (:119). Consumed through the closed ICommandHandler<TRedeemCommand, Result<AuthenticationResponse>> by SignInLinkControllerBase<TSendCommand, TRedeemCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/SignInLinks/SignInLinkControllerBase.cs:37, :45). Pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/SignInLinkHandlerBaseTests.cs:31 through test subclasses such as PasswordAccountRedeemHandler<TUser> (:686-692).

    • Caveats: the token is spent before the account is resolved, so a redemption that fails later (no account and no invitation profile, a refused password account) still consumes the link; the caller requests a new one. An app that overrides ProvisionUser returns an unsaved account: the workflow adds and saves it (:201-202).

Implements ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> closed over TCommand and Result (:49). Also uses Email, SignInLinkPurpose and UserEmailResources. Externals: Microsoft.Extensions.Options, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging ([LoggerMessage], :176-188) and System.Net.WebUtility.

    • Concept introduced: success-always as anti-enumeration. A disabled feature or missing SignInUrl (:64-68), a malformed address (:70-75), an address with no account (:77-83), a throttled token request (:85-92) and a failed send (:104-110) all log and return Result.Success(), so the response carries no signal about which addresses hold accounts (class remarks :24-28, the same rule ForgotPasswordHandlerBase follows). [Rubric §11: Security] assesses account-enumeration exposure. The no-account extension point runs inside NotifyNoAccountAsync (:164-174), which swallows and logs anything it throws other than a cancellation, so an override cannot reintroduce the signal through an exception; the audit lines carry no address (:182, :186). [Rubric §27: i18n] assesses whether user-facing text follows the user's culture. Subject and body are composed inside UserEmailResources.InRecipientCulture(user, ...) (:99-101), so the email reads in the account's stored culture rather than the request's.

    • Walkthrough: two protected members, four extension points, one public method.

      • UnitOfWork (:54, exposed so the lookup override can reach a read repository) and Settings (:57).
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:60-114): null-guards; gates on Settings.Enabled and a non-blank SignInUrl (:64); parses the address (:70); looks the account up untracked (:77), calling NotifyNoAccountAsync when there is none (:81); issues a token with SignInLinkPurpose.SignIn and no profile (:85-87); composes the link with Settings.ComposeLink (:95); sends the localized HTML email (:97-102); and logs the request (:112).

      • OnNoAccountAsync (:139, virtual no-op): lets an app re-issue a pending invitation for an address that holds none (remarks :30-34).
      • ComposeSubject (:146) and ComposeBody(string) (:151-161): virtual, resource-backed; the body HTML-encodes the link (:158) and states the lifetime from SignInLifetimeMinutes (:155, :159).
      • NotifyNoAccountAsync (:164-174, private): the exception-swallowing wrapper above.

    • Why it's built this way: this path never creates an account. Creating one is what an invitation does, and the app issues an invitation with SignInLinkPurpose.Invite through ISignInLinkTokenService directly (remarks :30-34). A send failure after the token is issued leaves that token valid, so the user can retry without the caller learning anything (:105-106).

    • Where it's used: subclassed by ADC's SendSignInLinkHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/SendSignInLink/SendSignInLinkHandler.cs:44), which overrides FindUntrackedByEmailAsync (:56) and OnNoAccountAsync (:68). Consumed through the closed ICommandHandler<TSendCommand, Result> by SignInLinkControllerBase<TSendCommand, TRedeemCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/SignInLinks/SignInLinkControllerBase.cs:36, :38, :42). Pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/SignInLinkHandlerBaseTests.cs:31 through TestSendSignInLinkHandler (:712-717) and NoAccountSendSignInLinkHandler (:737).

    ScheduledJobRunner

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Scheduling · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Scheduling/ScheduledJobRunner.cs:40 · Level 13 · class (sealed, partial, BackgroundService)

    • What it is: the framework's recurring job scheduler. A BackgroundService that runs the host's registered IScheduledJob implementations on their cron schedules, using a persistent job store (ScheduledJobEntry) and the outbox processor's claim-lease idiom so an occurrence executes exactly once across every replica.

    • Depends on: IServiceScopeFactory, ILogger<ScheduledJobRunner>, IOptions<SchedulerSettings> (SchedulerSettings), IDataSourceResolver, and an optional TimeProvider (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:40-45). At run time it resolves IDbContextFactory per cycle (:222) and works against ApplicationDbContext; it emits through SchedulerMetrics and returns its claim results as JobClaim. Externals: EF Core (ExecuteUpdateAsync), Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting, and Cronos, aliased as CronSchedule (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:13).

    • Concept introduced, the claim-lease scheduler. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether work survives failure: a schedule that lives in a timer dies with the process, so the schedule lives in a table and the loop only reads it. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses scale-out: an interval-driven hosted service runs on every replica, so scaling a service to three instances silently triples a purge. The fix is the outbox's claim: a single ExecuteUpdateAsync that stamps LockedUntil and LockToken over a Where admitting only unleased-or-expired rows, where the count of matched rows IS the race result (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:438-450). Two replicas both issue that update and exactly one matches. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: every branch that a human would need to explain later has a [LoggerMessage] line, including the ones that do nothing (disabled scheduler, duplicate job name, lease lost). [Rubric §14, Testability]: the injected TimeProvider plus an internal RunCycleAsync mean a test drives one whole cycle deterministically without waiting on wall-clock timers (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:215-216).

    • Walkthrough:

      • State and constants. _settings snapshots IOptions<SchedulerSettings>.Value once (ScheduledJobRunner.cs:47), and _timeProvider falls back to TimeProvider.System (:47). The three outcome strings Succeeded, Failed and Skipped are named constants (:50, :53, :59), MaxErrorLength is 2048 and matches the LastError column width (:62), StartupDelay is 15 seconds so the host finishes module registration and migration before the first cycle touches the table (:69), and MinimumWait is one second, the floor that stops an overdue row hot-looping the runner (:72). StampTimeout is five seconds (:80), the budget for recording an outcome after a job has returned (see ExecuteClaimedJobAsync below).
      • ExecuteAsync (:83-135), the loop. It returns immediately when Scheduler:Enabled is false, after one log line (:85-91), so a disabled scheduler is visible in the logs of a host that expected it without costing a line per cycle. Then the startup delay (:93-100), then forever: run a cycle, and swallow exceptions in two distinct ways. OperationCanceledException during shutdown breaks the loop (:109-113); any other exception is logged and the loop waits out the interval (:114-119), because one bad cycle (an unreachable database, a model mismatch) must not take the scheduler down for the life of the process.
      • The smart wait. ComputeWaitTime (:146-160) is a pure static function: the polling interval when nothing is registered, otherwise the time until the earliest upcoming occurrence, floored at MinimumWait and capped at the configured interval. This is the same "sleep until there is something to do" shape OutboxProcessor uses, and it is what keeps an idle scheduler from polling on a fixed tick.
      • RunCycleAsync (:213-236). One DI scope per cycle. It resolves the registered jobs (:216), returns early when there are none (:217-220), takes the context for the Default logical source on the configured engine through IDataSourceResolver (:222-224), reconciles registrations, runs due jobs, and finally reads back the earliest NextRunOn across the registered names (:229-235) which becomes the next wait.
      • ResolveRegisteredJobs (:243-258) groups GetServices<IScheduledJob>() by Name (ordinal) and keeps the first of each group, logging a collision rather than throwing (:251-254). Two jobs sharing a name would share one schedule row, and the design choice is that one mis-registered module must not stop every other job.
      • SyncRegistrationsAsync (:267-328) reconciles the table against the registered jobs. It reads the stored expressions once (:275-279), and for each job compares the resolved expression against the stored one: unchanged means leave the row alone (:287-293), with the comment naming the bug that would otherwise appear, recomputing NextRunOn every cycle would push every schedule forward forever and nothing would ever fire. A changed expression goes through the set-based UpdateScheduleAsync (:334-366) so a row another replica is currently executing is not disturbed by the change tracker; a new job is inserted (:307-319). An unparsable expression parks the row at DateTime.MaxValue and records Skipped instead of throwing (:295-316, and on the update path at :356-365).
      • ResolveCronExpression (:170-174) is the configuration override point: Scheduler:Jobs:{Name}:Cron when present and non-blank, otherwise the job's compiled-in default. TryGetNextOccurrence (:184-205) wraps Cronos and catches exactly CronFormatException and ArgumentException (:197), converting a malformed expression into a parked row plus an error message rather than a crashed runner.
      • RunDueJobsAsync (:373-401) claims and runs one row at a time, tracking an attempted set so each name is tried at most once per cycle (:378-390). A JobClaim with a null LockToken means another replica won that row, so it is skipped rather than retried (:392-399).
      • TryClaimNextDueAsync (:410-448) reads the earliest due, unleased row (:417-424), mints a Guid token and a lease of Scheduler:LeaseSeconds from now (:431-432), then issues the conditional claim update described above (:437-445).
      • ExecuteClaimedJobAsync (:462-521) records the lag (floored at zero so a clock adjustment cannot publish a negative duration, :472-475), invokes the job, records duration and the outcome-tagged counter (:477-482), then computes the next occurrence from the instant execution finished, not from the occurrence that just ran (:484-488). That is the missed-run policy: a host down for a day runs each job once on startup and returns to cadence instead of replaying a backlog. The final stamp is guarded by the claim token (:497-512): a replica whose lease expired mid-execution matches nothing, logs LogLeaseLost and drops its stale outcome (:514-518) rather than overwriting the current holder's record. That stamp runs under its own CancellationTokenSource(StampTimeout, _timeProvider) (:500, passed at :511) rather than the host stopping token (the source calls this "the outbox M8 shape"): the doc on StampTimeout (:74-79) explains that a completed occurrence must always advance its schedule and release its lease, or a graceful stop landing between the job and the stamp would leave the row leased and re-run work that already finished once the lease expires. Building the source from the injected TimeProvider keeps that budget testable on a fake clock.
      • InvokeJobAsync (:528-560) resolves the job in a fresh DI scope (:532-534), exactly like a request, so a job body gets scoped services (a unit of work, repositories, handlers) and the long-lived runner never captures a scoped dependency. A missing job returns Skipped with a message (:536-540); a cancellation during host shutdown is rethrown so the row stays leased and the occurrence is retried when the lease expires rather than being recorded as a failure it never was (:548-554); any other exception is logged and recorded as Failed (:555-559), so the schedule still advances and a permanently failing job cannot hot-loop. The two shutdown paths are deliberately different: a job interrupted mid-run is retried, while a job that ran to completion gets its stamp under StampTimeout regardless of the stopping token.
      • Log levels are a cost decision. The per-occurrence start and completion lines are Debug (:586-590) with the reason stated inline (a busy schedule would otherwise double this runner's steady-state log volume, [Rubric §31, Cost/FinOps], :583-585), while every failure line stays Error or Warning (:562-596).

    • Why it's built this way: ADR-074 records the decision to extend the durable polling loop already in production instead of adopting Hangfire or Quartz.NET, on the grounds that the missing piece was a cron expression, not a product, and that every extracted service host (ADR-008) would otherwise have to reason about a new dependency. Cron parsing is the one thing bought rather than built (Cronos, MIT, zero-dependency).

    • Where it's used: registered by AddScheduledJobs through TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IHostedService, ScheduledJobRunner>()) (MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:46-47), deliberately not AddHostedService, since the latter appends a descriptor per call and two modules calling it would run two runners racing for the same rows (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:44-46). The framework's own scheduled job is AuditTrailCleanupJob, registered by AddAuditTrail (DependencyInjection.Jobs.cs:124). ScheduledJobRunnerTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/ScheduledJobRunnerTests.cs:21) drives whole cycles through the internal entry point via a shared SchedulerTestHarness (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/SchedulerTestHarness.cs), and SchedulerModelGateTests (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Scheduling/SchedulerModelGateTests.cs:25) pins the model gate.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: which hosts actually call AddScheduledJobs and set Scheduler:Enabled lives in the downstream apps, not in this repository, so the set of deployments running a schedule today is Not determinable from source here.

Its one member, ConsumeAsync(IIntegrationEvent, IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> headers, CancellationToken) (IBrokerMessageConsumer.cs:19), lets BrokerReceivePipeline call the closed consumer for a subscription's runtime type without reflection per message (IBrokerMessageConsumer.cs:5-11).

The pipeline only learns the event's CLR type at run time (from the event-name header), so it cannot call a generic ConsumeAsync<TEvent> directly. Both consumers implement this interface explicitly and forward to their own typed method with one cast, so the typed API stays the public face and the pipeline resolves the consumer once per attempt as (IBrokerMessageConsumer)scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService(consumerType) (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:235).

    EventUpcasterStartupValidator

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Consumers · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:20 · Level 3 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: a one-method IHostedService whose entire job is to resolve IEventUpcasterRegistry at host start, so a bad upcaster registration graph fails the host instead of dead-lettering the first retired-contract message hours later (EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:7-12).
    • Depends on: IEventUpcasterRegistry as its single primary-constructor parameter (EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:20), Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting.IHostedService, and IIntegrationEvent as the type it probes with.
    • Concept introduced, validation by construction, forced by resolution. [Rubric §15, Best Practices and Code Quality] assesses whether invariants are checked at the earliest possible moment, and [Rubric §13, Observability and Operability] assesses whether a misconfiguration is discoverable. The validation itself does not live here: EventUpcasterRegistry validates its whole registration graph in its constructor, rejecting a duplicate source, a type mapped onto itself, and a cycle, with a message naming the offenders. Since DI is lazy, that constructor might not run until the first broker message arrives. This class exists purely to make it run at start. That is the fail-fast configuration posture of ADR-070 applied to a graph that options validation cannot express.
    • Walkthrough
      • StartAsync (EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:23-30) discards the result of upcasters.ResolveTerminalType(typeof(IIntegrationEvent)) (:27) and returns a completed task. The comment at :25-26 explains why the call exists at all: the real work happened in the injected registry's constructor, and reading one member is what makes the dependency impossible to elide.
      • StopAsync (EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:33) is a completed task. There is nothing to unwind.
    • Why it's built this way: the registration is the other half of the design, and its comment is explicit (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:227-231): TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IHostedService, EventUpcasterStartupValidator>()), not AddHostedService, because two modules calling AddInfrastructure must not run the same validation twice. TryAddEnumerable de-duplicates on the implementation type, which AddHostedService does not. The class doc adds the cost note (EventUpcasterStartupValidator.cs:13-17): a host with no upcasters resolves an empty registry, and the whole mechanism costs one no-op call at start (ADR-090).
    • Where it's used: registered once inside AddInfrastructure (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:231), so every host that calls it gets the check. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Consumers/EventUpcasterStartupValidatorTests.cs.

    [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] applies: this type sits on the path a message takes once it leaves the process (outbox, bus, consumer, or broker plumbing), which is what section 10 scores.

    • What it is: the unconfigured default for IFileStorageService. Uploads fail with a clear, stable error; deletes succeed, because there is nothing stored to delete (NullFileStorageService.cs:6-14).
    • Depends on: IFileStorageService as the contract and Result / Error for its returns.
    • Concept: the null-object default introduced at NullNativePushSender, with one instructive difference. [Rubric §29, Resilience and Business Continuity] assesses whether a missing capability degrades predictably. This null object is not uniformly silent: the two operations are treated asymmetrically because their meanings differ. A caller that wanted to store something and got nothing must be told (an upload that silently succeeded while storing nothing would leave a dangling URL in the database), whereas a caller that wanted something gone already has what it asked for.
    • Walkthrough
      • IsConfigured returns false (NullFileStorageService.cs:17), the flag the interface offers so a handler can gate a feature (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Storage/IFileStorageService.cs:17-18).

The options overload carries the same grandfathered RS0026 suppression as its Azure sibling (:21), since changing a shipped public signature would be a breaking change.

      • NotConfigured() (NullFileStorageService.cs:32-36) is the private helper both upload overloads share: a failed Result carrying Error.Failure with code FileStorage.NotConfigured, a message naming the actual condition ("No file storage is configured for this host"), and source set to the type name.     • Why it's built this way: the class doc says it directly (NullFileStorageService.cs:7-9), feature endpoints degrade cleanly. Because the failure is a Result and not an exception (ADR-013), an avatar upload in a host with no storage configured returns a clean error response instead of a 500, and the same code path works whether or not the deployment has provisioned a storage account (ADR-045).

Text that leaves the request (an email sent to someone else's address) should honor that person's locale. InRecipientCulture<T>(recipient, compose) (UserEmailResources.cs:29-44) saves CultureInfo.CurrentUICulture, switches it to the recipient's resolved preference when recipient is an IUserPreferences with a non-blank PreferredCulture, runs compose, and restores the previous culture in a finally. Without a stored preference the request's culture stays in force. Because it sets the current UI culture, both the default .resx text and any app override that reads the current UI culture speak the recipient's language.
