    ConsumerOriginRestore

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Consumers · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:20 · Level 6 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the consumer-side half of context propagation. It reads the five origin headers off a delivered message and restores them onto the per-message scope through AmbientOrigin.Restore, so a broker-delivered handler sees the identity, tenant and correlation id an in-process dispatch would have seen; a message carrying no headers (an older publisher, or an event raised with no user) leaves the scope's defaults untouched (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:7-12, :22-26).
    • Depends on: AmbientOrigin for the actual restore, MessageHeaders for the five header names, IServiceProvider, and the UserIdentifierType alias with its TryParse. The headers arrive as an IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string> (:31), the transport-neutral shape every transport hands the receive pipeline.
    • Concept introduced, parsing rather than trusting a typed header. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] assesses whether the pipeline handles transport differences correctly rather than assuming one broker's behavior. The user id is transported as text and parsed back with UserIdentifierType.TryParse under the invariant culture (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:37-43). A malformed value is treated as a publisher bug, not a reason to fail the consume, so it simply yields no identity rather than throwing (:35-36).
    • Walkthrough
      • Apply(headers, services, authenticationType) (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:31-53) throws on null headers (:33), parses MessageHeaders.UserId, defaulting to null on failure (:37-43), and returns an IDisposable: the handle that withdraws the published origin, which the caller holds for the whole consume (:30).
      • It returns AmbientOrigin.Restore with that id and the remaining four headers, UserRoles, UserPermissions, TenantId, and CorrelationId, read straight through as strings (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:45-52), so the handle is AmbientOrigin's own restore handle passed through unchanged.
      • Get(headers, name) (:55-56): TryGetValue, null when the header is absent.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the header-reading and the id-parsing in this one adapter, separate from AmbientOrigin itself, means the restore logic stays transport-agnostic while this class is the one step of the restore that knows about a transport (ConsumerOriginRestore.cs:14-18).
    • Where it's used: called by IntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> and UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:64), the two consumers BrokerReceivePipeline dispatches to, both before touching the inbox, so a retired contract is restored under the same identity and tenant its plain-consumer sibling would have used. Also referenced by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/BrokerMessageBusTests.cs.

    DeleteUserHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.DeleteUser · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:96 · Level 8 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared account-erasure workflow: authorize owner-or-privileged-role, soft-delete the account, run the app's tail hook, irreversibly anonymize the personal data in place, revoke and anonymize the account's refresh-session rows, blank its email on the support access log, schedule the deletion of its native-push installations, save, write the shared soft-deleted marker that revokes the account's already-issued access tokens, then drain a post-save queue (DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:14-26, :118-229). It exposes one abstract member and one virtual hook.

    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork, an ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter and an ILogger, then four optional parameters that default to null: an IRefreshSessionStore (refresh sessions are opt-in), a TimeProvider, an IViewAsGrantStore and an IInternalCommandScheduler (:96-103); implements ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> over Result (:103). The session helper is the shared RefreshSessionRevocation (:177-179). Constraints: TUser is an AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> implementing IErasableUser (:104), and TCommand is an IUserOwnedRequest (:105), not an IUserScopedCommand<out TRequest>: this workflow needs the caller as well as the target, and carries no request payload. It also uses UserOwnershipRule, Error and DeleteUserPushInstallationsInternalCommand, and logs through two private source-generated [LoggerMessage] methods, UserErased at Information (:262-263) and SoftDeletedMarkerFailed at Warning (:265-266), hence the partial declaration (:96). Externals: Microsoft.Extensions.Logging (:1).

    • Concept introduced: anonymize-in-place erasure, and why the row survives. Soft-delete (IsDeleted = true) hides a row but keeps its personal data, so it does not by itself satisfy a GDPR/CCPA erasure request; hard-deleting the row would break cross-context scalar references and destroy the audit trail. The framework's answer is the pair IAnonymizable plus IErasableUser: keep the row, overwrite the personal fields with non-identifying placeholders, and require Anonymize() to be idempotent (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Interfaces/IAnonymizable.cs:24-30). This handler is where that policy becomes a sequence (ADR-005).

      Concept introduced: interface dispatch as a correctness device. The comment at :148-150 states the rule briefly: the base calls Delete() through an IErasableUser local (:151-152), so interface dispatch runs the Delete() the app type maps onto IErasableUser, and a User that forgets the interface fails the TUser constraint at compile time. The reason it matters: an app's User may hide the base entity's Delete() with public new Result Delete(). A hidden method is not an override, and member lookup on a generic type parameter prefers the members of its class constraint, so a bare user.Delete() here would bind to AuditableBaseEntity<TIdentifierType>.Delete() and silently skip the app's version. The interface's own remarks record the same reasoning from the contract side (IErasableUser.cs:13-23), including the deliberate choice not to implement it on the base entity (IErasableUser.cs:18-19).

      Concept introduced: the post-save queue. OnAfterSoftDeleteAsync receives an ICollection<Func<CancellationToken, Task>> afterCommit (:255-260). Work that must not happen unless the erasure is actually saved (deleting a blob, notifying another system) is enqueued rather than run inline, and the base drains the queue in order after the save and the marker write (:221-224). The override can hand values it captured before anonymization to a post-save closure without parking them in mutable handler state (:53-55), which matters because a scoped handler's field would be shared mutable state for the whole request. The class summary is precise about what "after" means: under an ITransactional command the save is not the commit, so the marker and every afterCommit action run before the transaction commits, and only idempotent, retry-safe work belongs there; anything that must survive with the erasure should be scheduled as an internal command inside the unit instead (:22-25, repeated on the parameter at :245-252).

      Concept introduced: token revocation as part of the shared workflow, best effort and first. Between the save and the queued actions the base writes the shared soft-deleted marker through markerWriter.MarkDeletedAsync (:214), which is what stops an erased account's already-issued access token from working before the next database lookup would notice; the API middleware reads SoftDeletedUserCache on every host, and on a host without the soft-deleted-user validator query the marker is the only thing that rejects such a token (:29-32, ADR-047). The writer sizes the marker to outlive every access token issued before the erasure, and AddApplication registers it (:67-70). Two decisions are documented on the class and are worth reading as a pair. It is best effort (:33-37): the erasure is already saved, so a cache fault must not turn a successful, irreversible deletion into a failure the caller would retry, and the write is wrapped in a try/catch (excluding OperationCanceledException) that logs SoftDeletedMarkerFailed and continues (:212-219). The warning text states the consequence: the Identity host still rejects the deleted user's access token, but a host without the account-status query accepts it until it expires (:265-266). And it runs before the queued actions (:40-43), because that tail is unbounded app work and every second it takes is a second the deleted account's token still works. Owning the marker here rather than in each app's tail gives both apps the identical revocation window; the hook's own docs tell an override not to queue a marker write (:250-251).

      Concept introduced: personal data held beside the account is erased in the same unit. Three optional steps run after the user's own Anonymize() and before the save, each a no-op when the subclass forwards nothing:

      • Refresh sessions (:172-179): a session stores the IP address and user agent captured at sign-in, on revoked rows as much as live ones. RefreshSessionRevocation.RevokeAndAnonymizeAllAsync revokes every un-revoked session and anonymizes every row; the store hands back tracked rows on the same context factory, so the changes commit or roll back with the erasure in the one save (:206).
      • The support access log (:181-188): viewAsGrants.ForgetUserAsync blanks the account's email snapshot on every view-as grant naming it, as staff or as the viewed account; the grant rows themselves stay until ViewAs:RetentionDays sweeps them (ADR-137).
      • Native-push installations (:190-204): these live with the push provider, outside the unit of work, so the base schedules a DeleteUserPushInstallationsInternalCommand through the scheduler instead of calling the provider inline. The row commits with the erasure and the processor retries it until the provider answers (ADR-044, ADR-114). A scheduling failure fails the erasure (:200-203), because a partial erasure reported as a success is worse than a retryable failure (:193-194).

      [Rubric §30: Compliance, Privacy & Data Governance] assesses whether a data-subject erasure request is actually satisfiable. The sequence here is the mechanism behind both apps' published erasure promise: soft-delete, then irreversible anonymization of the account and the rows beside it, persisted in one save (:14-21).

      [Rubric §11: Security] assesses authorization placement. The very first thing the method does, before it touches the repository, is the ownership check (:124-134), so an unauthorized caller cannot even confirm that an account id exists. The privileged-role test is passed in already evaluated because each app owns its own role vocabulary (UserOwnershipRule.cs:14-18).

      [Rubric §1: SOLID] assesses the template-method shape. The invariant order (authorize, load, delete, tail, anonymize, session revoke-and-anonymize, view-as forget, push-deletion schedule, save, token revoke, queued actions) is fixed by the base; only the two hooks vary.

    • Walkthrough: two protected members, the handler method, two hooks and two log methods.

      • Primary constructor (:96-103): unitOfWork, markerWriter, logger, and the optional refreshSessions, timeProvider, viewAsGrants and internalCommandScheduler. UnitOfWork (:108) is protected specifically so a tail hook can enlist further aggregates.
      • HandlerName (:115): GetType().Name by default, so an app subclass named DeleteUserHandler reports that name as the error source (:110-114).
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:118-229):
        • Authorization first (:124-130) through UserOwnershipRule.CheckOwnership (UserOwnershipRule.cs:37), with the code "User.DeleteForbidden" and a message the caller sees; a non-null return is the failure (:131-134).
        • Load through the write repository (:136-137); Error.NotFound when absent (:140).
        • IErasableUser erasable = user; erasable.Delete() (:151-152) with the dispatch rationale above; a failure returns immediately (:153-156). The comment there points forward to the session handling: refresh sessions are revoked and anonymized further down, not left to the app (:145-146).
        • Allocate the afterCommit list and call OnAfterSoftDeleteAsync (:158-159); a failed tail aborts before anything is persisted (:160-163).
        • erasable.Anonymize() (:166), also short-circuiting on failure (:167-170).
        • RefreshSessionRevocation.RevokeAndAnonymizeAllAsync(refreshSessions, timeProvider, ...) (:177-179), a no-op when no store was forwarded; then ForgetUserAsync when a grant store was forwarded (:185-188); then the push-deletion schedule when a scheduler was forwarded (:195-204).
        • SaveChangesAsync (:206), then the best-effort marker write (:212-219), then the queued actions drained in order (:221-224), then the UserErased log (:226) and Result.Success() (:228).
      • HasDeletePrivilege(string? currentUserRole) (:237): protected abstract. Deliberately abstract rather than virtual-defaulting-to-false, so adopting the base forces an explicit answer about which role bypasses ownership; its XML doc names UserRole.IsAdmin(...) only as an example of "whatever the app's privileged role is" (:231-236).
      • OnAfterSoftDeleteAsync(user, command, afterCommit, cancellationToken) (:255-260): protected virtual, defaulting to Task.FromResult(Result.Success()); returning a failure aborts the erasure before anything is persisted (:240-241). Its position is load-bearing and documented: it runs after Delete() and before Anonymize() (:49-52), which is the only point where an override can both read personal data that anonymization is about to erase and enlist further aggregates in the same unit of work. Running it after Delete() rather than before means an already-deleted account fails with its own AlreadyDeleted error rather than one raised by a cascaded aggregate (:59-61).

    • Why it's built this way: the hook contract was derived from what the two apps actually needed, and both uses are visible in their overrides. ADC's override (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandler.cs:53-84) captures the avatar blob name before anonymization clears the URL (DeleteUserHandler.cs:61), raises the cross-service UserDeleted event on the aggregate so its outbox row is written by the very save that commits the erasure (:69), and schedules the avatar blob deletion as a durable internal command through IInternalCommandScheduler inside the erasure transaction rather than queueing it on afterCommit, so an erasure that persists can never lose the instruction to delete the photo (:71-81, :86 onward). Store instead cascades in the same unit of work, erasing the linked Customer that holds its name/email/address PII and returning the Customer's own failure untouched so nothing is persisted (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandler.cs:56 onward). One hook covers both because it can do work inline and schedule work for after the save.

    • Where it's used: subclassed once per app, each supplying its own privileged role to HasDeletePrivilege and forwarding what it has. ADC (MMCA.ADC/.../DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandler.cs:35-43) forwards the marker writer, the refresh-session store, the view-as grant store and its scheduler, with HasDeletePrivilege returning UserRole.IsOrganizer(...) (:49-50). Store (MMCA.Store/.../DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandler.cs:36-42) forwards the marker writer, the refresh-session store and the scheduler, but no grant store, with UserRole.IsAdmin(...) (:45-46); its own doc notes Store registers no push adapter, so the push command completes having deleted nothing there (:31-35). AddApplication() registers the push command's handler (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:64). Covered directly by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/DeleteUserHandlerBaseTests.cs, whose fixture user type is TestHidingDeleteUser (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/UserUseCaseTestDoubles.cs) precisely so the hidden-Delete() dispatch rule above is a regression test rather than a comment.

    • Caveats: queued afterCommit actions run after the erasure has been saved, so each one owns its own failure handling; the base does not wrap them (:221-224, and see the documented expectation at :245-252). Under an ITransactional command they, and the marker, run before the commit (:22-25). The one exception to "not wrapped" is the marker write the base performs itself, which it does wrap (:212-219). Both apps' DeleteUserCommand records are ICacheInvalidating, so the cache prefix they carry is invalidated by the decorator after the handler returns success, outside this class.

    UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Consumers · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:29 · Level 8 · class (public sealed partial, generic)

    • What it is: the draining consumer for a retired integration-event contract. It receives the old type from the host's queue, upcasts each message to its terminal contract, and invokes the handlers registered for that terminal contract, so handlers are written once against the newest event type while producers still publishing the old one (and messages already queued at the upgrade) keep being delivered (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:10-20).
    • Depends on: IEventUpcasterRegistry, IServiceProvider, IInboxStore, and ILogger<T> as its four primary-constructor parameters (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:30-33); implements IBrokerMessageConsumer (:33); EventNameResolver for the inbox key; ConsumerOriginRestore to restore the publisher's identity, tenant, and correlation id before the inbox is touched; UpcastDispatch for the per-terminal-type handler invoker.
    • Concept introduced, contract retirement without a coordinated deploy. [Rubric §6, CQRS and Event-Driven] assesses whether the event pipeline can evolve its contracts, and [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] assesses whether two services can be deployed independently. Renaming or reshaping an integration event across a distributed system normally forces a lockstep deploy, because in-flight messages of the old shape have no handler on the other side. ADR-090 resolves that with a registered IEventUpcaster chain plus this consumer: the old subscription stays bound and drains, each message walks the upcaster chain to the terminal type, and the handler code only ever knows the newest contract. The current contract keeps using the plain IntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent>, and the builder refuses to register both kinds for the same type (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:17-19; the check itself is BrokerConsumerBuilder's duplicate guard).
    • Concept, dedup keyed on the original message id. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether idempotency is applied uniformly rather than per handler. Idempotent consumption (ADR-021) keys on the message id carried in the envelope. The doc (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:22-25) records that the registry preserves the envelope across every upcast hop, so the id this consumer records is the same id a plain consumer would have recorded, and a redelivery is recognised whatever contract the handlers ultimately see.
    • Concept, restoring the publisher's origin before the inbox is touched. [Rubric §11, Security] and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] both apply here: under database-per-tenant, the inbox store's own routing depends on the tenant this restore sets. PrincipalAuthenticationType (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:36-41) is declared as the same constant IntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> uses, because an upcast changes the contract, never the hop the identity came back from. ConsumeAsync calls ConsumerOriginRestore.Apply (:59-64) before the dedup check for exactly the reason the sibling consumer does it in the same order: a retired contract is delivered with the same headers as a current one, so a consumer that skipped this would run its handlers anonymous while its sibling did not. The returned handle is bound with using var origin and so held for the whole consume (:63-64), which lets a handler's own scope inherit the origin too.
    • Walkthrough
      • ConsumeAsync(integrationEvent, headers, cancellationToken) (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:51-137) guards both arguments (:56-57), restores the publisher's origin first via ConsumerOriginRestore.Apply (:64), then takes integrationEvent.MessageId before any upcasting (:68), which is the point of the earlier concept paragraph on dedup.
      • The inbox key is EventNameResolver.GetInboxName(typeof(TEvent)) (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:72), the retired contract's [EventName] identity when it declares one and its short type name otherwise, which is what every row written so far holds (:70-71).
      • inbox.TryBeginAsync(...) returning false means already processed: log at Debug and return (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:76-80). TryBegin also stages the inbox row in the scope's unit of work; it is written by CompleteAsync once every handler has succeeded (:74-75), as in IntegrationEventConsumer.
      • With no upcaster registered for the type, the consumer logs at Information and continues (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:82-87). This is the documented degrade path: the registry returns the instance untouched, and handlers for the original type run as usual.
      • UpcastToTerminal produces the terminal instance, and a type change is logged at Debug with both contract names (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:89-95).
      • Handler dispatch is non-generic because the terminal type is only known at runtime: UpcastDispatch.For(terminalType) (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:97) returns the closed IIntegrationEventHandler<> interface and a compiled invoker, memoized per terminal type in UpcastDispatch, so reflection is paid once per contract instead of once per message. This mirrors what DomainEventDispatcher does for the in-process path.
      • The dispatch loop (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:101-125) counts handlers and awaits each invoker (:112). Its catch (:114-124) is the failure contract: inbox.Abandon(messageId) discards the staged row so the redelivery is reprocessed rather than skipped as a duplicate (:118), the handler failure is logged with the handler's full type name, and the exception is rethrown (:123) so the receive pipeline retries in a fresh scope, then redelivers or dead-letters (:120-121; the mechanism is BrokerReceivePipeline). OperationCanceledException is excluded from the catch filter, so a shutdown is not treated as a handler failure.
      • Zero handlers is an Information log, not an error (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:127-132): returning normally completes the message, and the comment states plainly that the broker will not retry.
      • inbox.CompleteAsync(...) (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:136) persists the staged row unless a handler's own save already committed it. The message is recorded only on a successful consume, because the failure path above rethrows.
      • The explicit IBrokerMessageConsumer.ConsumeAsync (UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumer.cs:140-144) casts the event to TEvent and forwards, which is how the non-generic pipeline reaches the typed method.
    • Why it's built this way: the alternative to a per-retired-type consumer is version-tolerant handlers, each branching on a schema version, which spreads the migration across every handler and never gets cleaned up. Concentrating it in one registered consumer per retired contract means the retirement is visible in one place in a host's broker registration and can be deleted when the old subscription is drained (ADR-010 sets the versioning policy, ADR-090 ships the mechanism, ADR-118 makes the transports framework code).
    • Where it's used: registered per retired type through RegisterUpcastedIntegrationEventConsumer<TEvent> on the IBrokerConsumerBuilder that AddBrokerMessaging hands its callback (BrokerConsumerBuilder, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:25-27), which maps the subscription to this closed type (:40-42) and has it registered scoped (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:105). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Consumers/UpcastingIntegrationEventConsumerTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: no host under MMCA.ADC/Source calls RegisterUpcastedIntegrationEventConsumer (MMCA.Store was not re-checked in this pass); the extension point is documented on BaseIntegrationEvent and on OutputCacheEvictionRequested as the path to take when a contract is retired. Its behavior is therefore established by the test suite rather than by production traffic.

    [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] applies: this type sits on the path a message takes once it leaves the process (outbox, bus, consumer, or broker plumbing), which is what section 10 scores.

    • What it is: the IBrokerConsumerBuilder that AddBrokerMessaging hands its configureConsumers callback. It collects one BrokerSubscription per registered event, in registration order, for the host's BrokerTopology (BrokerConsumerBuilder.cs:6-10).

    • Where it's used: constructed and invoked by AddBrokerMessaging (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:91-97), which then registers ConsumerTypeFor(subscription) scoped for every subscription (:103-106); BrokerReceivePipeline builds its dispatch table with ConsumerTypeFor (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:75-78).     BrokerReceivePipeline

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Messaging.Consumers · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:26 · Level 10 · class (internal sealed partial)

    • What it is: the framework's one IBrokerReceivePipeline, shared by every transport. Per delivered message it starts a Consumer span parented on the publisher's trace context, resolves the subscription from the event-name header, deserializes the body, and runs the subscription's consumer with in-process retry, each attempt in a fresh DI scope; when every retry fails it asks the transport for a second-level redelivery, and once those are spent it dead-letters the message with one Error log and one broker.fault.count (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:12-19).
    • Depends on: BrokerTopology, IServiceScopeFactory, MessageBusSettings, an optional transport redelivery-delay cap, TimeProvider and ILogger<T> (:55-61); BrokerTransportPolicies for the retry and redelivery schedule; BrokerConsumerBuilder for the consumer types; IBrokerMessageConsumer to call them; IncomingBrokerMessage in, BrokerDisposition out (DeadLetter, Redeliver); BrokerHeaders, BrokerWire (JSON options, ActivitySource) and BrokerMetrics. Externals: System.Text.Json, System.Diagnostics.
    • Concept introduced, the transport decides how, the pipeline decides what. [Rubric §10, Messaging & Integration Architecture] assesses whether retry, redelivery and dead-lettering are applied uniformly. Each transport only receives a message and applies the disposition this class returns; the policy (how many attempts, which delays, when to give up, what to log and count) lives here once (ADR-118). [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether failures are classified: a delivery no retry can fix (unknown event, undeserializable body) is dead-lettered at once, while a handler failure is retried, then redelivered, then dead-lettered. The pipeline never throws for a handler or payload failure; the only exception it lets out is the OperationCanceledException of the host's own token, and the transport then leaves the message unacknowledged so the broker redelivers it after the restart (:20-24). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] applies to the span and the single dead-letter Error row.
    • Walkthrough
      • Constants (BrokerReceivePipeline.cs:29-38): the dead-letter reasons "unknown-event", "poison" and "handler-failed", and MaxDetailLength = 1024, because brokers cap the description they store.
      • Constructor (:55-79): guards its arguments, builds the redelivery intervals with BrokerTransportPolicies.BuildRedeliveryIntervals(settings, maxRedeliveryDelay) (:72), and precomputes the dispatch table, event name to closed consumer type, with BrokerConsumerBuilder.ConsumerTypeFor under ordinal comparison (:75-78).
      • ProcessAsync(message, cancellationToken) (:82-105): starts the span (:86), rejects through TryResolve (:88-92), tags mmca.event.name, runs ConsumeWithRetryAsync (:96), returns BrokerDisposition.Complete on success (:100), otherwise AfterRetriesExhausted (:104).
      • TryResolve (:111-150): a missing event name or one with no subscription is dead-lettered as unknown-event with a Warning (:120-127); a JsonException or NotSupportedException from deserializing with BrokerWire.JsonOptions (:132) is dead-lettered as poison with the truncated message (:134-139), as is a body that deserializes to null (:141-146).
      • ConsumeWithRetryAsync (:184-224): up to RetryLimit + 1 attempts (:190, :193), waiting BrokerTransportPolicies.RetryDelay(settings, attempt) on the injected clock before each retry (:197-200). The catch filter (:211) lets a cancellation of the host's own token propagate and retries anything else, a handler's own timeout included (:213-214); each failed non-final attempt logs a Warning (:218). It returns null on success or the last exception.
      • ConsumeOnceAsync (:226-238): creates a fresh async scope (:232), resolves the consumer as IBrokerMessageConsumer (:235) and calls it, so the inbox, origin restore and handlers of one attempt never see another attempt's tracked state.
      • AfterRetriesExhausted (:156-177): while redeliveries remain it logs a Warning and returns Redeliver(delay, redeliveryCount + 1) (:162-167); otherwise it logs one Error with every exception message in the chain (Describe, :273-282), adds one to BrokerMetrics.FaultCounter tagged with event_type and queue (:171-174), and returns DeadLetter("handler-failed", detail) (:176).
      • StartConsumerActivity (:245-270): parses traceparent/tracestate from the headers into a remote parent (:248-255), so the publisher's sampling decision travels with the message, and starts a "{queue} process" Consumer span with the OpenTelemetry messaging tags (:257-266).
      • Five source-generated log methods (:287-300).
    • Why it's built this way: each attempt runs in a fresh scope so a failed attempt's tracked state (a staged inbox row, a dirty unit of work) cannot leak into the next one, and the second-level wait is a transport redelivery rather than an in-process delay, so a long backoff does not hold the receive call open.
    • Where it's used: registered as the singleton IBrokerReceivePipeline by AddBrokerMessaging (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Messaging.cs:109-115), with the selected transport's MaxRedeliveryDelay (:108) and TimeProvider.System when no clock is registered (:114). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Consumers/BrokerReceivePipelineTests.cs and MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/DependencyInjectionBrokerMessagingTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the default RetryLimit, the delay curve and the redelivery intervals are defined in MessageBusSettings and BrokerTransportPolicies, not read here; which transport receivers call ProcessAsync was not re-read for this section.

    ScopedUserOverride

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ScopedUserOverride.cs:27 · Level 5 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the scoped slot that lets a background scope act as a captured user. Principal is null by default, which means "read through to HTTP"; a caller sets it before any handler is resolved, and clears it afterward (ScopedUserOverride.cs:27-51).
    • Depends on: System.Security.Claims.ClaimsPrincipal (BCL), and AmbientOrigin for the seed value its Principal initializer reads (ScopedUserOverride.cs:30). It is a two-member holder with no other collaborators.
    • Concept introduced, the override slot behind a decorator. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether identity flows correctly across an async or process boundary rather than defaulting to anonymous or leaking across scopes. HTTP requests already have an ambient identity from the authentication middleware, but background work (the internal command processor, the outbox processor, a broker consumer) runs on a scope with no HTTP context at all. This class is the seam DI resolves per scope: when nothing has called Set, Principal stays null and ImpersonatingCurrentUserService reads through to whatever the inner ICurrentUserService would have returned anyway.
    • Walkthrough
      • Principal (ScopedUserOverride.cs:30) has a private setter, so Set and Clear are the only ways to change it after construction. Its initializer is AmbientOrigin.Current?.BuildPrincipal(): the scope reads the enclosing hop's published origin once, at construction, and owns its copy from then on (ScopedUserOverride.cs:20-26, :30). A scope a handler opens for itself from the root factory inside a delivery therefore starts as the original interaction, while an HTTP request (which never publishes an origin) starts null. Nothing is shared or mutated across scopes, which is the leak a live ambient override would have caused.
      • Set(principal) (ScopedUserOverride.cs:36-40) null-guards the argument and assigns it.
      • Clear() (ScopedUserOverride.cs:50) sets Principal back to null. Its doc comment names the scenario that makes it necessary rather than optional (:39-46): the outbox processor restores one captured identity per row on a scope it keeps for the whole batch, so without an explicit clear between rows, a row raised by a user would answer for every later row raised by the system.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-114 needs internal command handlers to see the identity that originally scheduled the work, through the same ICurrentUserService interface every other handler already depends on, rather than a parallel API only background code would use.
    • Where it's used: written by AmbientOrigin.Restore (set or cleared on every restore) and read by ImpersonatingCurrentUserService. Registered per scope in DependencyInjection.cs (2 references). Exercised directly by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Messaging/Consumers/IntegrationEventConsumerContextTests.cs (4), MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/Outbox/Processing/OutboxProcessorContextRestoreTests.cs (4), and MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/InternalCommands/InternalCommandTestHarness.cs (2).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: like TenantContext, it is not thread-safe, but as a scoped service on a single logical unit of work (one HTTP request, one dequeued message, one internal command) that is not a property it needs.

    AmbientOrigin

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/AmbientOrigin.cs:21 · Level 5 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the shared helper that flattens a capturing principal's roles and permission claims for storage, rebuilds a ClaimsPrincipal from what was stored, restores a captured user, tenant, and correlation id onto a fresh scope, and publishes that restored origin on the async flow so scopes opened inside the hop inherit it (AmbientOrigin.cs:21-344). It is the one place this logic exists; everything that later replays a captured origin, an internal command row, an outbox row, a broker message, calls into it.
    • Depends on: ScopedUserOverride and ITenantContext (from TenantContext) as the scope services it restores onto; OriginSnapshot as the published value and RestoreHandle as the disposable it returns; ICorrelationContext for the correlation id; the UserIdentifierType alias; System.Security.Claims for Claim/ClaimsIdentity/ClaimsPrincipal; System.Text.Json for the permissions array; AuthClaimTypes for the subject and permission claim types.
    • Concept introduced, one flatten/rebuild pair reused across every async boundary. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether identity propagation is centralized rather than reimplemented per call site, and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether the tenancy invariant holds even off the request path. MaxRolesLength (AmbientOrigin.cs:36-40, value 512) is the column width shared by InternalCommands.UserRoles and OutboxMessages.UserRoles; FlattenRoles fits the column rather than throw, by keeping only the whole leading roles that fit and dropping the trailing ones (:74-94): cutting a name mid-word would restore a role nobody holds and lose the real one. It is also explicitly null-tolerant even though ICurrentUserService.Roles is declared non-nullable, because Roles is a default interface member that runs against hand-written doubles and mocks that stub only the properties a caller touches (:47-53). A null there must read as "no roles", never as a capture that throws inside a save.
    • Concept, permissions travel at full fidelity as JSON. Roles alone no longer describe what a principal may do, so FlattenPermissions (AmbientOrigin.cs:110-126) captures the principal's distinct AuthClaimTypes.Permission claims, in claim order, as a JSON array of strings, and returns null when there are none. Unlike the roles list nothing is ever dropped or cut, because the UserPermissions columns are unbounded and a missing permission would deny a deferred command the inline request was allowed to run (:102-107); JSON rather than a delimited list because nothing constrains what a permission name may contain. ParsePermissions (:135-152) reads it back and treats a malformed value as a writer bug that yields no permissions rather than failing the hop, so deferred work is authorized by its roles alone, never by more than was captured.
    • Concept, the tenant is the one value Restore will not overwrite. Restore (AmbientOrigin.cs:254-288) documents an explicit asymmetry (:213-229): the principal and correlation id are set or cleared on every call, because a scope reused across several messages cannot let one message's user answer for the next, but ITenantContext is single-valued for the life of a scope by contract, since a scope whose tenant changed mid-flight has already read rows under the previous one. Restore therefore sets the tenant only when the scope has not already resolved a different one (:294-303); a host running database-per-tenant is unaffected, because its work is already one scope per tenant.
    • Concept, the restored origin is also published on the async flow. Integration event handlers are singletons that open their own scope from the root factory, a scope that never sees the Restore call. Restore therefore also writes an OriginSnapshot into a private AsyncLocal (AmbientOrigin.cs:26, :279-285), exposed read-only as Current (:34). TenantContext, ScopedUserOverride and CorrelationContext read Current once, at construction, and seed themselves from it (TenantContext.cs:19, ScopedUserOverride.cs:30, CorrelationContext.cs:13), so a handler's own scope runs as the original interaction (:231-241, the "Scopes opened inside the hop inherit it" remark). The snapshot carries the tenant and correlation id the restored scope ended up with, not the raw captured ones, so a database-per-tenant scope whose tenant was already fixed hands that tenant down (:282-283).
    • Walkthrough
      • FlattenRoles(roles) (AmbientOrigin.cs:60-95) joins the roles with a comma, keeps only the whole leading roles that fit MaxRolesLength, and returns null for a null or empty source (or when not even the first role fits).
      • FlattenPermissions(principal) (AmbientOrigin.cs:110-126) serializes the distinct permission claims to a JSON array; ParsePermissions(userPermissions) (:135-152) is its tolerant inverse.
      • BuildPrincipal(userId, userRoles, userPermissions, authenticationType) (AmbientOrigin.cs:179-206) returns null when userId is null, meaning no user was captured, and the execution stays anonymous rather than inventing an identity. Otherwise it builds a sub claim from the id, one role claim per comma-separated entry and one AuthClaimTypes.Permission claim per stored permission (:202-203), then wraps them in a ClaimsIdentity stamped with authenticationType, which is what makes IsAuthenticated true. The mfa claim is deliberately not propagated: a step-up proves a live interaction, deferred work runs later without that person present, so an IRequiresMfa command cannot run deferred and must run inline in the request that carried the step-up (:161-169).
      • Restore(services, userId, userRoles, userPermissions, tenantId, correlationId, authenticationType) (AmbientOrigin.cs:254-288) returns an IDisposable. It first saves the enclosing origin and withdraws it (:265-266), so a carrier constructed during this restore belongs to this hop and does not seed itself from the previous one. It resolves each of the three scope services with GetService rather than a required resolve, so a bare provider (a directly constructed test fixture) simply restores nothing rather than failing the hop (:226-229). It sets the tenant first via RestoreTenant (:270, :294-303), because it routes the scoped context factory to the right database and every repository resolved afterward reads its query filter from it; then sets or clears ScopedUserOverride via RestorePrincipal (:271, :306-320); then sets the correlation id when one was carried (:273-277); then publishes the new OriginSnapshot, now including the permissions, and returns a RestoreHandle that puts the previous origin back (:279-287). Callers dispose the handle when the message or row is done, so the next one cannot inherit it.
      • Suppress() (AmbientOrigin.cs:331-336) withdraws the published origin until the returned handle is disposed. It exists for the case where an explicit choice must win over an enclosing hop: its doc comment names TenantDataSourceTargets.CreateTenantScope (:325-329).
    • Why it's built this way: centralizing flatten, rebuild, and restore in one internal static class means every caller, the internal command scheduler, the outbox processor, the broker consumers, restores context identically; a divergence in any one of them would have been a silent identity or tenant leak rather than a compile error.
    • Where it's used: called by ConsumerOriginRestore (2 references) and directly by InternalCommandScheduler (2), InternalCommandProcessor (2), InternalCommandOriginCapture (2), TenantDataSourceTargets (2, the Suppress caller), BrokerMessageBus (1), DbContextFactory (1), and OutboxProcessor (1), all under MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure. The seeding readers are ScopedUserOverride, TenantContext and CorrelationContext. Exercised by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Context/TenantScopeInsideARestoredHopTests.cs (3).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: not determinable from this source whether a host could reasonably bypass Restore and set the three scope services directly; every first-party caller goes through this helper. The AsyncLocal is the one ambient value in this design, so a caller that drops the returned handle leaves the origin published for the rest of that async flow.

    OriginSnapshot

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/AmbientOrigin.cs:353 · Level 5 · record (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the immutable value AmbientOrigin publishes on the async flow while a background hop is running: the user id, roles, permissions, tenant, correlation id and authentication type the hop restored (AmbientOrigin.cs:353-364).
    • Depends on: the UserIdentifierType alias and System.Security.Claims.ClaimsPrincipal; its one method calls back into AmbientOrigin.BuildPrincipal (:363).
    • Concept introduced, a snapshot instead of a shared carrier. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether identity propagation avoids leaking across scopes. Publishing an immutable record rather than the live ScopedUserOverride or TenantContext means a scope that seeds from it copies values and then owns them; no mutable state is shared between the hop's scope and a scope a handler opens later.
    • Walkthrough
      • Positional members (AmbientOrigin.cs:353-359): UserId (nullable, null for system-raised work), UserRoles (the comma-separated list), UserPermissions (the permission claims as a JSON array, or null), TenantId, CorrelationId (both the values the restored scope ended up with) and a non-null AuthenticationType.
      • BuildPrincipal() (AmbientOrigin.cs:363) rebuilds the principal from the stored id, roles and permissions, or returns null when no user was captured. ScopedUserOverride calls it from its initializer (ScopedUserOverride.cs:30).
    • Why it's built this way: the roles and permissions stay in their flattened string forms so the snapshot carries exactly what the stored row or message header carried, and rebuilding stays in the one helper that already owns that logic.
    • Where it's used: only inside AmbientOrigin (Current, Restore) and by the three seeding carriers through Current; no other file names the type.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: none beyond the above.

    RestoreHandle

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/AmbientOrigin.cs:340 · Level 5 · class (private sealed, nested in AmbientOrigin)

    • What it is: the IDisposable that Restore and Suppress hand back; disposing it puts the previously published origin back (AmbientOrigin.cs:340-343).
    • Depends on: OriginSnapshot (the saved previous value) and the private CurrentOrigin AsyncLocal of its enclosing AmbientOrigin (:24).
    • Concept introduced, scoped publication through a disposable. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses whether a lifetime is expressed by the type system rather than by a convention. The handle makes "publish for the duration of this message or row" a using-shaped contract: Dispose is the single line CurrentOrigin.Value = previous (:242), so nesting restores correctly and the next message in a reused scope cannot inherit the last one's origin.
    • Walkthrough: a primary constructor capturing previous (AmbientOrigin.cs:340), and Dispose (:242) assigning it back. Restore passes the origin it displaced (:187) and Suppress passes the one it withdrew (:236).
    • Why it's built this way: a private nested class keeps the AsyncLocal writable only from AmbientOrigin, while callers see only IDisposable.
    • Where it's used: constructed in Restore and Suppress in the same file; callers hold it as IDisposable.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: not determinable from source whether every caller disposes it on all paths; that is each caller's responsibility.

    TenantContext

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Context · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/TenantContext.cs:13 · Level 6 · class (public sealed)

    • What it is: the scoped holder of "which tenant is this scope running as". It starts unresolved (unless it is created inside a background hop, below), is set exactly once per scope, and refuses to be changed to a different value afterwards (TenantContext.cs:6-13). A scope created while an outbox row, broker message or internal command is being delivered starts with the tenant that hop restored, so a handler that opens its own scope runs under the original tenant (TenantContext.cs:19).
    • Depends on: ITenantContext as the contract, System.Globalization for the exception message, and AmbientOrigin for the seed read in the constructor (TenantContext.cs:19). Otherwise it is a two-property object with one guarded setter.
    • Concept introduced, the ambient scope value with a write-once discipline. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether an isolation boundary can be crossed by accident, and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether the tenancy model is enforced by the infrastructure rather than by convention. Multi-tenancy here (ADR-073) is a shared-schema query filter plus database-per-tenant routing, which means the tenant value silently participates in every read (the named Tenant query filter), every write (the save interceptor), every tenant-scoped cache key, and the choice of physical database. Reassigning it mid-scope would therefore be catastrophic in a very quiet way: rows already tracked by the context were fetched under the old tenant, and the next save would attribute them to the new one. The exception message spells out exactly that (TenantContext.cs:45-51), and it ends with the remedy rather than just the complaint: start a new scope.
    • Walkthrough
      • The public parameterless constructor (TenantContext.cs:19) assigns TenantId = AmbientOrigin.Current?.TenantId, so the value is read once at construction and null outside a hop (every HTTP request).
      • TenantId has a private setter (TenantContext.cs:22), so the only way to write it after construction is through SetTenant.
      • IsResolved is TenantId is not null (TenantContext.cs:25). Note that "unresolved" is the normal, expected state for every background service, seeder, and design-time tool (:7-9): consumers of the value treat unresolved as "no tenancy" rather than as an error.
      • SetTenant(tenantId) (TenantContext.cs:28-52) has three branches. It null- and whitespace-guards the argument (:22); assigns and returns when nothing is set yet (:24-28); returns silently when the same value is re-asserted (:32-35); and throws InvalidOperationException on a genuine change (:37-43).
      • The idempotent middle branch is the load-bearing one, and the comment at :30-31 names the scenario: the resolution middleware and a background worker that re-asserts the tenant on the same scope must not fight each other. Same value is a no-op, different value is a hard failure.
    • Why it's built this way: the registration comment in AddInfrastructure explains why the class is always registered rather than opted into (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:344-348): everything that reads it treats an unresolved tenant as "no tenancy", so an always-on registration costs one object per scope and removes a whole class of "works until someone forgets the opt-in" bug. Only AddMultiTenancy(configuration) turns the mechanism itself on.
    • Where it's used: written by TenantResolutionMiddleware on the request path (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/TenantResolutionMiddleware.cs:71), and by the per-tenant background paths that create their own scope: database initialization (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/DatabaseInitializationExtensions.cs:212), OutboxProcessor, OutboxCleanupService, OutboxAdministration, and AuditTrailCleanupJob. It is read by DbContextFactory for routing, by TenantSaveChangesInterceptor, and by the caching decorators through TenantCacheKey. Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Context/TenantContextTests.cs, and exercised for routing by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/Tenancy/DbContextFactoryTenantTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the class is not thread-safe, and does not need to be as a scoped service on a request path, but two threads sharing one scope and racing on SetTenant with different values is not guarded against.

    ChangePreferencesCommandValidatorBase<TCommand>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Users.UseCases.ChangePreferences · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ChangePreferences/ChangePreferencesCommandValidatorBase.cs:29 · Level 6 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared FluentValidation rules for a change-preferences command: the request must be present, a supplied culture must be one the framework supports, and a supplied theme must be light or dark. A null field passes, because null is the documented "leave this preference unchanged" value (ChangePreferencesCommandValidatorBase.cs:8-13, :30-70).

    • Depends on: FluentValidation's AbstractValidator<TCommand> (:1, :30); TCommand is constrained to IUserScopedCommand<out TRequest> carrying a ChangePreferencesRequest (:31). The accepted values come from SupportedCultures.IsSupported (:51, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Globalization/SupportedCultures.cs:35) and CommonInvariants (LightTheme/DarkTheme in the message at :58, EnsurePreferredThemeIsValid at :67-69; MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Invariants/CommonInvariants.cs:16, :19, :158).

    • Concept introduced: a command validator that borrows the aggregate's own definition of valid. [Rubric §24: Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses whether bad input is rejected early, with a stable, client-readable reason. Each rule carries a fixed message and error code (User.Preferences.Required, User.PreferredCulture.Invalid, User.PreferredTheme.Invalid, :33-40), so a bad culture or theme is turned away before the handler runs instead of surfacing as an aggregate failure after a load. [Rubric §4: DDD] assesses whether invariants have one home. The validator does not restate the theme rule: BeAKnownTheme calls CommonInvariants.EnsurePreferredThemeIsValid and keeps only its IsSuccess (:64-69), and the culture rule uses the same SupportedCultures.IsSupported allowlist, so moving the rejection forward adds no second definition of what is valid (remarks at :22-27). Culture and theme are the ADR-027 and ADR-028 preferences (ADR-027, ADR-028; :9).

    • Walkthrough: three private error-code constants, a protected constructor, one private helper.

      • PreferencesRequiredCode, CultureInvalidCode, ThemeInvalidCode (:34, :37, :40).
      • Constructor (:43-62): RuleFor(c => c.Request).NotNull() (:45-46); then, only when the request is present (When, :48), a culture rule gated on Culture is not null (:50-54) and a theme rule gated on Theme is not null (:56-60). The outer When is what keeps a missing request down to the single "required" failure rather than a cascade of null dereferences.
      • BeAKnownTheme(string?) (:67-69): delegates to the domain invariant with an empty message and reads only the outcome.

    • Why it's built this way: it is a COMMAND validator rather than a request validator on purpose. The command carries its payload through IUserScopedCommand<out TRequest>, which does not opt it into the automatic CommandRequestValidator<TCommand, TRequest> bridge, so an IValidator<ChangePreferencesRequest> would never run (:16-19). It is abstract because module scanning registers validators from the app assemblies only: each app declares a one-line sealed subclass for its own command record, the same split as ChangePreferencesHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (:19-21). The remarks record that the app Identity modules carried near-identical copies before this base existed (:12-13).

    • Where it's used: ADC's MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ChangePreferences/ChangePreferencesCommandValidator.cs:10 is the one-line sealed subclass over ChangePreferencesCommand. Pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/UseCases/ChangePreferences/ChangePreferencesCommandValidatorBaseTests.cs:18 through an empty test subclass (:163): a null request yields only the required failure (:33), null fields pass (:48), every culture in SupportedCultures.All passes (:57), and two parity theories assert the validator agrees with CommonInvariants.EnsurePreferredThemeIsValid and EnsurePreferredCultureIsValid on edge inputs such as "DARK", " light", "es-MX" and "" (:102, :122).

A confirmation link opened twice, whether by a mail-client link prefetch or a user's double tap, is the most ordinary duplicate this feature sees, so the handler checks user.IsEmailConfirmed after resolving the account and returns success with no save when it is already true (:77-81, comment at :74-76).

      [Rubric §11: Security] assesses whether a rejected token leaks account state. Both rejection paths, an invalid or expired token and an account that no longer resolves, return the identical EmailConfirmationErrors.InvalidToken(HandlerName), differing only in a log reason string (:59-63, :68-72), so the response cannot be used to distinguish "bad token" from "account gone" the way ResetPasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> closes the same gap for password resets. The rejection log itself carries the reason and nothing else, no address and no account id, as the comment on its declaration records (:98-101).

      • UnitOfWork (:41): exposed for app-level extensions, same shape as the other Users bases.
      • HandlerName (:47): protected virtual, defaulting to GetType().Name.
      • HandleAsync(TCommand, CancellationToken) (:50-93): null-guard (:52); redeem the token via ValidateAndConsumeAsync(request.Email, request.Token, ...) (:56-58), failing generically on rejection (:59-63); load the resolved account through the write repository (:65-67), failing generically again if it is gone (:68-72); short-circuit on an already-confirmed address (:77-81); call user.ConfirmEmail() (:83), returning its failure untouched (:84-87); save (:89); log EmailConfirmed and return the aggregate's success result (:91-92).

    • Where it's used: subclassed by ADC (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ConfirmEmail/ConfirmEmailHandler.cs:1). Covered by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/EmailConfirmationHandlerBaseTests.cs.

It also uses the Email value object (:59), and logs through three private source-generated [LoggerMessage] methods (:157-166), hence the partial declaration (:37).
